children.title: Global-Constraint Foundations
children.top_down_role: The modeling, propagation-strength, representation, and complexity distinctions needed before individual global families.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Relation Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines globality semantically, independently of a particular propagator or decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\). A global constraint with scope \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) denotes one relation \(R\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), and an assignment \(a\) satisfies it exactly when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_n))\in R\). Its global scope is the entire ordered tuple \(X\): the relation is specified and reasoned about as one combinatorial object, even when an equivalent conjunction of lower-arity constraints exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global constraint is one relation over an entire variable tuple, treated as a single combinatorial object even if it admits a lower-arity decomposition.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\models R(X)\iff (a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_n))\in R\).

notation.meaning: Relation represented by the global constraint.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relational semantics are coherent and fit the leaf, but no cited source establishes the stronger characterization of globality as treatment of the full relation as one combinatorial object.

knowledge_statements.title: Specialized Global Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the semantic obligation and possible strength advantage of a specialized propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a relation \(R\) and current domain store \(D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)\), a specialized global propagator \(P_R\) must be contracting and solution preserving: \(P_R(D)\subseteq D\) componentwise and \(R\cap\prod_i P_R(D)_i=R\cap\prod_iD_i\). It may exploit a joint structure of \(R\), such as matching, counting, or ordering, and can therefore delete values that remain supported in every member of a chosen lower-arity decomposition considered separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Specialized propagation contracts domains without losing solutions and may infer more than separate propagation of an equivalent decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\) is a finite-domain relation.
\(P_R\) is invoked on a current domain store \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_R(D)\subseteq D\) and \(R\cap\prod_iP_R(D)_i=R\cap\prod_iD_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The propagator conditions are mathematically coherent and the principle fits the leaf, but the claimed advantage over separately propagated decompositions requires a specific source or catalog example.

children.title: Global-Constraint Recognition Cues
children.top_down_role: Structural cues indicating a catalogued global relation.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Recognition Cues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficient modeling cues for seeking a catalogued global relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model fragment is a candidate for global-constraint recognition when there exist variables \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), parameters \(\theta\), and a catalogued relation family \(\{R_\theta\}\) such that the fragment's feasible assignments projected onto \(X\) equal \(R_\theta\), while its constraints jointly express a shared invariant such as distinctness, cardinality, sequencing, packing, or connectivity. Recognition is semantic only after the projected feasible-set equality has been established; common vocabulary or overlapping scopes alone are merely cues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared combinatorial invariants suggest a global constraint, but recognition requires equality between the fragment’s projected feasible set and a catalogued relation.
assumptions_latex: The model fragment and catalog relation have finite domains.
Auxiliary variables, if present, are eliminated by projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_X(F)=R_\theta\) is required for semantic recognition.

notation.meaning: Feasible-assignment relation of the model fragment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Projected feasible-set equality is a precise semantic matching condition, but the proposed recognition framework and listed cues have no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Catalog Matching
children.top_down_role: Matching model structure to available global-constraint families.

knowledge_statements.title: Catalog Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matches a model fragment to a parameterized global-constraint signature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a fragment relation \(F\), exposed variables \(X\), and catalog families \(\{R^k_\theta\}\). For each family, unify its signature with the types, arity, and index structure of \(X\); infer admissible parameters \(\theta\); then test \(\operatorname{proj}_X(F)=R^k_\theta\), or record a separately verified one-way implication if equivalence is not established. Return every pair \((k,\theta)\) passing equality, together with the variable permutation and parameter map; return no match when every candidate fails or remains unverified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unify signatures, infer parameters, and accept a catalog entry only after its instantiated relation equals the fragment’s projected feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Catalog entries specify typed signatures and relational semantics.
Equality testing is exact or accompanied by a checkable equivalence certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M=\{(k,\theta):\operatorname{proj}_X(F)=R^k_\theta\}\).

notation.meaning: Instance of catalog family k with parameters theta.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Catalog Matching, but exact relation equality and the proposed equivalence-certificate alternative require a sourced, specified decision or certification procedure.

children.title: Global-Constraint Selection Criteria
children.top_down_role: Propagation strength, computational cost, backend support, and modeling fit.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Selection Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects among semantically equivalent global encodings and decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Among candidate encodings \(E\) with the same projected feasible relation on decision variables \(X\), select a global constraint only after comparing propagation strength, filtering cost, incremental-update cost, memory use, explanation support, and solver availability. If \(P_E\) denotes the associated propagator, semantic equivalence requires \(\operatorname{proj}_X(E)=R\); stronger filtering means \(P_{E_1}(D)\subseteq P_{E_2}(D)\) for every admissible store \(D\). No single criterion implies universal superiority because propagation gained may be offset by execution cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose among equivalent encodings by propagation strength, runtime, incrementality, memory, explanations, and implementation support; no one encoding is universally best.
assumptions_latex: All compared encodings project to the same relation \(R\) on \(X\).
Propagators are sound and evaluated on the same domain stores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E^*\in\arg\min_{E:\operatorname{proj}_X(E)=R}\operatorname{Cost}(E)\), subject to the required filtering strength.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The criteria and filtering-strength order are plausible, but the scalar cost optimization does not fully formalize the listed tradeoffs and no source supports the selection principle.

children.title: Misrecognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where superficial similarity leads to an unsuitable global constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Misrecognition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that semantic equivalence does not imply equal propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) each have domain \(\{1,2\}\). The global constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) is infeasible because three variables must take distinct values from a two-value set. Its logically equivalent pairwise decomposition \(x_1
eq x_2\), \(x_1
eq x_3\), \(x_2
eq x_3\) is arc consistent at the same store: every value of either endpoint of each binary constraint has the opposite value as support. Thus recognizing only the decomposed syntax, or treating decomposition propagation as interchangeable with global propagation, misses immediate failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three two-valued variables make AllDifferent impossible, yet every pairwise disequality remains arc consistent; equivalent syntax can therefore yield weaker propagation.
assumptions_latex: All three variables have domain \(\{1,2\}\).
Binary disequalities are propagated separately to arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) is inconsistent, while its pairwise decomposition is arc consistent.

notation.meaning: Relation requiring pairwise distinct assigned values.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The AllDifferent counterexample is mathematically correct and counterexample is the appropriate content kind, but the record supplies no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses generalized arc consistency for a finite-domain relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq U_1\times\cdots\times U_n\) constrain variables with current domains \(D_i\subseteq U_i\). The constraint is domain consistent if, for every index \(i\) and every value \(v\in D_i\), there exists a tuple \(a\in R\cap\prod_{j=1}^nD_j\) with \(a_i=v\). Such a tuple is a support for \(v\). Enforcing domain consistency deletes exactly those current values having no support in the current domains; an empty resulting domain certifies failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is domain consistent when every current value of every variable occurs in a satisfying tuple using only current-domain values.
assumptions_latex: Every universe \(U_i\) and current domain \(D_i\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\,\forall v\in D_i\,\exists a\in R\cap\prod_jD_j:\ a_i=v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a precise standard finite-domain definition of domain consistency, but no authoritative source and locator are supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Range Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the integer interval-hull version of range consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) constrain variables with finite nonempty domains \(D_i\), and let \(I_i=[\min D_i,\max D_i]\cap\mathbb Z\). The constraint is range consistent if, for every index \(i\) and every value \(v\in D_i\), there exists \(a\in R\cap\prod_{j=1}^n I_j\) satisfying \(a_i=v\). Thus the tested value must belong to its actual domain, while the remaining coordinates need only belong to the integer interval hulls of their domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every actual domain value must have a satisfying support when other variables may use any integer between their current minimum and maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).
Each \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\,\forall v\in D_i\,\exists a\in R\cap\prod_jI_j:\ a_i=v\).

notation.meaning: Integer interval hull of the current domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-hull formulation is internally precise, but range-consistency terminology varies in the literature, so this exact convention needs a specific source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounds Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses integer bounds consistency with interval-hull supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) constrain variables with finite nonempty domains \(D_i\), and set \(I_i=[\min D_i,\max D_i]\cap\mathbb Z\). The constraint is bounds consistent if, for every index \(i\) and each endpoint \(b\in\{\min D_i,\max D_i\}\), there exists a tuple \(a\in R\cap\prod_{j=1}^n I_j\) with \(a_i=b\). Only current lower and upper bounds require support, and supporting coordinates may lie in domain holes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each variable’s current minimum and maximum must extend to a satisfying integer tuple within all variables’ interval hulls.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).
Each \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\,\forall b\in\{\min D_i,\max D_i\}\,\exists a\in R\cap\prod_jI_j:\ a_i=b\).

notation.meaning: Integer interval hull of the current domain.
A current lower or upper domain bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integer interval-support variant is coherent, but bounds-consistency conventions differ over integer versus real supports and therefore require an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Entailment Detection
children.top_down_role: Detection of permanently satisfied constraint states.

knowledge_statements.title: Entailment Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a relation against the Cartesian product of a nonfailed current domain store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint relation \(R\) and a current nonfailed store \(D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)\), inclusion \(\prod_i D_i\subseteq R\) certifies entailment: every completion allowed by the store satisfies the constraint. Emptiness \(R\cap\prod_i D_i=\varnothing\) certifies disentailment: no allowed completion satisfies it. If neither predicate holds, the constraint is undecided. Under monotone domain contraction that preserves nonemptiness, an entailed constraint remains entailed; if a domain becomes empty, store failure is reported before this three-way classification is applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonfailed store, a constraint is entailed when every current completion satisfies it, disentailed when none does, and otherwise undecided; an empty domain is handled as store failure first.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\) is finite and nonempty.
Subsequent store updates only remove values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a nonfailed store, \(\prod_i D_i\subseteq R\Rightarrow\text{entailed}\), while \(R\cap\prod_i D_i=\varnothing\Rightarrow\text{disentailed}\).

children.title: Incremental Filter State
children.top_down_role: Reusable filtering state across domain changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Filter State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the invariant required of cached propagator state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_R(D)\) be the result of rebuilding a specified sound filter for relation \(R\) on store \(D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)\). For every contraction \(D'=(D'_1,\ldots,D'_n)\subseteq D\), define the removed-value event tuple by \(\Delta(D,D')=(D_1\setminus D'_1,\ldots,D_n\setminus D'_n)\). An incremental state consists of a summary \(S(D)\) and update map \(U\) such that \(S'=U(S(D),\Delta(D,D'))\) is valid for \(D'\), and the incremental filter returns exactly \(F_R(D')\). Cached supports, counters, matchings, or residual graphs are admissible summaries only while this invariant holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached propagation data are valid only if every domain contraction updates them so that filtering agrees with a complete rebuild on the new store.
assumptions_latex: Domain evolution is monotone: \(D'_i\subseteq D_i\) for every \(i\).
\(F_R\) is a specified reference rebuild filter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{IncFilter}(D',U(S(D),\Delta(D,D')))=F_R(D')\).

notation.meaning: Cached filter summary valid for store D.
Specified reference filter obtained by rebuilding.
Tuple of values removed from each domain during the contraction.

children.title: Event-Driven Refiltering
children.top_down_role: Filtering activation under variable-domain events.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Driven Refiltering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines queue-based propagation under complete event subscriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite-domain store \(D\), deterministic propagators \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\), and complete subscriptions that map each domain-change event to every active propagator whose output may change because of that event. Initialize a queue with all active propagators. Repeatedly remove \(P_k\), replace \(D\) by \(P_k(D)\), report failure if a domain becomes empty, and enqueue every subscribed active propagator for each newly generated event. Stop when the queue is empty and return the resulting store. A propagator certified entailed may be deactivated. If every propagator is contracting and the queue eventually processes every enqueued propagator, finite domains imply termination; at normal termination the returned store is a common fixed point of all active propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run every propagator initially and wake every active propagator affected by later domain events. With finite domains, contracting deterministic propagators, complete subscriptions, and fair queue processing, normal termination returns a common propagation fixed point.
assumptions_latex: Every domain is finite.
Each \(P_k\) is a deterministic, contracting, solution-preserving store map.
Subscriptions enqueue every active propagator whose output may change after an event.
Every enqueued propagator is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At normal termination, \(D^*\subseteq D\) and \(P_k(D^*)=D^*\) for every active propagator \(P_k\).

notation.meaning: Store returned when the event queue becomes empty.

children.title: Incremental-State Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Stale state, excessive maintenance cost, and weak event granularity.

assumptions_latex: Variable domains only shrink during propagation.
The incremental filter is intended to reproduce a specified from-scratch filter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An incremental state is sound only while its update invariant is preserved; otherwise missed deletion events can make its output differ from fresh filtering.

notation.meaning: cached incremental state after processing D

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers soundness failure caused by stale state, omitted events, or invalid restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a deterministic filtering operator and let an incremental implementation return \(F_S(D)\) from domains \(D\) and cached state \(S\). Its state invariant requires \(F_S(D)=F(D)\) after every processed domain deletion. If some deletion changing a support recorded in \(S\) is neither reported nor reconstructed, there can be a reachable state \(D'\subseteq D\) for which \(F_S(D')\ne F(D')\). The stale implementation may retain an unsupported value or fail to detect inconsistency. Backtracking likewise crosses the boundary unless \(S\) is restored, trailed, or recomputed consistently with the restored domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental filtering can become unsound when a relevant deletion or restoration is absent from the cached state, causing disagreement with fresh filtering.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental-State Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and content kind are plausible, but the stale-support and backtracking claims require a specific incremental-propagation source.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Equivalence of Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic equivalence concerns accepted assignments, independently of propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be the assignment space of the original variables \(X\). For \(i\in\{1,2\}\), let \(\mathcal Y_i\) be the assignment space of auxiliary variables \(Y_i\), and let \(\Delta_i(X,Y_i)\) be a conjunction of constraints. Define \[R_i=\{x\in\mathcal X:\exists y_i\in\mathcal Y_i\;\Delta_i(x,y_i)\}.\] The decompositions are semantically equivalent when \(R_1=R_2\), equivalently when, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\bigl(\exists y_1\in\mathcal Y_1\;\Delta_1(x,y_1)\bigr)\Longleftrightarrow\bigl(\exists y_2\in\mathcal Y_2\;\Delta_2(x,y_2)\bigr).\] This permits different auxiliary spaces and does not imply equal pruning under a local propagation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two decompositions are semantically equivalent when existentially eliminating their explicitly declared auxiliary-variable spaces yields exactly the same assignments to the original variables.
assumptions_latex: The assignment spaces \(\mathcal X\), \(\mathcal Y_1\), and \(\mathcal Y_2\) are declared.
All auxiliary variables are existentially quantified over their declared assignment spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decompositions are semantically equivalent exactly when their projections onto \(\mathcal X\) coincide.

notation.meaning: original variables with assignment space \(\mathcal X\)
auxiliary variables with assignment space \(\mathcal Y_i\)
decomposition \(i\) as a conjunction of constraints
relation on original assignments induced by decomposition \(i\)

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Propagation Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Decompositions matching the filtering strength of a global representation.

assumptions_latex: Both propagators are applied to the same domain states on the original variables.
Auxiliary domains, if present, are initialized canonically and propagation reaches a common fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation equivalence holds exactly when both propagation systems induce the same original-variable domain closure on every input state.

notation.meaning: admissible domain states of the original variables
fixpoint closure induced by propagator or decomposition i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixpoint equivalence is measured after projecting away auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be monotone, contracting propagation systems over finite domains, possibly using different auxiliary variables. For each original-variable domain state \(D\in\mathcal D\), initialize auxiliaries by the prescribed canonical rule and iterate each system to a fixpoint. The systems are propagation equivalent on \(\mathcal D\) when \[\pi_X(P_1^*(D))=\pi_X(P_2^*(D))\qquad\text{for every }D\in\mathcal D.\] Equality includes simultaneous failure, represented by an empty domain. Agreement only on complete assignments establishes semantic equivalence, not propagation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two propagation systems are equivalent when every initial domain state produces identical fixpoint domains on the original variables, including identical failure detection.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixpoint definition fits the container and is internally coherent, but no source supports the chosen auxiliary-initialization and projected-closure formulation.

children.title: Propagation Loss
children.top_down_role: Domain pruning unavailable after decomposition.

assumptions_latex: The compared propagation systems are sound for the same constraint relation.
Both are run to fixpoint from the same original-variable domain state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A propagation loss is witnessed by a value removed by one fixpoint closure but retained by the other.

notation.meaning: strong and weak projected fixpoint closures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss is relative to a fixed propagation regime, schedule-to-fixpoint convention, and input class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_s^*\) and \(P_w^*\) denote projected fixpoint closures, ordered by componentwise domain inclusion, with smaller domains meaning stronger pruning. The weak system has no greater strength than the strong system when \(P_s^*(D)\preceq P_w^*(D)\) for every admissible \(D\). It incurs propagation loss when the inclusion is strict for some \(D\): there exist an original variable \(x\) and value \(a\) such that \[a\notin P_s^*(D)(x)\quad\text{and}\quad a\in P_w^*(D)(x).\] The witness may instead be failure detected only by \(P_s^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation loss occurs when one sound fixpoint system retains a value, or misses failure, that a stronger system eliminates on the same domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The witness formulation is plausible, but the relative-strength convention and treatment of failure need a cited propagation-strength source.

children.title: Strength-Separation Cases
children.top_down_role: Instance families exposing propagation differences.

assumptions_latex: Both systems are sound for the same semantic relation.
The comparison uses identical input states and projected fixpoint semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict strength separation is certified by universal dominance together with one explicit strict witness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the certificate form for strict separation rather than a particular global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To establish that propagation system \(A\) is strictly stronger than \(B\) on a class \(\mathcal D\), it suffices to establish \[P_A^*(D)\preceq P_B^*(D)\qquad\text{for all }D\in\mathcal D\] and provide one \(D_0\in\mathcal D\) for which equality fails. A checkable strictness witness is a variable-value pair \((x,a)\) satisfying \(a\notin P_A^*(D_0)(x)\) and \(a\in P_B^*(D_0)(x)\), or a state where \(A\) detects failure and \(B\) does not. Reversing witnesses on different states shows incomparability rather than dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation requires dominance on all tested states and one state where the stronger system deletes more or alone detects failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Strength-Separation Cases

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the plain statement says dominance on all tested states whereas the mathematical statement requires all states in the declared class. A source and aligned wording are required.

children.title: Redundant Views
children.top_down_role: Additional representations retained for complementary propagation.

assumptions_latex: Each added view is semantically implied by the base model together with its channeling constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A redundant view preserves projected solutions but may strengthen propagation when its propagators communicate through channeling constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy is semantic; usefulness depends on the induced fixpoint propagation.

source_refs.locator: 8.1 Implicit equalities and redundant constraints p. 99
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(X)\) be a base constraint model. A view \(V(Y)\), connected by channeling constraints \(H(X,Y)\), is redundant when \[\pi_X\{(x,y):M(x)\land H(x,y)\land V(y)\}=\{x:M(x)\}.\] Thus adding the view neither creates nor removes complete solutions on \(X\). Nevertheless, propagating \(M\), \(H\), and \(V\) jointly may produce a strictly smaller domain fixpoint than propagating \(M\) alone, because deductions expressible in the \(Y\)-representation can return through \(H\). Semantic redundancy therefore does not imply propagation redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant view leaves original solutions unchanged but can improve pruning by expressing deductions in another representation and returning them through channeling.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Views

source_witnesses.locator: 8.1 Implicit equalities and redundant constraints p. 99
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the cited polyhedral section on redundant constraints does not specifically support channelled redundant views or the claimed propagation strengthening.

children.title: Channeling Views
children.top_down_role: Linked representations exposing alternative variable perspectives.

assumptions_latex: The two views represent the same underlying object.
Each complete assignment in either view has at least one compatible assignment in the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Channeling constraints define the compatibility relation through which assignments and domain reductions are transferred between views.

notation.meaning: relations represented in the two views

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers exact semantic channeling; propagation completeness is a separate property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_X\) and \(R_Y\) be two representations of one solution object. A channeling relation \(H(X,Y)\) is exact when \[x\in R_X\Longleftrightarrow \exists y\in R_Y\;H(x,y),\qquad y\in R_Y\Longleftrightarrow \exists x\in R_X\;H(x,y).\] The combined model is \(R_X(X)\land H(X,Y)\land R_Y(Y)\). Propagation of \(H\) transfers incompatible assignments or values between the views. Exactness guarantees agreement of complete solutions under projection, but local propagation on \(H\) need not transfer every deduction obtainable in either representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact channeling relates two representations so their complete solutions project consistently, while its propagator transfers domain reductions between them.
knowledge_statements.title: Channeling Views

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and exact projection conditions are plausible, but the semantic and propagation roles of channeling constraints require a specific source.

children.title: Cross-View Propagation
children.top_down_role: Propagation transferred through representation links.

assumptions_latex: All component propagators are monotone, contracting, and sound.
Domains are finite, and every effective reduction reschedules all affected propagators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fair cross-view iteration terminates at the greatest common fixpoint below the initial domain state.

notation.meaning: finite family of view and channel propagators
propagator selected from the work queue

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worklist iteration across multiple views and their channeling propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite joint domain state \(D_0\) and propagators \(\mathcal P\) for every view and channel. Initialize \(D\leftarrow D_0\) and enqueue every \(p\in\mathcal P\). Repeatedly remove a queued \(p\), compute \(D'\leftarrow p(D)\), and stop with failure if \(D'\) contains an empty domain. If \(D'\ne D\), set \(D\leftarrow D'\) and enqueue every propagator whose watched variables changed; otherwise continue. When the queue is empty, output \(D\). Under fair scheduling, the output is the greatest common fixpoint of \(\mathcal P\) contained in \(D_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-view propagation repeatedly runs view and channel propagators after relevant domain changes until failure or a common fixpoint is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-View Propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits cross-view propagation, but the greatest-common-fixpoint conclusion is a theorem-level guarantee requiring a precise chaotic-iteration or constraint-propagation citation.

children.title: View-Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Memory, wake-up, and propagation costs from additional views.

assumptions_latex: Every maintained view and channel has explicitly represented state.
Propagation uses a work queue and finite shrinking domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Additional views are beneficial only when pruning or search savings exceed their representation, update, and scheduling overhead.

notation.meaning: number of stored view and channel objects

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized overhead boundary; it does not assert a universal runtime improvement from added views.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a multi-view system stores \(S\) view, channel, and propagator-state objects. If at most \(E\) effective domain events occur along a propagation episode and processing all propagators awakened by one event costs at most \(U\), then its bookkeeping space is \(O(S)\) plus stored domains, and its event-processing time is \(O(EU)\), excluding search-tree changes. Because a redundant view can leave the fixpoint unchanged, it may add this cost without reducing search. Its use crosses the practical overhead boundary when the saved propagation or search work is no larger than its added construction, maintenance, and scheduling work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A view may cost linear stored state and event-triggered update work without improving pruning; it pays only when those costs are offset elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.title: View-Overhead Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Counting state objects does not imply \(O(S)\) space unless their representation sizes are bounded. The parameterized time and practical break-even claims also require an explicit cost model and source.

assumptions_latex: The backend encoding preserves the original model under projection.
Auxiliary variables are existentially quantified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Backend-specific decomposition requires semantic preservation, while propagation strength and computational cost remain backend-dependent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic correctness from backend-dependent propagation and encoding cost.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a target backend \(B\), a decomposition \(\Delta_B(X,Y_B)\) of a global constraint \(C(X)\) is semantically correct when \[C(x)\Longleftrightarrow \exists y_B\;\Delta_B(x,y_B)\qquad\text{for every assignment }x.\] The primitive constraints, auxiliary variables, and redundant structure may depend on \(B\). Semantic correctness alone does not ensure that backend inference reaches the same domain closure as a native propagator or another encoding. Consequently, backend selection must separately compare projected propagation strength, encoding size, update cost, and the backend's available inference regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A backend-specific encoding must preserve projected solutions, but its pruning strength, size, and update cost depend on the backend's inference mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.title: Backend-Specific Decomposition

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the topic, but a general MINLP decomposition chapter does not specifically support projected correctness and propagation comparisons for constraint-programming backends.

children.title: Bipartite-Matching Filters
children.top_down_role: Filtering architectures based on matching structure.

assumptions_latex: Variables have finite domains.
Filtering targets domain consistency for an all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matching-based filtering fails exactly without a covering matching and deletes precisely edges belonging to no covering matching.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-consistency characterization for finite-domain all-different constraints.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X\) with domains over values \(V\), construct the bipartite graph \(G_D=(X\cup V,E)\), where \((x,a)\in E\) exactly when \(a\in D(x)\). Compute a matching \(M\) covering every vertex of \(X\); if none exists, report failure. Otherwise retain an edge \((x,a)\) exactly when it belongs to at least one matching covering \(X\), and delete \(a\) from \(D(x)\) for every other edge. Alternating-path and alternating-cycle structure relative to \(M\) can identify all retained edges without recomputing a matching for each value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all-different, build the variable-value graph, fail without a matching covering all variables, and remove edges absent from every such matching.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite-Matching Filters

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically plausible for finite-domain all-different, but the cited matching and matching-polytope sections do not establish the exact domain-consistency filtering rule or its alternating-path/cycle implementation.

children.title: Network-Flow Filters
children.top_down_role: Filtering architectures based on capacitated flow structure.

assumptions_latex: The constraint's solutions correspond exactly to integral feasible flows in the constructed network.
Arc bounds and node balances are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flow-based filtering rejects infeasible networks and removes values whose corresponding arcs occur in no feasible integral flow.

notation.meaning: lower and upper capacity of arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic integral-flow filtering template; the value-to-arc encoding is constraint-specific.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_refs.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode the current domains as a directed network \(N=(V,A)\) with integral bounds \(\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\) and prescribed node balances, so that feasible integral flows project exactly to satisfying assignments. Find one feasible flow \(f\); if none exists, report failure. For each value represented by an arc or designated arc set, test whether the residual network admits a balance-preserving adjustment that forces that representation while respecting all bounds. Delete the value when no such adjustment exists. Output the remaining domains when every retained value extends to a feasible integral flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode solutions as integral flows, fail if none exists, and remove each value that cannot be forced within any feasible residual-flow adjustment.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Filters

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

children.title: Matching–Flow Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representational links between matching-based and flow-based reasoning.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) has finite domains \(D_i\subseteq V\).
All network capacities are integral and equal to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a matching saturating \(X\) if and only if \(N\) has an \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(n\).

notation.meaning: Edge joining variable i to an allowed value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-capacity correspondence underlying matching-based global-constraint filters.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct \(N\) with arcs \((s,x_i)\), \((x_i,v)\) for every \((x_i,v)\in E\), and \((v,t)\), all of capacity one. Every matching \(M\) saturating \(X\) defines an integral flow of value \(n\) by sending one unit along \(s,x_i,v,t\) whenever \((x_i,v)\in M\). Conversely, the variable-to-value arcs carrying one unit in any integral flow of value \(n\) form a matching saturating \(X\). Hence \((x_i,v)\) is supported by the all-different relation exactly when some value-\(n\) flow uses arc \((x_i,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-saturating bipartite matching is exactly an integral unit-capacity flow of full value; supported assignments are precisely edges used by some full flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Flow Correspondence

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Incremental Graph Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Reuse of graph certificates across domain changes.

assumptions_latex: A matching \(M\) saturating all variables is available before an edge deletion.
Only domain-edge deletions occur between maintenance steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update either returns a matching saturating every variable or certifies that no such matching remains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-edge decremental maintenance of a variable-saturating matching.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete \(e\) from \(E\). If \(e\notin M\), retain \(M\). If \(e\in M\), set \(M\leftarrow M\setminus\{e\}\) and search the alternating graph for a path beginning at the now-unmatched variable \(x_i\) and ending at an unmatched value. When such a path \(P\) exists, replace \(M\) by the symmetric difference \(M\mathbin{\triangle}E(P)\). When none exists, report failure. Subsequent support tests may reuse the repaired matching and the updated alternating or residual graph rather than reconstructing them from the original domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unmatched-edge deletion changes nothing; deleting a matched edge triggers one augmenting-path repair, whose failure certifies that no variable-saturating matching remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Graph Maintenance

children.title: Automaton-Based Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering through layered state-transition representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Automaton-Based Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-consistency filtering for a finite-automaton sequence constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(R_0=\{q_0\}\) and, for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute \(R_i=\{q'\in Q\mid q\in R_{i-1},\ a\in D_i,\ (q,a,q')\in\delta\}\). Initialize \(B_n=F\) and, for \(i=n,\ldots,1\), compute \(B_{i-1}=\{q\in Q\mid a\in D_i,\ q'\in B_i,\ (q,a,q')\in\delta\}\). Retain \(a\in D_i\) exactly when there are \(q\in R_{i-1}\) and \(q'\in B_i\) such that \((q,a,q')\in\delta\). The retained values are precisely those occurring on accepting paths compatible with the current domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward reachable-state sets retain exactly the domain values that label transitions on accepting paths compatible with all current domains.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are variables with finite domains \(D_i\subseteq\Sigma\).
\(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)\) is a finite automaton with transition relation \(\delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), and accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(a\in D_i\), the value \(a\) is retained if and only if it labels the layer-\(i\) transition of an accepting path compatible with all current domains.

notation.meaning: States reachable after the first i variables
States from which an accepting suffix of length n-i exists

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering through staged state aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete filtering on an explicit finite layered dynamic-program representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(F_0=\{s_0\}\) and, for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute \(F_i=\{s'\in S_i\mid s\in F_{i-1},\ a\in D_i,\ (s,a,s')\in\Gamma_i\}\). Set \(C_n=T\) and, for \(i=n,\ldots,1\), compute \(C_{i-1}=\{s\in S_{i-1}\mid a\in D_i,\ s'\in C_i,\ (s,a,s')\in\Gamma_i\}\). Retain \(a\in D_i\) exactly when some \((s,a,s')\in\Gamma_i\) has \(s\in F_{i-1}\) and \(s'\in C_i\). Report inconsistency exactly when \(F_n\cap T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward passes through a finite layered dynamic program retain precisely the values belonging to feasible initial-to-accepting paths.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
The constraint has finite state layers \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\), initial state \(s_0\in S_0\), accepting set \(T\subseteq S_n\), and transition relations \(\Gamma_i\subseteq S_{i-1}\times D_i\times S_i\).
Feasible assignments are exactly the label sequences of paths from \(s_0\) to \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the retained values in \(D_i\) are exactly those occurring at layer \(i\) on a feasible dynamic-program path.

notation.meaning: States at layer i that can reach acceptance

children.title: State-Space Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Links between automaton states and dynamic-programming states.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path semantics for exact layered state-machine and dynamic-program representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) have state layers \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\) and labeled arc sets \(A_i\subseteq S_{i-1}\times D_i\times S_i\). An assignment \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) belongs to the represented relation \(R\) if and only if \(H\) has a path from \(s_0\) to a state in \(T\) whose layer-\(i\) arc is labeled \(a_i\) for every \(i\). Consequently, \(a\in D_i\) has support in \(R\) under the current domains if and only if a layer-\(i\) arc labeled \(a\) lies on such an accepting path whose other labels also belong to their current domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assignments in the represented relation correspond exactly to accepting labeled paths, and a value is supported exactly when its layer arc belongs to a domain-compatible accepting path.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite current domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
\(H\) is a finite layered directed graph with state layers \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\), initial state \(s_0\in S_0\), accepting set \(T\subseteq S_n\), and layer-\(i\) arcs labeled by values in \(D_i\).
\(H\) is an exact representation of a relation \(R\) on the variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible assignments correspond exactly to \(s_0\)-to-\(T\) labeled paths, and value supports correspond exactly to layer arcs on domain-compatible \(s_0\)-to-\(T\) paths.

notation.meaning: Accepting states in the final layer
Relation represented by the labeled paths

children.title: State-Representation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Size, sparsity, reuse, and propagation considerations.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Representation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision-size tradeoff induced by merging states in layered representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Create an abstract arc \((\pi_{i-1}(s),a,\pi_i(s'))\) for every exact arc \((s,a,s')\). Every exact accepting path maps to an abstract accepting path, so filtering on the abstract graph cannot delete a value supported in the exact graph. The abstraction gives the same value filtering as the exact graph if and only if, for every layer \(i\) and label \(a\), an abstract accepting path using label \(a\) at layer \(i\) exists exactly when an exact accepting path using that label at that layer exists. Requiring every abstract accepting path to have a label-preserving exact lift is a sufficient, but not necessary, condition for this equality. Coarser merging may reduce representation size while retaining unsupported values introduced by spurious abstract paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State merging is a sound relaxation that may retain unsupported values; filtering remains exact precisely when the abstract and exact graphs support the same label at every layer.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite exact layered state representation with layers \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\).
For each \(i\), \(\pi_i:S_i\to\bar S_i\) is a layerwise state-merging map.
The abstract initial and accepting states are the images of the exact initial and accepting states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: State merging is sound for value filtering, and it is filtering-exact if and only if the exact and abstract representations have the same supported layer-label pairs.

assumptions_latex: A finite relation \(R\subseteq D_1^0\times\cdots\times D_n^0\) is stored extensionally.
Current domains satisfy \(D_i\subseteq D_i^0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(a\in D_i\) if and only if some currently valid tuple \(t\in R\) satisfies \(t_i=a\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized arc consistency for an extensionally represented relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the active tuples as \(R_D\). For every literal \((i,a)\), maintain the active members of \(L_{i,a}\). Delete \(a\) from \(D_i\) whenever \(L_{i,a}\cap R_D=\varnothing\). Whenever a value is deleted, deactivate every tuple containing that value and update the support lists of all literals occurring in those tuples. Continue until no value is deleted. If some domain becomes empty, return inconsistency; otherwise return the fixed-point domains, which are generalized-arc-consistent for \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain valid allowed tuples and delete each value whose support list becomes empty, updating affected tuples until generalized arc consistency is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Tuple-Support Architectures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tuple-support algorithm is mathematically standard and fits the architecture leaf, but the cited general CP section does not specifically substantiate generalized-arc-consistency maintenance for extensional relations.

assumptions_latex: Task \(i\) has duration \(p_i>0\), demand \(r_i>0\), and start domain \([\operatorname{est}_i,\operatorname{lst}_i]\).
A renewable resource has capacity \(C\), and \(\operatorname{lct}_i=\operatorname{lst}_i+p_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible schedule satisfies \(\sum_i r_i e_i(a,b)\le C(b-a)\) for every interval \([a,b)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum processing of task i forced into the interval

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic envelope condition for a nonpreemptive cumulative resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each interval \([a,b)\) with \(a<b\), task \(i\) must execute within that interval for at least \(e_i(a,b)=\max\{0,\min\{b-a,p_i,\operatorname{est}_i+p_i-a,b-\operatorname{lst}_i\}\}\) time units. Its forced energy is therefore \(r_i e_i(a,b)\). The resource envelope condition is \(\sum_i r_i e_i(a,b)\le C(b-a)\). Violation for any interval certifies infeasibility. A filtering architecture may additionally tighten start bounds or delete values whose hypothetical inclusion makes this inequality fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every interval must have enough capacity for the minimum task energy forced into it; an overloaded interval certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Envelope Architectures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The energetic necessary condition and forced-overlap formula are plausible for nonpreemptive cumulative scheduling, but the cited general CP locator is too indirect to validate this specialized formula and its scheduling assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Complete-Filtering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle characterization of polynomial complete domain filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complete domain filtering can be performed with at most \(M\) fixed-literal support queries and \(O(M)\) additional bookkeeping. If each support query takes time \(T(N)\), the resulting running time is \(O(MT(N)+M)\). Conversely, a complete-filtering procedure decides whether a designated literal has support by determining whether that literal is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete filtering and designated-value support testing are polynomial-time equivalent up to one support query per current domain literal and linear bookkeeping.
assumptions_latex: The represented instance has encoded size \(N\).
The current domains contain \(M=\sum_i|D_i|\) variable-value pairs, with \(M\) polynomially bounded in \(N\).
Existence of a satisfying completion for any fixed variable-value pair is decidable in time \(T(N)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete domain filtering is computable in \(O(MT(N)+M)\) time and is polynomial-time computable whenever \(T(N)\) is polynomially bounded.

notation.meaning: Running time of one fixed-literal support query

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Complete-Filtering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness boundary induced by NP-complete support existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any represented constraint family in which designated-literal support is NP-complete, an algorithm enforcing complete filtering also decides designated-literal support by whether it retains that literal. Complete filtering for the family is therefore NP-hard. This hardness applies to complete filtering and does not preclude polynomial-time sound propagation that retains some unsupported values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NP-complete designated-value support makes complete filtering NP-hard, although weaker sound propagation may remain polynomial.
assumptions_latex: For the represented constraint family, deciding whether a designated variable-value pair has a satisfying completion is NP-complete.
Complete filtering must remove every unsupported value and retain every supported value.
Running time is measured in the encoded instance size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete filtering for the family is NP-hard and has no polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Filtering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-parameter tractability inherited from support testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complete filtering can be implemented with one parameterized support query per current variable-value pair and \(O(M)\) additional bookkeeping. If one query takes time \(f(k)N^c\), the total running time is \(O(Mf(k)N^c+M)\). Under a polynomial bound on \(M\), this is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT support test yields an FPT complete filter when the represented number of domain literals is polynomially bounded in the input size.
assumptions_latex: Instances have encoded size \(N\), parameter \(k\), and \(M=\sum_i|D_i|\) current variable-value pairs.
There is a constant \(d\), independent of \(k\), such that \(M=O(N^d)\).
A fixed-literal support query is decidable in time \(f(k)N^c\), where \(f\) is computable and \(c\) is independent of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete filtering is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to \(k\), with running time \(O(Mf(k)N^c+M)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit versus succinct encoding of a finite Boolean relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicit list of allowed Boolean tuples with \(L\) stored literal occurrences, all supported variable-value pairs can be identified in \(O(L+n)\) time. For a relation \(R=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n\mid C(x)=1\}\) represented by a Boolean circuit \(C\), deciding support for a designated value is NP-complete, and complete filtering is NP-hard. Thus the same filtering specification can be polynomial for an extensional encoding and intractable for a succinct circuit encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit Boolean tuples permit linear-time support scanning in the representation size, while a succinct circuit encoding makes value support and complete filtering intractable unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The relation is over \(n\) Boolean variables.
In the explicit representation, \(L\) is the total number of stored tuple entries.
In the succinct representation, a Boolean circuit \(C\) decides membership in the relation.
Complexity is measured in the length of the selected encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete filtering is computable in \(O(L+n)\) time for an explicit tuple list but is NP-hard for a Boolean-circuit representation unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Boolean circuit encoding membership in the relation

children.title: Hall Sets
children.top_down_role: Variable subsets paired with restricted value neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Hall Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the equality form of a Hall-tight variable set for finite-domain AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite set of variables, let \(V\) be a finite set of values, and let each \(x\in X\) have a domain \(D(x)\subseteq V\). For each nonempty set \(S\subseteq X\), define \(N(S)=\bigcup_{x\in S}D(x)\). The set \(S\) is a Hall set, also called a Hall-tight set, exactly when \(|N(S)|=|S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hall set is a nonempty variable subset having exactly as many collectively available values as variables.
assumptions_latex: The variable set \(X\) and value set \(V\) are finite.
Each variable \(x\in X\) has a domain \(D(x)\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonempty set \(S\subseteq X\) is a Hall set exactly when \(|N(S)|=|S|\).

notation.meaning: Values available to at least one variable in S.

children.title: Hall Deficiency Certificates
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood shortages certifying infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Hall Deficiency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bipartite Hall-violation certificate for infeasibility of AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite set of variables, let each domain satisfy \(D(x)\subseteq V\), and define \(N(S)=\bigcup_{x\in S}D(x)\) and \(\delta(S)=|S|-|N(S)|\) for every \(S\subseteq X\). A Hall deficiency certificate is a set \(S\subseteq X\) satisfying \(\delta(S)>0\), equivalently \(|N(S)|<|S|\). The existence of such a certificate implies that the AllDifferent constraint on \(X\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable subset with fewer available values than variables is a Hall deficiency certificate and implies that the AllDifferent constraint is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The variable set \(X\), value set \(V\), and all domains \(D(x)\subseteq V\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If some \(S\subseteq X\) satisfies \(|N(S)|<|S|\), then the AllDifferent constraint is infeasible.

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of values available to variables in S.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65

children.title: Minimal Deficient Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion-minimal structures exposing Hall deficiency.

assumptions_latex: The variable set \(X\) and all domains \(D(x)\subseteq V\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimal deficiency means \(|N(S)|<|S|\) while \(|N(T)|\ge |T|\) for every proper subset \(T\subsetneq S\).

notation.meaning: Values adjacent to variables in S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-minimal, rather than minimum-cardinality, deficient variable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N(S)=\bigcup_{x\in S}D(x)\) for \(S\subseteq X\). A set \(S\subseteq X\) is deficient when \(|N(S)|<|S|\). It is a minimal deficient set when it is deficient and no proper subset is deficient; equivalently, \(|N(S)|<|S|\) and \(|N(T)|\ge |T|\) for every \(T\subsetneq S\). Thus \(S\) is an inclusion-minimal Hall deficiency certificate, although another minimal deficient set may have smaller cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal deficient set violates Hall's inequality, while each of its proper subsets satisfies the inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Deficient Sets

assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite integer domain \(D(x)\subseteq\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval \([a,b]\) is Hall when \(|H[a,b]|=b-a+1\).

notation.meaning: Variables whose entire current domains lie in the integer interval.
Integer interval from a through b.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-domain Hall intervals used in interval-based AllDifferent propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(a\le b\), write \([a,b]=\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}\) and define \(H[a,b]=\{x\in X:D(x)\subseteq[a,b]\}\). The interval \([a,b]\) is a Hall interval when \(|H[a,b]|=b-a+1\). In any injective assignment, the variables in \(H[a,b]\) must occupy every value of \([a,b]\); consequently, values in \([a,b]\) are unavailable to every variable in \(X\setminus H[a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hall interval contains the entire domains of exactly as many variables as the interval contains integer values.
knowledge_statements.title: Hall Intervals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is plausible, but Hall-interval terminology and the stated pruning consequence require a direct constraint-programming source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Domain Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal-cardinality variable and value sets with all domains contained in the common universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(V\) be finite sets with \(|X|=|V|=n\), and let \(D(x)\subseteq V\) for every \(x\in X\). An assignment \(f:X\to V\) satisfies AllDifferent exactly when \(f(x)\in D(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(f\) is injective. Under these equal-cardinality assumptions, every satisfying assignment is a bijection from \(X\) to \(V\), so it uses every value in \(V\) exactly once and is a domain-feasible permutation of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With equally many variables and possible values, every AllDifferent solution uses every value exactly once and is a domain-feasible permutation.
assumptions_latex: The finite sets \(X\) and \(V\) satisfy \(|X|=|V|=n\).
Every domain satisfies \(D(x)\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every satisfying assignment is a bijection \(f:X\to V\), hence a domain-feasible permutation of \(V\).

notation.meaning: Assignment value chosen for variable x.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65

knowledge_statements.title: Variable–Value Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bipartite representation of finite-domain AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite set of variables, let \(V\) be a finite set of values, and let \(D(x)\subseteq V\) for every \(x\in X\). Define the bipartite variable–value graph \(G=(X\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\) with \(E=\{(x,v)\in X\times V:v\in D(x)\}\). Domain-respecting injective assignments \(f:X\to V\) correspond bijectively to matchings in \(G\) that cover every vertex of \(X\), via \(f\mapsto\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent each permitted variable-value pair by an edge; AllDifferent solutions correspond bijectively to matchings that cover every variable vertex.
assumptions_latex: The variable set \(X\), value set \(V\), and domains \(D(x)\subseteq V\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Domain-respecting injective assignments correspond bijectively to matchings in \(G\) that cover \(X\).

source_refs.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Matching Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching-size certificate for feasibility or infeasibility of finite-domain AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(X\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\) be the finite variable–value graph and let \(M\) be a maximum-cardinality matching in \(G\). The AllDifferent constraint is feasible if and only if \(|M|=|X|\), equivalently if and only if \(M\) covers every variable vertex. Thus a maximum matching of size \(|X|\) certifies feasibility, while a certified maximum matching with \(|M|<|X|\) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified maximum matching establishes feasibility exactly when it covers every variable; a smaller certified maximum matching establishes infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The finite variable–value graph is \(G=(X\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\).
The matching \(M\) has certified maximum cardinality in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: AllDifferent is feasible if and only if \(|M|=|X|\).

source_refs.locator: Section 4.2, Bipartite Maximum Cardinality Matching, p. 65
