children.title: Alternating-Path Support
children.top_down_role: Matching-edge support exposed through alternating paths.

assumptions_latex: A matching \(M\) covers every variable vertex of the finite bipartite graph \(G\).
The path is simple, begins at an \(M\)-free value, and alternates between edges outside and inside \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every edge on an even-length such path belongs to some matching covering \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support obtained by flipping an even alternating path between value vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) cover \(X\), and let \(P\) be an even-length \(M\)-alternating path whose endpoints are value vertices and whose first edge is outside \(M\), with its initial value endpoint unmatched by \(M\). Flipping membership along the path gives \(M'=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(P)\). The matching \(M'\) still covers every variable, its terminal value becomes free, and every nonmatching edge of \(P\) belongs to \(M'\). Hence each edge of \(P\), whether retained in \(M\) or introduced in \(M'\), has AllDifferent support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge on an appropriate alternating path from a free value is supported because flipping that path preserves coverage of all variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Path Support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alternating-path claim depends on precise orientation, parity, and endpoint conventions. The conclusion's phrase “every edge on an even-length such path” is also less precise than the statement's distinction between edges retained in the reference matching and introduced after flipping. A direct Régin-style support characterization with a specific theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Alternating-Cycle Support
children.top_down_role: Matching-edge support exposed through alternating cycles.

assumptions_latex: A matching \(M\) covers every variable vertex of the finite bipartite graph \(G\).
The cycle \(C\) alternates between edges in \(M\) and edges outside \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every edge of \(C\) belongs to some matching covering \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support obtained by flipping an alternating cycle relative to a covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching covering \(X\), and let \(C\) be an even cycle whose edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\). Then \(M'=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(C)\) is also a matching covering \(X\): every vertex of \(C\) exchanges one matched incident edge for the other. Every edge of \(C\setminus M\) belongs to \(M'\), while every edge of \(C\cap M\) belongs to \(M\). Consequently every edge on the alternating cycle occurs in a satisfying AllDifferent matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every edge on an alternating cycle is supported, since flipping the cycle produces another matching that still covers all variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Cycle Support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alternating-cycle support fact is mathematically plausible, but the generic matching citation does not specifically locate the AllDifferent edge-support characterization. A direct source is required before relying on this formulation in the Régin container.

children.title: Unsupported-Edge Separation
children.top_down_role: Edges excluded from feasible matching support.

assumptions_latex: A matching \(M\) covers every variable vertex of the finite variable-value graph.
Support means membership in at least one matching that covers all variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An edge is unsupported exactly when it is in none of \(M\), an \(M\)-alternating cycle, or an eligible \(M\)-alternating path from a free value.

notation.meaning: Edges belonging to at least one variable-covering matching.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete edge-support separation relative to one variable-covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a matching \(M\) covering \(X\). The supported edge set \(E_{\mathrm{sup}}\) consists exactly of the edges in \(M\), the edges lying on an \(M\)-alternating cycle, and the edges lying on an even \(M\)-alternating path that begins at an \(M\)-free value with a nonmatching edge. Therefore any edge \(e\in E\setminus E_{\mathrm{sup}}\) belongs to no matching covering \(X\). Deleting every such edge preserves all solutions and establishes domain consistency for the AllDifferent constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edges outside the reference matching, its alternating cycles, and eligible alternating paths occur in no solution and may be removed.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported-Edge Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a complete if-and-only-if support separation and domain-consistency claim, not merely a sufficient alternating-path or cycle observation. Its exact reachability, parity, and orientation conventions require a direct authoritative Régin source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: A current matching \(M\) covers every variable before domain edges are deleted.
Domain updates only remove edges from the finite variable-value graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After each deletion batch, the procedure either restores a matching covering \(X\) or certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-only repair of a maintained variable-covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G\), a matching \(M\) covering \(X\), and a batch \(F\) of deleted domain edges. Set \(G'=G-F\) and \(M'=M-F\). For each variable exposed by deletion of its matched edge, search in \(G'\) for an \(M'\)-augmenting path and replace \(M'\) by its symmetric difference with that path. If no augmenting path exists, output infeasible. Otherwise, after all exposed variables are rematched, output \(M'\); optionally recompute alternating support information and delete unsupported edges before the next update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain unaffected matched edges, repair each deleted matched edge by augmentation, and report infeasibility when a covering matching cannot be restored.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Matching Maintenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the leaf, but the deletion-batch repair procedure and its infeasibility guarantee require a direct incremental matching source. The optional unsupported-edge filtering step also invokes a separate characterization that is not sourced here.

assumptions_latex: Each variable \(x\in X\) has a nonempty finite integer domain with bounds \(\ell_x=\min D(x)\) and \(u_x=\max D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounds consistency holds exactly when both \(\ell_x\) and \(u_x\) have interval-hull injective supports for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Lower and upper domain bounds of variable x.
Integer interval hull of the domain of x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-hull definition of bounds consistency for integer AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The AllDifferent constraint is bounds consistent when, for every variable \(x\in X\) and each bound \(b\in\{\ell_x,u_x\}\), there exists an injective map \(f:X\to\mathbb Z\) such that \(f(x)=b\) and \(\ell_y\le f(y)\le u_y\) for every \(y\in X\). Such a map is a bounds support: values assigned to other variables need only lie in their integer interval hulls, not necessarily in their possibly nonconvex current domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each lower and upper domain bound must extend to an injective assignment using values within every variable's current integer bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounds-Consistent AllDifferent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Bounds consistency has convention-sensitive definitions, especially concerning interval-hull values outside current nonconvex domains. A direct constraint-programming source with a precise definition or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Range-Consistent AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range consistency defined using each variable’s current domain and the interval hulls of all other domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite integer domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\), and let \(R_i=[\min D_i,\max D_i]\cap\mathbb Z\). The constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is range consistent if, for every \(i\) and every \(v\in D_i\), there exist values \(a_j\in R_j\) for all \(j\ne i\) such that the tuple defined by \(a_i=v\) has pairwise distinct components. Equivalently, every current domain value has an AllDifferent support when the other domains are replaced by their integer interval hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AllDifferent is range consistent when every current value extends to a pairwise-distinct assignment using values from the interval hulls of the other domains.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) and each \(D_i\subset\mathbb Z\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\( orall i\; orall v\in D_i\;\exists (a_j)_{j
e i}\in\prod_{j
e i}R_j:\ a_i=v\ \land\  orall p<q,\ a_p
e a_q.\)

notation.meaning: current finite domain of variable x_i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the consistency-regime leaf, but no citation supports the precise range-consistency convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Disequality Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical decomposition of finite-arity AllDifferent; propagation strength is distinguished from solution-set equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) over arbitrary domains, the global constraint has the exact logical representation
\[\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigwedge_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_i\ne x_j).\]
Thus the global constraint and its binary decomposition admit exactly the same complete assignments. This equivalence does not imply equal propagation strength: enforcing arc consistency separately on all binary disequalities can leave values that generalized arc consistency on the global AllDifferent constraint removes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AllDifferent equals the conjunction of all pairwise disequalities, although propagation on the global constraint can be strictly stronger than propagation on the binary decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sol}(\operatorname{AllDifferent})=\operatorname{sol}(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j)\), while binary arc consistency need not imply global generalized arc consistency.

notation.meaning: set of complete assignments satisfying constraint C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and distinction between solution equivalence and propagation strength fit the leaf, but the strict propagation comparison requires an inspectable source.

children.title: Excepted-Value AllDifferent
children.top_down_role: AllDifferent variants permitting designated repeated values.

knowledge_statements.title: Excepted-Value AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AllDifferent with a designated set of repeatable exception values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) take values in a set \(V\), and let \(E\subseteq V\) be the exception set. The constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferentExcept}(x_1,\ldots,x_n;E)\) holds exactly when any two variables assigned the same value receive an exception value:
\[\forall i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad i<j\ \land\ x_i=x_j\ \Longrightarrow\ x_i\in E.\]
Values in \(E\) may occur any number of times, whereas each value in \(V\setminus E\) occurs at most once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonexception values must be pairwise distinct; designated exception values may be repeated without restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\), \(x_i\in V\), and \(E\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall v\in V\setminus E,\ \lvert\{i:x_i=v\}\rvert\le 1.\)

notation.meaning: set of values exempt from distinctness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and appropriately typed, but the named variant's convention for repeatable exception values is unsupported.

children.title: Optional AllDifferent
children.top_down_role: AllDifferent variants with conditionally participating variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity-indexed AllDifferent in which only active variables participate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be variables and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\{0,1\}\) be activity indicators. The optional AllDifferent constraint holds when every pair of active variables takes different values:
\[\operatorname{OptionalAllDifferent}(x,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall i<j,\ (y_i=1\land y_j=1)\Longrightarrow x_i\ne x_j.\]
No distinctness restriction is imposed between two variables when at least one is inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables marked active must have pairwise-distinct values; inactive variables do not participate in distinctness.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) and \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i<j,\ y_i y_j=1\Longrightarrow x_i\ne x_j.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The activity-indexed semantics are coherent and fit the leaf, but no source establishes that this is the intended Optional AllDifferent convention.

children.title: Exception–Optional Interaction
children.top_down_role: Variants combining value exceptions with optional participation.

knowledge_statements.title: Exception–Optional Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined semantics when both exception values and optional participation are present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\subseteq V\) be exception values and let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate participation of \(x_i\). Combining exception and optional semantics yields
\[\forall i<j,\quad (y_i=1\land y_j=1\land x_i=x_j)\Longrightarrow x_i\in E.\]
Equivalently, for every nonexception value \(v\in V\setminus E\), at most one active variable may equal \(v\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\,\mathbf 1[x_i=v]\le 1.\]
Consequently, inactive variables and occurrences of exception values do not consume the nonexception uniqueness capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among active variables, only exception values may repeat; inactive variables and exception-valued assignments are ignored by the uniqueness count.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in V\), \(E\subseteq V\), and \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall v\in V\setminus E,\ \sum_i y_i\mathbf 1[x_i=v]\le 1.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula correctly combines the two stated candidate definitions and property is the appropriate kind, but both conventions and their named interaction remain unsourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Involutive-permutation form of symmetric AllDifferent on a common index and value set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have domains contained in \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The symmetric AllDifferent constraint holds exactly when
\[\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\quad\land\quad\forall i,j\in I,\ x_i=j\Longrightarrow x_j=i.\]
Because an injective self-map of the finite set \(I\) is bijective, a satisfying assignment represents an involutive permutation \(\pi:I\to I\), with \(\pi(i)=x_i\) and \(\pi(\pi(i))=i\). Fixed points are permitted unless separately excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variables form an involutive permutation: values are all distinct, and assigning j to position i forces i at position j.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) and \(D(x_i)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(i)=x_i\) defines a permutation satisfying \(\pi^2=\operatorname{id}_I\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The involutive-permutation formulation is internally coherent and fits the leaf, but an authoritative source is required to confirm the exact Symmetric AllDifferent convention.

children.title: Partial AllDifferent
children.top_down_role: AllDifferent restrictions applied to selected assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AllDifferent restricted to a specified subset of variable indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be variables and let \(S\subseteq\{1,ldots,n\}\) be the participating index set. The partial AllDifferent constraint on \(S\) holds exactly when
\[\forall i,j\in S,\quad i<j\Longrightarrow x_i\ne x_j.\]
Variables indexed outside \(S\) are unrestricted by this constraint and may equal participating or nonparticipating variables. When \(S=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the constraint specializes to ordinary AllDifferent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only variables whose indices belong to the designated subset must be pairwise distinct.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\{x_i:i\in S\}\rvert=\lvert S\rvert.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed subset-participation meaning is not established for the named variant, and the statement also contains the malformed set expression \(\{1,ldots,n\}\), which should be \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) once the semantics are sourced.

children.title: Precedence-Constrained AllDifferent
children.top_down_role: AllDifferent assignments restricted by value or variable precedence.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Constrained AllDifferent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AllDifferent augmented by strict value-order constraints from an acyclic precedence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) take values in a totally ordered set \((V,<)\), and let \(P\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\) be a directed acyclic precedence relation. The precedence-constrained AllDifferent constraint holds exactly when
\[\left(\forall i<j,\ x_i\ne x_j\right)\quad\land\quad\left(\forall(i,j)\in P,\ x_i<x_j\right).\]
Thus every feasible assignment is injective and is order-preserving on each specified precedence arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All variables take distinct values, and every specified precedence arc requires the predecessor’s value to be strictly smaller.
assumptions_latex: \((V,<)\) is totally ordered and every \(x_i\in V\).
\(P\) is a directed acyclic relation on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x)\land\bigwedge_{(i,j)\in P}(x_i<x_j).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conjunction of AllDifferent with value-order inequalities is coherent, but no source confirms that this is the intended meaning of Precedence-Constrained AllDifferent.

children.title: Partial–Precedence Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined participation and precedence restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial–Precedence Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined semantics for subset participation and precedence arcs among participating variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be the participating indices and let \(P\subseteq S\times S\) be an acyclic precedence relation. Over a totally ordered value set, the combined constraint is
\[\left(\forall i,j\in S,\ i<j\Longrightarrow x_i\ne x_j\right)\quad\land\quad\left(\forall(i,j)\in P,\ x_i<x_j\right).\]
Indices outside \(S\) neither consume distinct values nor participate in precedence arcs. Feasibility therefore requires every directed path in \(P\) to map to a strictly increasing sequence of distinct values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Participating variables are distinct and respect their precedence arcs; variables outside the selected subset are ignored.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(P\subseteq S\times S\) is acyclic.
The common value set is totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}((x_i)_{i\in S})\land\bigwedge_{(i,j)\in P}(x_i<x_j).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interaction property follows from the proposed component semantics and fits the leaf, but those named semantics are ambiguous and unsupported.

children.title: Bounded Occurrences
children.top_down_role: Value multiplicities governed by lower and upper limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Occurrences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global cardinality constraint with lower and upper occurrence bounds for designated values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) take values in \(V\), let \(W\subseteq V\) be the values whose occurrences are constrained, and assign integers \(0\le \ell_v\le u_v\le n\) to every \(v\in W\). The bounded global cardinality constraint holds exactly when
\[\forall v\in W,\qquad \ell_v\le \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i=v]\le u_v.\]
Values outside \(W\) have no occurrence restriction unless the modeling convention separately forbids them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each designated value must occur between its specified lower and upper counts.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\), \(W\subseteq V\), and \(x_i\in V\).
\(0\le \ell_v\le u_v\le n\) for every \(v\in W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall v\in W,\ \ell_v\le \operatorname{occ}_x(v)\le u_v.\)

notation.meaning: number of indices i with x_i=v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-occurrence definition is standard-looking and fits the leaf, but no inspectable global-cardinality source is cited, particularly for the treatment of values outside \(W\).

children.title: Exact Occurrences
children.top_down_role: Value multiplicities fixed to specified counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Occurrences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global cardinality constraint prescribing an exact multiplicity for every designated value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) take values in \(V\), let \(W\subseteq V\), and let \(c_v\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) be prescribed for every \(v\in W\). The exact-occurrence global cardinality constraint holds exactly when
\[\forall v\in W,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i=v]=c_v.\]
If \(W=V\), feasibility additionally forces \(\sum_{v\in V}c_v=n\). If values outside \(W\) are permitted, their total occurrence equals \(n-\sum_{v\in W}c_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every designated value occurs exactly its prescribed number of times.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\), \(W\subseteq V\), and \(x_i\in V\).
\(c_v\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) for every \(v\in W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall v\in W,\ \operatorname{occ}_x(v)=c_v.\)

notation.meaning: prescribed occurrence count of value v
number of variables assigned value v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-count definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but the convention for designated versus undesignated values lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Bound-to-Exact Specialization
children.top_down_role: Structural transition from occurrence intervals to fixed counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-to-Exact Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global cardinality is the equal-bound specialization of bounded global cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each constrained value \(v\in W\), set the bounded-occurrence parameters equal, \(\ell_v=u_v=c_v\). Then
\[\ell_v\le \operatorname{occ}_x(v)\le u_v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{occ}_x(v)=c_v.\]
Consequently, the exact-occurrence global cardinality constraint is precisely the specialization of bounded global cardinality obtained by imposing equal lower and upper bounds for every constrained value. Conversely, any bounded instance with \(\ell_v=u_v\) for all \(v\in W\) is an exact-occurrence instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal lower and upper occurrence bounds turn bounded global cardinality exactly into prescribed cardinalities.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_v=u_v=c_v\) for every \(v\in W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{GCC}_{[\ell,u]}(x;W)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{GCC}_{=c}(x;W).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-bound specialization is mathematically correct relative to the two proposed definitions and property is the proper kind, but those global-cardinality conventions have no supporting source.

children.title: Open Global Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality regimes permitting values outside the listed occurrence map.

knowledge_statements.title: Open Global Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open GCC constrains multiplicities only for an explicitly listed value set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be finite-domain variables, let \(V\) be a finite set of distinguished values, and let \(\ell_v,u_v\in\mathbb Z\) satisfy \(0\leq \ell_v\leq u_v\leq n\) for every \(v\in V\). The open global-cardinality constraint \(\operatorname{ogcc}(X;V,\ell,u)\) holds exactly when
\[
\ell_v\leq \left|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=v\}\right|\leq u_v\qquad(v\in V).
\]
Values in \(\bigcup_i D(x_i)\setminus V\) remain admissible and their individual occurrence counts are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open GCC bounds occurrences of listed values but permits unlisted domain values without imposing individual count bounds on them.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) consists of finitely many finite-domain variables.
\(V\) is finite and \(0\leq \ell_v\leq u_v\leq n\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ogcc}(X;V,\ell,u)\iff \forall v\in V:\ \ell_v\leq |\{i:x_i=v\}|\leq u_v\).

notation.meaning: current finite domain of variable x_i
values whose occurrence counts are constrained

children.title: Closed Global Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality regimes restricting assignments to listed values.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Global Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed GCC additionally excludes every value absent from its value-count table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), let \(V\) be finite, and let \(0\leq \ell_v\leq u_v\leq n\) be integer bounds for \(v\in V\). The closed global-cardinality constraint \(\operatorname{cgcc}(X;V,\ell,u)\) holds exactly when
\[
\bigl(\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\in V\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\forall v\in V:\ell_v\leq |\{i:x_i=v\}|\leq u_v\bigr).
\]
Thus every assigned value must occur in the explicit count table.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed GCC bounds the occurrence of every listed value and requires every variable to take one of those listed values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) consists of finitely many finite-domain variables.
\(V\) is finite and each pair \((\ell_v,u_v)\) is integral with \(0\leq\ell_v\leq u_v\leq n\).

children.title: Closure-Sensitivity Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open and closed GCC diverge precisely when an unlisted value remains assignable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For identical data \(X,V,\ell,u\), every closed-GCC solution is an open-GCC solution. The converse holds if \(D(x_i)\subseteq V\) for every \(i\), but can fail otherwise. Concretely, take one variable with \(D(x_1)=\{a,b\}\), let \(V=\{a\}\), and impose \(\ell_a=u_a=0\). The assignment \(x_1=b\) satisfies the open GCC because the count of \(a\) is zero, whereas it violates the closed GCC because \(b\notin V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed GCC implies open GCC. They coincide when all domains lie in the count table; otherwise unlisted values can separate their solution sets.
assumptions_latex: Open and closed constraints use the same variables, listed values, and occurrence bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(\operatorname{cgcc})\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}(\operatorname{ogcc})\), with equality when \(\bigcup_iD(x_i)\subseteq V\); strict inclusion is possible otherwise.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Cardinality Flow Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed GCC feasibility is represented by an integral lower-capacitated bipartite flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed GCC on variables \(X\) and values \(V\), form a directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), variable vertices \(x_i\), and value vertices \(v\). Give \((s,x_i)\) lower and upper capacity \([1,1]\); include \((x_i,v)\) with capacity \([0,1]\) exactly when \(v\in D(x_i)\cap V\); and give \((v,t)\) capacity \([\ell_v,u_v]\). Then the GCC is satisfiable exactly when this network has a feasible integral flow. An assignment and flow correspond through \(x_i=v\iff f(x_i,v)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed GCC is feasible exactly when its source–variable–value–sink network admits an integral flow respecting occurrence lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: The GCC is closed and all domains and value sets are finite.
Occurrence bounds are integral and satisfy \(0\leq\ell_v\leq u_v\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cgcc}(X;V,\ell,u)\) is satisfiable \(\iff\) the constructed network admits a feasible integral flow of value \(n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Flow Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An integral feasible flow is a directly checkable certificate of GCC satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the GCC network, a certificate consists of integers \(f(e)\) for every arc. It is valid when each arc satisfies \(\ell(e)\leq f(e)\leq u(e)\), flow is conserved at every variable and value vertex, and the source emits total flow \(n\). These checks are linear in the number of arcs. A valid certificate induces the assignment selecting, for each \(i\), the unique \(v\) with \(f(x_i,v)=1\); its value-node flows certify all prescribed occurrence bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Network Support Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual cycles characterize assignment edges that can belong to another feasible GCC flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a feasible integral flow of the GCC network and let \(R_f\) be its residual digraph, including forward residual arcs below upper capacity and reverse residual arcs above lower capacity. For an assignment arc \(e=(x_i,v)\), the literal \(x_i=v\) has a GCC support if and only if either \(f(e)=1\), or \(f(e)=0\) and the endpoints of \(e\) lie in the same strongly connected component of \(R_f\). Equivalently, an unused assignment arc is supportable exactly when it belongs to a directed residual cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A used assignment edge is supported; an unused one is supported exactly when it closes a residual cycle, equivalently when its endpoints share an SCC.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible integral flow in the GCC network.
\(R_f\) respects both lower and upper residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=v\) is supported \(\iff f(x_i,v)=1\) or \(x_i\) and \(v\) belong to one strongly connected component of \(R_f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental GCC Flow Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain deletions are handled by residual rerouting before support SCCs are refreshed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible integral GCC flow \(f\) and a deleted assignment arc \((x_i,v)\). If \(f(x_i,v)=0\), remove the arc and retain \(f\). If \(f(x_i,v)=1\), first cancel its unit; then search the remaining residual digraph for a directed path from \(x_i\) to \(v\). Augment one unit along such a path and delete the original arc. If no path exists, report infeasibility. Finally recompute or incrementally update strongly connected components and delete every unused assignment arc whose endpoints are in distinct components. Output the repaired flow and filtered domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After an edge deletion, preserve an unused flow or reroute a deleted used unit through the residual graph, then refresh SCC-based support pruning.
assumptions_latex: The maintained flow is feasible before the domain deletion.
The deletion removes an assignment arc from the GCC network.

children.title: Bounds Filtering for GCC
children.top_down_role: Global-cardinality filtering over variable bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounds Filtering for GCC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds consistency requires support for each current endpoint, not every interior domain value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every integer variable \(x_i\) have current domain \(D(x_i)\), with bounds \(m_i=\min D(x_i)\) and \(M_i=\max D(x_i)\). A GCC is bounds consistent when, for every \(i\) and each endpoint \(a\in\{m_i,M_i\}\), there exists a complete GCC-satisfying assignment \(y\) such that \(y_i=a\) and \(m_j\leq y_j\leq M_j\) for every \(j\). Bounds filtering repeatedly removes an unsupported endpoint and updates the affected bound until this predicate holds or some domain becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GCC bounds filtering removes a variable’s minimum or maximum whenever that endpoint lacks a solution using the other variables’ current intervals.
assumptions_latex: All variables are integer-valued with finite nonempty domains.
Support for other variables is tested over their current bound intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After reaching a fixed point, every \(a\in\{\min D(x_i),\max D(x_i)\}\) has a GCC support within all current bounds.

notation.meaning: current lower and upper bounds of x_i

children.title: Interval Filtering for GCC
children.top_down_role: Global-cardinality filtering over value intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Filtering for GCC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval filtering uses interval-relaxed supports while testing every retained domain value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite integer domains, write \(I_j=[\min D(x_j),\max D(x_j)]\cap\mathbb Z\). A GCC is interval consistent, also called range consistent, when for every variable \(x_i\) and every \(a\in D(x_i)\), there exists a complete GCC-satisfying assignment \(y\) such that \(y_i=a\) and \(y_j\in I_j\) for all \(j\neq i\). Interval filtering deletes each value lacking such an interval-relaxed support and iterates until this condition holds or a domain is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval filtering tests every retained value, allowing the other variables any integer between their current bounds, and deletes values without such support.
assumptions_latex: All variables have finite nonempty integer domains.
Other variables are relaxed to the integer hulls of their domains during support tests.

children.title: GCC Filtering-Strength Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relative pruning power and computational regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: GCC Filtering-Strength Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The comparison uses domain, interval/range, and bounds consistency under common domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a GCC over finite integer domains, domain consistency implies interval consistency, and interval consistency implies bounds consistency:
\[
\operatorname{DC}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{IC}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{BC}.
\]
The first implication holds because a support using actual domains also uses their interval hulls; the second holds because interval consistency tests every retained value, including each endpoint. Neither converse holds in general when domains contain holes: interval-relaxed supports may use absent interior values, while bounds consistency need not support retained nonendpoint values. Hence the implications are strict over general finite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain consistency is at least as strong as interval consistency, which is at least as strong as bounds consistency; domain holes can make both implications strict.
assumptions_latex: All three consistencies concern the same GCC and current finite integer domains.
Interval consistency uses integer interval hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{DC}\Rightarrow\operatorname{IC}\Rightarrow\operatorname{BC}\), and both reverse implications fail for some finite-domain GCC instances.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: implication chain follows from support-set containment

knowledge_statements.title: Costed Global Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Costed GCC augments occurrence bounds with assignment-dependent costs and a total-cost variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be finite-domain variables, let \(V\) carry occurrence bounds \(\ell_v,u_v\), let \(c_{i,v}\in\mathbb R\) be defined whenever \(v\in D(x_i)\cap V\), and let \(z\) be a real-valued cost variable. The costed global-cardinality constraint \(\operatorname{costgcc}(X,z;V,\ell,u,c)\) holds exactly when the underlying closed GCC holds and
\[
z=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,x_i}.
\]
For fixed \(L,U\in\mathbb R\) with \(L\leq U\), a bounded-cost variant instead requires \(L\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,x_i}\leq U\). In the flow representation, \(c_{i,v}\) is the cost of assignment arc \((x_i,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A costed GCC enforces value-occurrence bounds and makes a real-valued cost variable equal to the sum of the selected assignment costs; a bounded variant instead constrains that sum to a fixed interval.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) consists of finitely many finite-domain variables and the underlying GCC is closed.
Every admissible pair \((i,v)\) has a cost \(c_{i,v}\in\mathbb R\).
\(z\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{costgcc}(X,z;V,\ell,u,c)\iff \operatorname{cgcc}(X;V,\ell,u)\land z=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,x_i}\).

notation.meaning: real cost of assigning value v to variable x_i

knowledge_statements.title: Among Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Among counts how many variables take a value from a designated set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be finite-domain variables, let \(S\) be a set of values, and let \(N\) be an integer variable. The constraint \(\operatorname{among}(N,X,S)\) holds exactly when
\[
N=\left|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\in S\}\right|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i\in S].
\]
If constants \(L,U\) are used instead of \(N\), the bounded form requires \(L\leq |\{i:x_i\in S\}|\leq U\). Values outside \(S\) contribute zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among equates an integer variable to the number of variables assigned a value from a specified set, with an optional bounded-count form.

\(S\) is a fixed value set and \(N\) is integer-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) taking values in a finite set \(V\), the count constraint associates each selected value \(v\in V\) with an integer variable \(c_v\) and requires
\[
c_v=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i=v]=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=v\}|.
\]
Thus \(0\le c_v\le n\). If counts are specified for every value that can occur, then \(\sum_{v\in V}c_v=n\). A single-value count constraint is obtained by retaining only one designated \(v\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between an among-style membership count and exact-value count variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq U\), define exact-value counts \(c_v=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i=v]\) for \(v\in U\). The membership count of \(S\) satisfies
\[
N=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1[x_i\in S]=\sum_{v\in S}c_v.
\]
Conversely, a count constraint for one value \(v\) is the membership-count constraint for the singleton \(S=\{v\}\). Hence any prescribed bounds \(L\le N\le H\) translate exactly into \(L\le\sum_{v\in S}c_v\le H\).

The NVALUE constraint on \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and \(N\) holds exactly when

N=|\{x_i:i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\}|,

The distribution constraint \(\operatorname{distribution}(x_1,\ldots,x_n;v_1,\ldots,v_m;c_1,\ldots,c_m)\) holds when, for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\),

children.title: Balance Constraints

assumptions_latex: \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) are nonnegative integer frequencies with \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j=n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric frequency-balancing form; other catalogued BALANCE signatures may use value intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A distribution vector \((c_1,\ldots,c_m)\) is balanced when
\[
\max_{1\le j\le m}c_j-\min_{1\le j\le m}c_j\le 1.
\]
Writing \(n=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\), this is equivalent to requiring exactly \(r\) components to equal \(q+1\) and the remaining \(m-r\) components to equal \(q\). Applied to assignment variables, the balance constraint requires their value-frequency vector to satisfy this predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced distribution assigns each represented value either the floor or the ceiling of the average frequency, so no two frequencies differ by more than one.

children.title: Spread Constraints
children.top_down_role: Restrictions on dispersion across assigned values.

assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are integer variables.
\(S\) and \(Q\) are integer variables representing the sum and squared sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\) and \(Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2\), equivalently \(nQ-S^2=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_i-x_j)^2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common SPREAD global constraint uses sum and sum-of-squares statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum-and-squared-sum form of SPREAD for integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The spread constraint \(\operatorname{spread}(x_1,\ldots,x_n;S,Q)\) requires
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i,\qquad Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2.
\]
Its induced dispersion is
\[
nQ-S^2=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_i-x_j)^2\ge 0.
\]
Thus fixing or bounding \(Q\) while fixing \(S\) fixes or bounds the variance, since \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-S/n)^2=Q/n-(S/n)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SPREAD links a variable sequence to its sum and squared sum, thereby representing its variance or pairwise squared dispersion.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: discrete convex equalization minimizes sum of squared frequencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic regularity link between a distribution histogram and balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\). Every nonnegative integer frequency vector \(c\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j=n\) obeys
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j^2\ge r(q+1)^2+(m-r)q^2.
\]
Equality holds exactly when every \(c_j\in\{q,q+1\}\), equivalently when \(\max_j c_j-\min_j c_j\le 1\). Hence a balance constraint selects precisely the distributions of minimum quadratic concentration, linking count-based distribution regularity to a spread statistic on the count vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among fixed-total integer histograms, the balanced histograms are exactly the minimizers of the sum of squared frequencies, connecting balance to a quadratic spread measure.

The permutation constraint on \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) holds exactly when the map \(i\mapsto x_i\) is a bijection from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to itself. Equivalently,

x_i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\quad\text{for all }i,\qquad x_i\ne x_j\quad\text{whenever }i\ne j.

The inverse constraint \(\operatorname{inverse}(x,y)\) holds when
\[
\forall i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},qquad x_i=j\Longleftrightarrow y_j=i.
\]
Consequently both \(x\) and \(y\) are permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the represented maps are mutual inverses: \(y_{x_i}=i\) for every \(i\) and \(x_{y_j}=j\) for every \(j\). The biconditional is part of the constraint, so information may propagate in either direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: INVERSE channels two permutation arrays so that assigning value j at position i in one array assigns value i at position j in the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The biconditional gives the standard symmetric INVERSE semantics, introduces its indices and domains, and fits the definition leaf. No inspectable source is supplied, so the catalog semantics cannot yet be source-reviewed.

\[
x_i=j
\]
means that item \(i\) is assigned to position or resource \(j\). If the assignment is bijective and \(|I|=|J|\), the variables must additionally satisfy \(x_i\ne x_{i'}\) whenever \(i\ne i'\); then \(i\mapsto x_i\) is a bijection.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets of equal cardinality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Bidirectional assignment channeling imposes, for every \(i\in I\) and \(j\in J\),
\[
x_i=j\Longleftrightarrow y_j=i.

Equivalently, \(y_{x_i}=i\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(x_{y_j}=j\) for every \(j\in J\). The channeling constraint makes the two arrays mutual inverses and therefore represents one bijective assignment in both item-indexed and position-indexed coordinates. Domain deletion of \(j\) from \(x_i\) is equivalent to deletion of \(i\) from \(y_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidirectional channeling equates each primal assignment literal with its dual inverse literal, making the two arrays exact inverse representations of one bijection.

children.title: Asymmetric Domain Effects

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Domain Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of exact primal–dual assignment channeling when values and variable positions are not symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite domains contained in a value set \(V\), and suppose a dual variable \(y_v\) is intended to identify the unique index assigned value \(v\). The equivalence \(x_i=v\iff y_v=i\) is well-defined and bidirectional only when every feasible assignment uses each represented value exactly once. If values may be unused or repeated, a single index-valued \(y_v\) cannot encode the primal assignment without an unused-value sentinel or a set-valued representation. Consequently, pruning a primal domain \(D(x_i)\) and pruning a dual domain \(D(y_v)\) need not have symmetric meanings outside the bijective case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index-valued dual variables exactly mirror primal assignments only for bijections. Optional or repeated values require sentinels or set-valued duals, so domain pruning becomes asymmetric.
assumptions_latex: \(D(x_i)\subseteq V\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each \(y_v\), if scalar, ranges over variable indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalar channel \(x_i=v\iff y_v=i\) is an exact two-way representation precisely under unique, exhaustive value use.

children.title: Sorting Channels

knowledge_statements.title: Sorting Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-statistic channel from an assignment vector to a nondecreasing sorted vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) over a totally ordered finite set, a sorting channel introduces variables \(s_1,\ldots,s_n\) satisfying \(s_1\leq\cdots\leq s_n\) and preserving multiplicities: for every value \(v\), \[\bigl|\{i:x_i=v\}\bigr|=\bigl|\{k:s_k=v\}\bigr|.\] Equivalently, for every complete assignment, \(s_k\) equals the \(k\)-th order statistic of the multiset \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\). The channel records the sorted value sequence but, in the presence of equal values, does not by itself identify which original index occupies each sorted position.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sorting channel equates a nondecreasing auxiliary vector with the ordered multiset of assigned values while preserving every value multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: The common value universe is finite and totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \((s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) is the nondecreasing rearrangement of \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).

children.title: Rank Channels
children.top_down_role: Links between values or variables and positional ranks.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tie-broken permutation channel assigning each original variable a unique sorted position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For assignment variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), define rank variables \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\) by ordering the pairs \((x_i,i)\) lexicographically. Thus \[r_i=1+\bigl|\{j:x_j<x_i\}\bigr|+\bigl|\{j<i:x_j=x_i\}\bigr|.\] Then \((r_1,\ldots,r_n)\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(s_1\leq\cdots\leq s_n\) is the corresponding sorted vector, channeling requires \(s_{r_i}=x_i\) for every \(i\). The index tie-break makes the representation single-valued even when assignments contain equal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank variables give each original variable a unique sorted position, resolving equal-value ties by original index and channeling each value to that position.
assumptions_latex: The value universe is totally ordered.
Ranks use increasing original index to break equal-value ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ranks form a permutation and satisfy \(s_{r_i}=x_i\) for all \(i\).

notation.meaning: tie-broken sorted rank of original position i

children.title: Sorting–Rank Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Sorting–Rank Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between sorted-position values and a tie-broken rank permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let ranks be defined by lexicographically sorting \((x_i,i)\), and let \(p\) be their inverse permutation, so \(r_{p_k}=k\). The sorting and rank views determine one another through \[s_k=x_{p_k}\quad\text{and}\quad s_{r_i}=x_i.\] Conversely, a rank permutation satisfying \(x_{p_1}\leq\cdots\leq x_{p_n}\), together with \(p_k<p_{k+1}\) whenever \(x_{p_k}=x_{p_{k+1}}\), induces the unique tie-broken ranks and the sorted vector. Without a fixed tie rule, sorted values determine only equivalence classes of ranks among equal-valued variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tie-broken rank permutation maps original variables bijectively to sorted positions; sorted values and ranks then channel through inverse permutations.
assumptions_latex: Values belong to a totally ordered set.
Equal values are ordered by increasing original index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identities \(s_k=x_{p_k}\) and \(s_{r_i}=x_i\) give the exact sorting–rank correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Tables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional constraint represented by its permitted tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be finite-domain variables and let \(T^+\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) be a finite set of tuples. The positive table constraint \(\operatorname{Table}^+(X,T^+)\) is satisfied by an assignment \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) exactly when \[a\in T^+.\] Under current domains \(D(x_i)\subseteq D_i\), a tuple \(t\in T^+\) is currently valid when \(t_i\in D(x_i)\) for every \(i\). A value \(v\in D(x_i)\) has table support when some currently valid tuple satisfies \(t_i=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive table explicitly lists all permitted tuples; a current value is supported when it occurs in a listed tuple compatible with every domain.
assumptions_latex: Every \(D_i\) is finite.
All tuples in \(T^+\) have arity \(n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Negative Tables

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be finite-domain variables with initial Cartesian universe \(U=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), and let \(T^-\subseteq U\) be finite. The negative table constraint \(\operatorname{Table}^-(X,T^-)\) is satisfied by an assignment \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in U\) exactly when \[a\notin T^-.\] Thus the represented relation is \(U\setminus T^-\). Current domain restrictions alter the feasible Cartesian product but do not change the forbidden relation: a current complete assignment is accepted precisely when it lies in the current product and is absent from \(T^-\).

children.title: Table-Polarity Conversion
children.top_down_role: Conversion regimes between permitted-tuple and forbidden-tuple representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Table-Polarity Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement conversion between allowed-tuple and forbidden-tuple tables over a fixed finite universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix finite domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\) and the tuple universe \(U=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\). A positive table \(T^+\subseteq U\) and a negative table \(T^-\subseteq U\) represent the same relation exactly when \[T^-=U\setminus T^+,\qquad T^+=U\setminus T^-.\] Conversion therefore consists of complementing the tuple set relative to the declared universe. The universe must remain fixed: complementing relative only to current, reduced domains changes the stored relation and is not generally equivalent to the original constraint after backtracking or domain restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive and negative tables are converted by set complementation over the fixed initial Cartesian universe, not over transient current domains.
assumptions_latex: Each declared domain \(D_i\) is finite.
Both polarities use the same fixed tuple universe \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent polarities satisfy \(T^-=U\setminus T^+\).

children.title: Polarity-Size Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation growth caused by an unsuitable table polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Polarity-Size Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case storage expansion caused by complementing a finite extensional relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), let \(N=|U|=\prod_{i=1}^n|D_i|\), and let a relation contain \(m\) allowed tuples. Its explicit positive representation has \(m\) tuples, whereas its explicit negative representation has \(N-m\) tuples. Hence polarity conversion by enumeration requires \(\Theta(N)\) membership examinations and may require \(\Theta(N-m)\) output storage. In particular, when domains have uniform size \(d\), \(N=d^n\); converting a polynomial-size table can therefore produce an exponentially large complement in the arity \(n\). The smaller explicit polarity contains \(\min\{m,N-m\}\) tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing a table can expand storage from a small relation to nearly the full Cartesian product, which is exponential in arity for fixed nontrivial domain size.
assumptions_latex: Tuples are stored explicitly.
Tuple membership tests take constant or amortized constant time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complement enumeration costs \(\Theta(N)\) tests and the smaller polarity has size \(\min\{m,N-m\}\).

notation.meaning: number of tuples in the Cartesian universe

children.title: Tuple-Support Search
children.top_down_role: Search regimes for currently valid tuple supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Tuple-Support Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support lookup for generalized arc consistency on a positive table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a positive table \(T^+\), current domains \(D(x_1),\ldots,D(x_n)\), and a queried pair \((i,v)\) with \(v\in D(x_i)\). Inspect tuples \(t\in T^+\) satisfying \(t_i=v\) until finding one for which \(t_j\in D(x_j)\) for every \(j\). Return that tuple as a support. If no such tuple exists, delete \(v\) from \(D(x_i)\). Repeat for affected variable-value pairs until no deletion occurs or some domain becomes empty. At termination without failure, every remaining value has a currently valid supporting tuple, so the positive table is generalized arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search tuples containing a queried value, retain the value if a domain-compatible tuple exists, and otherwise delete it; iterate to generalized arc consistency.
assumptions_latex: \(T^+\) is a finite positive table.
Domain deletion is monotone during one propagation branch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed point retains exactly values having at least one currently valid tuple support.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard support-based table filtering scheme
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Residue Caching
children.top_down_role: Reuse of previously located supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Caching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Last-support caching for repeated positive-table support queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable-value pair \((i,v)\), maintain either no residue or a tuple index \(R[i,v]\) naming the most recently found support in \(T^+\). On a support query, first test whether \(R[i,v]\) still indexes a tuple \(t\) with \(t_i=v\) and \(t_j\in D(x_j)\) for all \(j\). If so, accept it without further search. Otherwise search candidate tuples containing \(v\); on success set \(R[i,v]\) to the discovered tuple, and on failure delete \(v\). A residue is a search hint only: its presence never establishes support without the validity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cache each value's last supporting tuple, reuse it after checking current validity, and search anew only when the cached support has become invalid.
assumptions_latex: Tuple indices remain stable while residues refer to them.
Current tuple validity can be tested against all variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residues preserve filtering correctness while potentially avoiding repeated scans for unchanged supports.

notation.meaning: cached tuple index for variable-value pair

children.title: Residue Invalidation

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Invalidation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity predicate determining when a cached tuple may still certify support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A residue \(R[i,v]=q\) is valid under current domains exactly when the indexed tuple \(t^q\) exists, satisfies \(t^q_i=v\), and obeys \[t^q_j\in D(x_j)\quad\text{for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.\] It is invalidated when its tuple is removed from the active table, when any component \(t^q_j\) is deleted from \(D(x_j)\), or when the index no longer denotes the same tuple. An invalid residue cannot justify retaining \(v\); it triggers a fresh support search. After backtracking, a residue may be reused only after reevaluating this predicate against the restored state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached support remains valid only while its tuple still exists and every tuple component belongs to the corresponding current domain.
assumptions_latex: \(R[i,v]\) refers to an indexed tuple \(t^q\).
Residue validity is evaluated in the current propagation state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residue is usable if and only if \(t^q_i=v\) and \(t^q_j\in D(x_j)\) for every \(j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Tabular Reduction Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone active-tuple filtering for generalized arc consistency on positive tables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite-domain variables \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and an allowed table \(T^+\). Initialize the active set \(A:=T^+\). Whenever a domain loses values, remove from \(A\) every tuple \(t\) for which \(t_i\notin D(x_i)\) for some \(i\). Then, for each \(i\) and \(v\in D(x_i)\), delete \(v\) when no tuple \(t\in A\) satisfies \(t_i=v\). Repeat tuple removal and value deletion until a fixed point or an empty domain is reached. Output failure in the latter case; otherwise output the reduced domains and active table. Reversible state restores removed tuples during backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain compatible allowed tuples, delete unsupported values, and iterate these reductions to a fixed point; restore reversible tuple state when backtracking.
assumptions_latex: \(T^+\) is finite.
Domain reductions are monotone between backtracking events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a nonfailure fixed point, every remaining value occurs in at least one active tuple.

children.top_down_role: Active-tuple filtering using compact extensional state.

assumptions_latex: A positive table constraint has variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), current domains \(D_i\), and allowed tuples \(T\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^n U_i\).
Each tuple of \(T\) has a fixed bit position, and \(M_{i,a}\) is the bitset of tuples assigning value \(a\) to position \(i\).

notation.meaning: support bitset for value \(a\) at position \(i\)

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the Compact-Table algorithm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive extensional constraints with reversible tuple bitsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the reversible current-table bitset by \(S\leftarrow T\). After a domain change at position \(i\), update \[S\leftarrow S\cap\bigcup_{a\in D_i}M_{i,a}.\] For every position \(j\) and value \(b\in D_j\), test whether \(S\cap M_{j,b}\neq\varnothing\), optionally beginning from a saved supporting word. If the intersection is empty, delete \(b\) from \(D_j\); otherwise retain \(b\) and save a nonzero intersecting word as its residue. Repeat updates and value tests until no domain changes. Failure is reported exactly when \(S=\varnothing\).

assumptions_latex: Allowed tuples have fixed bit positions and are represented by a bitset \(B_T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the compatible-tuple bitset \[S=B_T\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^n\left(\bigcup_{a\in D_i}M_{i,a}\right).\] The constraint fails if \(S=\varnothing\). Otherwise, for every \(i\) and \(a\in D_i\), retain \(a\) exactly when \(S\cap M_{i,a}\neq\varnothing\), and delete it otherwise. Each union, intersection, and emptiness test is executed wordwise over the bitset representation. Recompute or incrementally update \(S\) after deletions until a fixed point is reached; the resulting domains are generalized-arc-consistent with respect to the represented positive table.

children.title: Sparse–Dense Execution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Implementation choices under changing active-tuple density.

assumptions_latex: The current tuple set is stored over \(m\) machine words, of which \(k\) are nonzero.
A sparse index list of nonzero words and a dense contiguous word array are both available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sparse execution costs \(O(k)\) word operations, dense execution costs \(O(m)\), and choosing the smaller estimated cost preserves filtering semantics.
review_flags: The exact switching policy is implementation-dependent and unsupported by supplied locators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive traversal of tuple bitsets by current density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any mask intersection or support scan, dense execution visits all \(m\) words, whereas sparse execution visits only the \(k\) indices whose current-table words are nonzero. Thus their respective word-operation bounds are \(O(m)\) and \(O(k)\), with additional sparse-index maintenance determined by the implementation. A hybrid regime may select sparse traversal when \(k/m\leq\tau\) and dense traversal otherwise. Because both regimes apply the same Boolean operation to every nonzero current-table word, switching representations changes execution cost but not the resulting feasible-tuple set or deleted values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traverse only nonzero words when the live tuple bitset is sparse, but scan its contiguous array when density makes sparse bookkeeping more expensive.
