intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind matches the leaf and the overload implication is plausible, but the exact minimum-overlap certificate has no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Energetic Bound Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Start-bound propagation by energetic infeasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each activity \(k\), test candidate lower and upper start bounds. To test \(s_k\le v\) or \(s_k\ge v\), add that temporary restriction to the current domains and, for selected windows \([a,b)\), compute \(q_i(a,b)=\min_s\lvert[s,s+p_i)\cap[a,b)\rvert\) over the temporarily restricted domain of each \(s_i\). If \(\sum_i h_iq_i(a,b)>C(b-a)\), the tested restriction is infeasible. Remove the corresponding unsupported bound values, update the start domain, and repeat until all selected tests pass or a domain becomes empty. A complete implementation specifies the finite family of tested windows and candidate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporarily restrict a start bound, compute forced energy in selected windows, and discard the bound whenever some window is overloaded.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive with fixed positive durations and demands.
The resource has constant capacity \(C>0\).
Every computed \(q_i\) is a valid minimum overlap under the temporary restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An energetic overload under a temporary bound restriction proves that restriction unsupported and justifies its removal.

notation.meaning: processing forced into the tested window

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the tested windows and candidate restrictions determine the actual filtering algorithm and are left unspecified and uncited.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Activity Energetic Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic propagation for activities governed by presence variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate each activity \(i\) with a presence variable \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\). For a window \([a,b)\), let \(q_i(a,b)\) be its minimum overlap when present. The energy forced by mandatory activities is \(E_1(a,b)=\sum_{i:z_i=1}h_iq_i(a,b)\). If \(E_1(a,b)>C(b-a)\), report infeasibility. For an undecided activity \(k\), if \(E_1(a,b)+h_kq_k(a,b)>C(b-a)\) for some window, infer \(z_k=0\). When \(z_k=1\) is fixed, apply ordinary energetic start-bound filtering to \(k\); iterate presence and bound deductions to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory activities must fit energetically; an optional activity is excluded when assuming its presence creates a window overload.
assumptions_latex: Presence \(z_i=0\) removes all processing and demand of activity \(i\).
Present activities are nonpreemptive with fixed positive durations and demands.
The renewable resource has constant capacity \(C>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If adding optional activity \(k\)'s forced energy overloads a window, every feasible solution satisfies \(z_k=0\).

notation.meaning: energy forced by presently mandatory activities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits and the stated presence inference is plausible, but its precise optional-activity semantics and energetic propagation variant require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Cumulative Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued extension of the cumulative scheduling constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite activity set and \(R\) a finite resource set. Activity \(i\) starts at \(s_i\), has duration \(p_i>0\), and consumes \(h_{ir}\ge0\) units of resource \(r\) throughout \([s_i,s_i+p_i)\). Capacities are \(C_r(t)\ge0\). The multiple-cumulative constraint holds exactly when, for every resource \(r\in R\) and time \(t\), \[\sum_{i\in I:t\in[s_i,s_i+p_i)}h_{ir}\le C_r(t).\] An activity may use several resources simultaneously, but feasibility is checked componentwise against each resource’s capacity profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each active activity consumes a demand vector, and at every time every resource component must remain within its own capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(R\) are finite.
Activities are nonpreemptive.
All demands and capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule is feasible precisely when all componentwise cumulative inequalities hold for every \(r\in R\) and time \(t\).

notation.meaning: demand of activity i on resource r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and componentwise formulation fit the leaf, but no scheduling source is cited for this multiple-resource cumulative formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Reservoir Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven bounded stock with production and consumption changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let events \(e\in E\) occur at times \(t_e\) and change a stock by signed amounts \(\Delta_e\), with positive values denoting production. Given initial level \(L_0\), define the right-continuous reservoir level by \[L(t)=L_0+\sum_{e\in E:t_e\le t}\Delta_e.\] The reservoir constraint requires \(L^{\min}(t)\le L(t)\le L^{\max}(t)\) for every time \(t\). If simultaneous events are atomic, their changes are summed before testing the bounds; if an application orders simultaneous changes, that event order must instead be supplied as part of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reservoir tracks cumulative signed event changes and requires the resulting stock to remain between prescribed lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: The event set \(E\) is finite.
Every event has a defined time and signed stock change.
The convention for simultaneous events is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The event schedule satisfies the reservoir constraint exactly when \(L^{\min}(t)\le L(t)\le L^{\max}(t)\) at all times.

notation.meaning: signed stock change at event e
reservoir level after events through time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but reservoir constraints have convention-sensitive simultaneous-event and level-testing semantics that require a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Function Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant resource state constrained by activity requirements and transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state function is a right-continuous, piecewise-constant map \(x:T\to Q\) over a time horizon \(T\), where \(Q\) is a finite set of states. Each scheduled activity \(i\) may require \(x(t)\in Q_i\) throughout \([s_i,s_i+p_i)\). Consecutive constant segments with states \(q,q'\in Q\) must satisfy an allowed-transition relation \((q,q')\in A\); a transition may additionally require a prescribed nonnegative duration during which no incompatible activity executes. The state-function constraint holds when all interval requirements, transition admissibility conditions, and transition-duration exclusions are simultaneously satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-constant state must meet every activity’s interval requirement and may change only through allowed transitions with any required transition time.
assumptions_latex: The state set \(Q\) is finite.
Activities are nonpreemptive intervals.
Transition semantics and transition durations are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(x(t)\in Q_i\) during every activity \(i\) and \((q,q')\in A\) at every state change.

notation.meaning: states permitted while activity i executes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but the proposed state-function and transition-duration semantics are model-dependent and unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Resource Calendars
children.top_down_role: Availability patterns induced by working periods, closures, or shifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Calendars
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Availability calendar for a renewable scheduling resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scheduling horizon \(T\), a resource calendar is a measurable availability function \(a:T\to[0,1]\), commonly piecewise constant and binary. A value \(a(t)=0\) marks resource closure, while \(a(t)=1\) marks full availability; fractional values encode proportional availability when the model permits it. Given nominal capacity \(C_0\ge0\), the usable capacity at time \(t\) is \(C(t)=C_0a(t)\). A schedule respecting the calendar must satisfy its resource-load inequality against \(C(t)\), including zero load during every closed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource calendar maps time to availability and scales nominal capacity, forcing zero use during closures and reduced use during partial availability.
assumptions_latex: The horizon \(T\) is measurable.
The nominal capacity satisfies \(C_0\ge0\).
Fractional availability is used only when proportional capacity is meaningful.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calendar induces usable capacity \(C(t)=C_0a(t)\), against which the resource load must be bounded.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but treating a resource calendar as a measurable fractional multiplier is a particular convention requiring source support.

children.title: Variable-Capacity Resources
children.top_down_role: Resources whose usable capacity changes over time.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Capacity Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cumulative renewable resources whose capacity depends on time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:T\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be a specified measurable capacity function. Activities \(i\in I\) start at \(s_i\), have durations \(p_i>0\), and consume fixed demands \(h_i\ge0\) throughout their nonpreemptive execution intervals. The variable-capacity cumulative constraint is \[\sum_{i\in I:t\in[s_i,s_i+p_i)}h_i\le C(t)\qquad\text{for every }t\in T.\] For piecewise-constant \(C\), it suffices to check intervals separated by activity endpoints and capacity breakpoints. Capacity changes do not interrupt an activity unless preemption is separately modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every time, the load of active activities must not exceed the resource’s time-dependent capacity.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive with fixed durations and demands.
The capacity function \(C\) is specified and nonnegative.
All execution intervals lie within the horizon \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule is feasible exactly when its active load is at most \(C(t)\) for every \(t\in T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and pointwise capacity inequality fit the leaf, but the formulation and breakpoint-checking claim lack a supporting scheduling citation.

children.title: Calendar-Induced Capacity Profiles
children.top_down_role: Capacity profiles arising from calendar-based availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Calendar-Induced Capacity Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity profile obtained by combining nominal capacity with calendar availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let resource \(r\) have nominal capacity \(C_r^0\ge0\) and calendar availability \(a_r(t)\in[0,1]\). Its calendar-induced capacity profile is represented by \[C_r(t)=C_r^0a_r(t).\] More generally, if the calendar specifies additive capacity increments \(\delta_{rk}\) on calendar intervals \(J_{rk}\), then \[C_r(t)=C_r^0+\sum_k\delta_{rk}\mathbf{1}_{J_{rk}}(t),\] provided the resulting profile is nonnegative. The cumulative load \(L_r(t)\) is calendar-feasible exactly when \(L_r(t)\le C_r(t)\) for every time in the scheduling horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calendar becomes a time-indexed capacity profile by scaling nominal capacity or adding interval-specific capacity changes; resource load is bounded by that profile.
assumptions_latex: Nominal capacities and resulting profiles are nonnegative.
Calendar intervals and endpoint conventions are specified.
Availability scaling and additive adjustments are not applied simultaneously unless explicitly intended.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Calendar feasibility is equivalent to the pointwise inequality \(L_r(t)\le C_r(t)\) over the horizon.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the scaling and additive calendar representations use distinct conventions whose applicability and combination rules require a source.

children.title: Setup Resources
children.top_down_role: Resource requirements associated with preparing activities or machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Setup Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Renewable-resource semantics for setup operations inserted between consecutive scheduled activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let activities be assigned to machines, and let \(y_{ij}=1\) mean that activity \(j\) immediately follows activity \(i\) on their common machine. A setup resource of capacity \(C^{\mathrm{set}}\) is modeled by an optional setup interval \(S_{ij}\) for each admissible pair \((i,j)\). Its presence is equivalent to \(y_{ij}=1\), its duration is \(s_{ij}\ge 0\), and it lies temporally between the activities: \(\operatorname{end}(i)\le \operatorname{start}(S_{ij})\) and \(\operatorname{end}(S_{ij})\le \operatorname{start}(j)\). If present, it demands \(q_{ij}\ge 0\), and feasibility requires \[\sum_{(i,j):\,t\in S_{ij}}q_{ij}\le C^{\mathrm{set}}\quad\text{for every time }t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected machine succession creates a setup interval whose timing, duration, and resource demand must respect the setup-resource capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) encodes immediate succession.
\(s_{ij},q_{ij}\ge 0\) and \(C^{\mathrm{set}}\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_{ij}=1\) activates a capacity-feasible setup interval between activities \(i\) and \(j\).

notation.meaning: optional setup interval induced by succession from activity i to activity j

review_flags: Exact setup-resource global-constraint semantics require an authoritative scheduling reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this particular optional-interval formulation, including immediate succession, temporal placement, and renewable setup-resource capacity semantics.

children.title: Transition Resources
children.top_down_role: Resource requirements associated with changes between activity states.

knowledge_statements.title: Transition Resources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource capacity consumed while equipment changes state between consecutive activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(i)\) and \(m(j)\) denote the states required by consecutive activities \(i\) and \(j\), and let \(y_{ij}=1\) encode their immediate succession. A transition resource of capacity \(C^{\mathrm{tr}}\) associates with every selected arc \((i,j)\) an interval \(T_{ij}\) of duration \(\tau_{m(i),m(j)}\ge 0\) and demand \(r_{m(i),m(j)}\ge 0\). The interval must occur after \(i\) and before \(j\). The transition-resource constraint holds exactly when every present \(T_{ij}\) respects these temporal links and \[\sum_{(i,j):\,t\in T_{ij}}r_{m(i),m(j)}\le C^{\mathrm{tr}}\quad\text{for every time }t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each selected state-changing succession activates a transition interval, and all simultaneous transitions must fit the shared transition-resource capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) identifies immediate successors.
Transition durations and demands depend on the ordered state pair \((m(i),m(j))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected transition is temporally placed and the aggregate active transition demand never exceeds \(C^{\mathrm{tr}}\).

notation.meaning: transition interval associated with selected succession (i,j)
duration of changing from state a to state b

review_flags: Exact transition-resource template and its distinction from setup resources need a scheduling source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative scheduling source is required to establish this transition-resource template and distinguish it from setup-resource semantics.

children.title: Sequence-Dependent Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling between activity order and setup or transition consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Dependent Resource Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling immediate-successor decisions to transition timing and renewable-resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For activities \(i,j\), let \(y_{ij}=1\) precisely when \(j\) immediately follows \(i\). Given pair-dependent duration \(s_{ij}\) and demand \(q_{ij}\), sequence-dependent resource coupling requires \[y_{ij}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{start}(j)\ge \operatorname{end}(i)+s_{ij}\] and activates a resource interval \(R_{ij}=[\operatorname{end}(i),\operatorname{end}(i)+s_{ij})\) with demand \(q_{ij}\). For resource capacity \(C\), the complete coupling additionally requires \[\sum_{(i,j):\,y_{ij}=1,\ t\in R_{ij}}q_{ij}\le C\quad\text{for every time }t.\] Thus both temporal separation and resource consumption are selected by the same ordered adjacency decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The chosen immediate successor determines both the required separation time and the capacity consumed during the intervening setup or transition.
assumptions_latex: \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) forms a valid immediate-successor relation.
\(s_{ij},q_{ij}\ge 0\) are specified for every admissible ordered pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selected adjacencies simultaneously enforce pair-dependent separation and capacity-feasible resource use.

notation.meaning: resource interval induced by selected adjacency (i,j)

review_flags: The precise global-constraint formulation needs an authoritative sequence-dependent scheduling reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim fixes the resource interval at the predecessor's end, which is stronger than generic sequence-dependent coupling. A source is needed to confirm that convention and the complete formulation.

children.title: Graph-Network Global Constraint Family
children.top_down_role: Graph-variable constraints and sequence encodings for paths, circuits, connectivity, trees, and flows.

children.title: Circuit Constraints
children.top_down_role: Single-cycle structures over the selected graph domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successor-variable definition of a single directed Hamiltonian circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(x_i\in V\) be the successor of vertex \(i\). The constraint \(\operatorname{circuit}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) holds if and only if the mapping \(i\mapsto x_i\) is a permutation of \(V\) and consists of exactly one directed cycle. Equivalently, there exists an ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices such that \[x_{v_k}=v_{k+1}\quad(1\le k<n),\qquad x_{v_n}=v_1.\] Hence every vertex has exactly one successor and one predecessor, and every vertex belongs to the same circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The successor variables form one directed cycle visiting every vertex exactly once.
assumptions_latex: Each successor variable has domain contained in \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arcs \(\{(i,x_i):i\in V\}\) form one directed Hamiltonian cycle on \(V\).
review_flags: A constraint-programming specification is needed to certify the selected circuit convention, including self-loop treatment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is standard under one circuit convention, but no cited specification establishes the intended convention, particularly treatment of self-loops and the restriction n at least 2.

children.title: Subcircuit Constraints
children.top_down_role: Cycle structures permitted to cover only a selected subset.

knowledge_statements.title: Subcircuit Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successor-variable subcircuit with fixed points representing vertices outside the selected tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with successor variables \(x_i\in V\). The constraint \(\operatorname{subcircuit}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) holds if and only if there exists a subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that \(x_i=i\) for every \(i\notin S\), while the restriction \(i\mapsto x_i\) on \(S\) is one directed cycle through all vertices of \(S\). Formally, when \(S\ne\varnothing\), there is an ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_k)\) of \(S\) satisfying \[x_{v_j}=v_{j+1}\quad(1\le j<k),\qquad x_{v_k}=v_1.\] No second nontrivial cycle is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected vertices form one directed cycle; every unselected vertex is represented by a self-loop.
assumptions_latex: Successor variables have domains contained in \(V\).
Fixed points encode vertices excluded from the nontrivial circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The non-fixed successor arcs form at most one directed circuit, and all remaining vertices are fixed points.

notation.meaning: successor of vertex i, or i itself when excluded

review_flags: Subcircuit conventions differ on whether an empty or singleton selected circuit is allowed; an authoritative specification is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source must determine whether empty and singleton selected sets are allowed. For a singleton, the displayed cycle is a fixed point and conflicts with the stated selected-versus-excluded interpretation.

children.title: Circuit–Subcircuit Coverage Boundary
children.top_down_role: Coverage distinctions separating full-cycle and partial-cycle regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Subcircuit Coverage Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between mandatory full coverage and optional coverage encoded by fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For successor variables \(x_i\in V\), a circuit constraint requires every vertex to lie on one common directed cycle. A subcircuit constraint relaxes coverage by allowing \(x_i=i\) for excluded vertices while requiring all non-fixed vertices to lie on one common directed cycle. Therefore, \[\operatorname{circuit}(x)\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{subcircuit}(x)\] under the convention that the selected set of a subcircuit may equal \(V\). The converse fails whenever a proper subset is selected: for \(V=\{1,2,3\}\), the assignment \(x_1=2\), \(x_2=1\), and \(x_3=3\) is a subcircuit but not a circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Circuit requires all vertices; subcircuit permits fixed-point exclusions. A two-cycle plus an excluded fixed vertex separates the two notions.
assumptions_latex: Subcircuit exclusion is encoded by self-loops.
A circuit contains no excluded vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full vertex coverage is exactly the additional requirement separating circuit from subcircuit semantics.
review_flags: The boundary depends on the adopted subcircuit convention and needs a matching constraint-language specification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary and counterexample are correct only for the stated fixed-point subcircuit convention, whose empty, singleton, and self-loop cases remain unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Successor–Predecessor Tour Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent successor and predecessor encodings of a directed tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A directed tour may be represented by successor variables \(s_i\in V\) or predecessor variables \(p_j\in V\). The views are mutually inverse precisely when \[s_i=j\ \Longleftrightarrow\ p_j=i\qquad(i,j\in V).\] If \(s\) is a permutation consisting of one cycle, these channeling equivalences uniquely determine \(p=s^{-1}\), and \(p\) also consists of one cycle. Conversely, any single-cycle predecessor permutation uniquely determines its successor inverse. Thus either view specifies the same directed Hamiltonian circuit, while maintaining both views exposes incoming and outgoing adjacency information simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successor and predecessor tour encodings are inverse permutations linked by bidirectional channeling equations.
assumptions_latex: \(s\) and \(p\) range over the same finite vertex set \(V\).
The tour is a single-cycle permutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=s^{-1}\), and the successor and predecessor arcs describe the same directed tour.
review_flags: A global-constraint or graph-modeling reference is needed for the dual-view channeling formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-permutation representation is mathematically plausible and fits the container, but no inspectable citation supports its use as the intended tour-view channeling formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Side-Constraint Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Channeling circuit arcs to variables used by costs, capacities, and other side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let successor variables \(s_i\in V\) define a circuit, and introduce arc indicators \(z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). Exact channeling requires \[z_{ij}=1\ \Longleftrightarrow\ s_i=j\qquad(i,j\in V).\] Consequently, side constraints may address the selected circuit through \(z\); for example, an additive tour attribute with arc data \(a_{ij}\) is \[A=\sum_{i\in V}\sum_{j\in V}a_{ij}z_{ij}.\] Bounds, resource constraints, forbidden-arc conditions, and objective terms imposed on \(z\) therefore constrain the same arcs as the circuit variables. Bidirectional equivalence is required if propagation must pass from side constraints back to the successor view.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc indicators are equated with successor choices so circuit arcs can participate exactly in cost, capacity, and compatibility constraints.
assumptions_latex: The successor variables satisfy a circuit constraint.
Each \(z_{ij}\) is binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every side constraint on \(z\) applies to exactly the arcs selected by the successor circuit.

notation.meaning: indicator that directed arc (i,j) is selected
an additive attribute of the selected tour

review_flags: An authoritative constraint-modeling source is needed for exact circuit-to-arc channeling semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact arc channeling equations are plausible, but no cited modeling source supports the formulation or the statement about bidirectional propagation.

children.title: Directed Paths
children.top_down_role: Path constraints respecting arc orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple directed path induced by selected arcs in a directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and let \(s,t\in V\). A directed simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) path is a sequence \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) of pairwise distinct vertices satisfying \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), and \((v_{r-1},v_r)\in A\) for every \(r=1,ldots,k\). Equivalently, its selected-arc indicators \(z_a\in\{0,1\}\) describe a connected acyclic support with net outflow \(1\) at \(s\), net inflow \(1\) at \(t\), and balanced flow at every other selected vertex. Arc orientation must agree with traversal from \(s\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path follows oriented arcs from its source to its target without repeating vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(s,t\in V\) are designated endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) connects \(s\) to \(t\) using only forward-oriented arcs and no repeated vertex.

notation.meaning: ordered vertex sequence of the path

review_flags: A graph or global-constraint source is required for the selected simple-path semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. The range contains the malformed text “1,ldots,k”, and the claimed indicator equivalence needs a precise definition of selected support, connectivity, and net flow.

children.title: Undirected Paths
children.top_down_role: Path constraints over orientation-free edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple path induced by selected edges in an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and let \(s,t\in V\). An undirected simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) path is a sequence \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) of pairwise distinct vertices satisfying \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), and \(\{v_{r-1},v_r\}\in E\) for every \(r=1,\ldots,k\). Its selected-edge subgraph is connected, has degree \(1\) at \(s\) and \(t\), degree \(2\) at each internal path vertex, and degree \(0\) at every unselected vertex. Because edges are unordered, either traversal direction represents the same path support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected path connects two endpoints through unordered edges without repeating vertices; reversing its traversal does not change the path.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(s,t\in V\) are distinct designated endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected edges form one simple undirected chain between \(s\) and \(t\).
review_flags: A graph or global-constraint source is required for the selected simple-path semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simple-path definition and degree characterization are standard and fit the container, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Orientation-Sensitive Path Semantics
children.top_down_role: Modeling distinctions caused by directed versus undirected graph structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitive Path Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How reversing traversal affects directed and undirected path feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) and let \(P^{\mathrm{rev}}=(v_k,\ldots,v_0)\). In an undirected graph, \(P\) is a path if and only if \(P^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is a path, because \(\{u,v\}=\{v,u\}\). In a directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), \(P^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is feasible if and only if \((v_r,v_{r-1})\in A\) for every \(r=1,\ldots,k\). Hence directed reachability need not be symmetric: the existence of a directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) does not imply one from \(t\) to \(s\), whereas an undirected path certifies connectivity in both traversal directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path reversal always preserves undirected feasibility but preserves directed feasibility only when every reverse arc exists.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a simple path in the relevant graph.
Directed arcs are ordered; undirected edges are unordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Undirected path feasibility is reversal-invariant, while directed path feasibility is generally orientation-sensitive.

notation.meaning: the reverse ordering of path P

review_flags: A standard graph-theory source with an exact locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orientation comparison is mathematically standard and the property kind fits the boundary-style container, but no source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Bounded Paths
children.top_down_role: Paths restricted by length, hop count, or related limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-bounded simple paths, distinct from bounds on accumulated edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed or undirected graph, let \(s,t\in V\), and let \(L\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\). A path \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) is an \(L\)-bounded \(s\)-to-\(t\) path when it satisfies the applicable directed or undirected simple-path conditions and \[k=|E(P)|\le L.\] In an arc- or edge-indicator representation \(z_e\in\{0,1\}\), the bound is equivalently \[\sum_{e\in E}z_e\le L,\] provided the remaining constraints ensure that the selected support is exactly one simple \(s\)-to-\(t\) path. knowledge_statements.title: Directed-Acyclicity Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\) and selected arcs \(A_x\subseteq A\), the selected digraph \((V,A_x)\) is acyclic if and only if there exists an injective ordering \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\) satisfying \[\pi(u)<\pi(v)\quad\text{for every }(u,v)\in A_x.\] Thus directed acyclicity is represented by strict precedence along each selected arc; applying an undirected cycle test instead would not exclude all directed-regime distinctions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(R\subseteq V\) be nonempty, and fix \(r\in R\). For binary variables \(z_v\) and \(y_e\), define \(V_z=\{v\in V:z_v=1\}\) and \(E_y=\{e\in E:y_e=1\}\). The selected subgraph \(H=(V_z,E_y)\) is a tree containing every vertex of \(R\) if and only if
\[z_v=1\quad(v\in R),\qquad y_{uv}\le z_u,\quad y_{uv}\le z_v\quad(uv\in E),\]
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}y_e\ge z_v\quad(S\subseteq V,\ v\in S,\ r\notin S),\qquad \sum_{e\in E}y_e=\sum_{v\in V}z_v-1.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Network-Flow Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated directed flow with prescribed node supplies and demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\), and balances \(b_v\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), a feasible network flow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) such that
\[\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=b_v\quad(v\in V).\]
Positive \(b_v\) denotes supply and negative \(b_v\) denotes demand. A feasible-network-flow global constraint holds precisely when its flow variables admit values satisfying all arc bounds and node-balance equalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow respects every arc’s lower and upper bounds and realizes the prescribed net supply or demand at every node.

knowledge_statements.title: Costed Network-Flow Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost channel attached to a feasible capacitated network flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a feasible network-flow system and arc costs \(c_a\in\mathbb{R}\), introduce a cost variable \(C\). The costed network-flow constraint is represented by all flow bounds and node-balance equations together with
\[C=\sum_{a\in A}c_af_a.\]
If a budget \(K\) is imposed, the additional condition is \(C\le K\). If cost is optimized, its optimal value is
\[C^*=\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_af_a: f\text{ satisfies the flow bounds and balances}\right\}.\]
Thus feasibility and cost accounting share the same arc-flow variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A costed flow is a feasible network flow whose total cost is channeled to a variable, optionally bounded or minimized.
assumptions_latex: The feasible-flow system of \(D=(V,A)\) is nonempty.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).

Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with nonnegative capacities \(u_a\), distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and required flow value \(d\ge0\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\) is an infeasibility certificate for a value-\(d\) flow whenever
\[u(\delta^+(S)):=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a<d.\]
Equivalently, a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(d\) exists if and only if
\[u(\delta^+(S))\ge d\quad\text{for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }s\in S\text{ and }t\notin S.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-variable representation of identical-capacity one-dimensional bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let items \(i=1,\ldots,n\) have sizes \(s_i>0\), and let \(m\) candidate bins have common capacity \(C>0\). In the bin-assignment view, each variable \(b_i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) names the bin receiving item \(i\). Feasibility requires
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_i\mathbf{1}[b_i=j]\le C\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
Equivalently, binary variables \(x_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[b_i=j]\) satisfy
\[\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{ij}=1\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}s_ix_{ij}\le C\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each item chooses exactly one of the candidate bins, and the total size assigned to each bin does not exceed its capacity.

Let items \(i=1,\ldots,n\) have sizes \(s_i>0\), and let \(b_i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) assign each item to one of \(m\) bins. Define the load of bin \(j\) by
\[L_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_i\mathbf{1}[b_i=j]\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
The bin-load representation imposes
\[0\le L_j\le C\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
Given the assignments, the load vector is uniquely determined. With binary assignment indicators \(x_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[b_i=j]\), the same channel is
\[L_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_ix_{ij}\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]

Let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate assignment of item \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to bin \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether bin \(j\) is used. The capacity channel is

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For binary assignment indicators \(x_{ij}\), define the cardinality of bin \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) by
\[N_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}.\]
If \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) records bin use, exact usage channeling is
\[y_j\le N_j\le ny_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
Thus \(y_j=1\) if and only if at least one item is assigned to bin \(j\). If explicit cardinality limits \(q_j^-\) and \(q_j^+\) are specified, impose
\[q_j^-y_j\le N_j\le q_j^+y_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each bin's cardinality equals its number of assigned items, and its use indicator is one exactly when that cardinality is positive.

children.title: Capacity–Cardinality Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions between load aggregates and item-count aggregates.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity–Cardinality Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid inequalities coupling each bin’s load, cardinality, and capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose every item size satisfies \(0<s_{\min}\le s_i\le s_{\max}\le C\). For each bin \(j\), let \(N_j=\sum_i x_{ij}\) and \(L_j=\sum_i s_ix_{ij}\). Then
\[s_{\min}N_j\le L_j\le s_{\max}N_j,\qquad L_j\le Cy_j.\]
Consequently,
\[N_j\le \left\lfloor C/s_{\min}\right\rfloor y_j.\]
These inequalities are valid for every integral assignment and couple propagation on load, item count, and bin use; tighter bin-specific size bounds may replace \(s_{\min}\) and \(s_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum and maximum item sizes bound load by cardinality; capacity then bounds how many items a used bin can contain.
assumptions_latex: \(0<s_{\min}\le s_i\le s_{\max}\le C\).
\(L_j\le Cy_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_{\min}N_j\le L_j\le s_{\max}N_j\) and \(N_j\le\lfloor C/s_{\min}\rfloor y_j\).

notation.meaning: global lower and upper item-size bounds

children.title: Packing Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounding structures derived from packing capacity and item structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary lower bounds for identical-capacity one-dimensional bin packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B^*\) be the minimum number of bins of capacity \(C\) needed for items with \(0<s_i\le C\). Every feasible packing satisfies the volume bound
\[B^*\ge \left\lceil\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_i}{C}\right\rceil.\]
Moreover, no bin can contain two items larger than \(C/2\), so
\[B^*\ge \left|\{i:s_i>C/2\}\right|.\]
Thus the combined computable lower bound is the maximum of these two quantities. Any feasible packing using \(B\) bins supplies the upper bound \(B^*\le B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total volume and the number of items exceeding half capacity give lower bounds; any constructed packing gives an upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) and \(C>0\).
\(0<s_i\le C\) for every item \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\lceil\sum_i s_i/C\rceil,\ |\{i:s_i>C/2\}|\}\le B^*\le B\) for every feasible \(B\)-bin packing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation of the assignment formulation for bin packing.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation, and Bounds p. 25

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\) items and \(m\) candidate bins, the assignment formulation uses binary variables \(x_{ij}\) and \(y_j\), minimizes \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}y_j\), and imposes
\[\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{ij}=1\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\]
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_ix_{ij}\le Cy_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\qquad x_{ij}\le y_j\quad(i=1,\ldots,n;\ j=1,\ldots,m).\]
Its continuous packing relaxation replaces integrality by
\[0\le x_{ij}\le1\quad(i=1,\ldots,n;\ j=1,\ldots,m),\qquad 0\le y_j\le1\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\]
while leaving the objective and other constraints unchanged. If \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is the relaxed optimum and \(B^*\) is the integral optimum, then \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le B^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous packing relaxation permits fractional assignment and bin-use variables while retaining the assignment, capacity, linking constraints, and minimization objective; its optimum is a lower bound on the integral optimum.

children.title: Relaxation-Bound Strength
children.top_down_role: Comparative strength of bounds supplied by different packing relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Bound Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-region inclusion orders lower-bound strength for minimization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the feasible set of a minimization problem with objective \(f\), and let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be relaxations satisfying \(X\subseteq P_1\subseteq P_2\). Define \(\beta_k=\inf\{f(x):x\in P_k\}\) and \(z^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X\}\). Then
\[\beta_2\le\beta_1\le z^*.\]
Accordingly, \(P_1\) is at least as strong as \(P_2\) for lower bounding. Strict inclusion need not yield a strictly better bound for a particular objective, although it cannot worsen the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, the smaller relaxation gives a lower bound at least as strong as that from a containing relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P_1\subseteq P_2\).
The same objective \(f\) is minimized over all three sets.
The displayed infima are well-defined in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P_2}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in P_1}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).

children.title: Weight Aggregation

knowledge_statements.title: Weight Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear weight aggregation for a finite-domain knapsack global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite item set \(I\), integer decision variables \(x_i\in D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), and fixed integer weights \(w_i\ge 0\), the aggregate weight variable \(W\) is defined by \[W=\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_i.\] If the knapsack has capacity \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), feasibility additionally requires \(W\le C\). Thus every assignment to the item variables determines exactly one aggregate weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate weight is the weighted sum of selected item quantities; a capacity-constrained knapsack also requires that sum not to exceed its capacity.

\(w_i,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).

Every assignment to the item variables therefore fixes exactly one aggregate profit.

children.title: Weight–Profit Tradeoff Channels
children.top_down_role: Channels connecting resource consumption with aggregate item value.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight–Profit Tradeoff Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Channeling between item decisions and the two aggregate coordinates of a knapsack constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite, with variables \(x_i\in D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), weights \(w_i\ge0\), and profits \(p_i\in\mathbb Z\). A weight–profit channel is the simultaneous system \[W=\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_i,\qquad P=\sum_{i\in I}p_i x_i.\] Consequently the attainable aggregate pairs are exactly \(\mathcal A=\{(\sum_i w_i x_i,\sum_i p_i x_i):x_i\in D_i\}\). Capacity and profit requirements restrict this channel by \(W\le C\) and \(P\ge L\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared item variables channel every feasible selection to one attainable weight–profit pair, on which capacity and profit bounds can be imposed.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and every domain \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) are finite.
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(p_i\in\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((W,P)\in\mathcal A\), with \(W\le C\) and \(P\ge L\) when those bounds are present.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Bound Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound bound filtering using residual capacity and an upper profit bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given current finite domains \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), capacity \(C\), weights \(w_i>0\), profits \(p_i\ge0\), and target \(L\), initialize \(\ell_i=\min D_i\). Let \(R=C-\sum_iw_i\ell_i\); fail if \(R<0\). Replace each upper bound by \(\min\{\max D_i,\ell_i+\lfloor R/w_i\rfloor\}\). Compute any valid upper bound \(U\) on \(\max\{\sum_i p_i x_i:x_i\in D_i,\sum_iw_i x_i\le C\}\), for example the fractional-knapsack relaxation; fail if \(U<L\). Iterate after each domain change and return the resulting domains at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tighten quantities using residual capacity, detect overload, and reject a node when a valid relaxation cannot attain the required profit.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) are finite and nonempty.
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(p_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\).
\(U\) is a valid upper bound under the current domains and capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned domains contain every assignment satisfying \(\sum_iw_ix_i\le C\) and \(\sum_ip_ix_i\ge L\); either failure test certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: capacity remaining after mandatory lower-bound quantities

However, the cited branch-and-bound section does not inspectably establish this particular constraint-propagation algorithm or its fixed-point formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Diffn Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard axis-aligned multidimensional nonoverlap constraint with boundary touching allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) axis-aligned boxes in \(d\) dimensions, let \(o_{ik}\in\mathbb R\) be the origin coordinate and \(s_{ik}\in\mathbb R_{>0}\) the size of box \(i\) on axis \(k\). The constraint \(\operatorname{diffn}((o_i,s_i)_{i=1}^n)\) holds exactly when, for every distinct \(i,j\), \[\bigvee_{k=1}^{d}\bigl(o_{ik}+s_{ik}\le o_{jk}\ \lor\ o_{jk}+s_{jk}\le o_{ik}\bigr).\] Hence every box pair is separated on at least one coordinate axis; equality permits boundary contact without interior overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DIFFN requires every pair of positive-size axis-aligned boxes to be separated along at least one axis, while permitting boundary contact.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(o_{ik}\in\mathbb R\) and \(s_{ik}\in\mathbb R_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every pair of represented boxes has disjoint interiors.

notation.meaning: origin of box i on axis k
positive extent of box i on axis k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard DIFFN semantics for positive-size axis-aligned boxes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula gives a standard positive-size, axis-aligned DIFFN semantics with boundary contact allowed, but no authoritative global-constraint specification is cited. A source is needed to confirm that this is the intended DIFFN variant for the leaf.

children.title: Strict Nonoverlap
children.top_down_role: Nonoverlap regimes excluding boundary contact.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Nonoverlap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-gap separation for closed axis-aligned boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let box \(i\) be \(B_i=\prod_{k=1}^{d}[o_{ik},o_{ik}+s_{ik}]\), where every \(s_{ik}>0\). Boxes \(B_i\) and \(B_j\) satisfy strict nonoverlap when \[\bigvee_{k=1}^{d}\bigl(o_{ik}+s_{ik}<o_{jk}\ \lor\ o_{jk}+s_{jk}<o_{ik}\bigr).\] The strict inequality gives a positive gap on at least one axis, so the boxes are disjoint and cannot touch at a face, edge, or corner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed axis-aligned boxes strictly nonoverlap when a positive gap separates their projections on at least one axis.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(o_{ik}\in\mathbb R\) and \(s_{ik}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\), with positive separation on at least one axis.

notation.meaning: origin and extent of box i on axis k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strict interval separation uses a strict endpoint inequality
local meaning of strict nonoverlap requires authoritative confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict endpoint-separation condition correctly yields a positive gap and disjoint closed boxes. Because strict versus nonstrict nonoverlap terminology varies across sources, an authoritative citation is required to establish the intended local convention.

children.title: Nonstrict Nonoverlap
children.top_down_role: Nonoverlap regimes permitting boundary contact.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstrict Nonoverlap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-disjoint axis-aligned boxes under weak endpoint separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let box \(i\) be \(B_i=\prod_{k=1}^{d}[o_{ik},o_{ik}+s_{ik}]\), where every \(s_{ik}>0\). Boxes \(B_i\) and \(B_j\) satisfy nonstrict nonoverlap when \[\bigvee_{k=1}^{d}\bigl(o_{ik}+s_{ik}\le o_{jk}\ \lor\ o_{jk}+s_{jk}\le o_{ik}\bigr).\] Their interiors are then disjoint. Equality on a separating axis is admissible and represents boundary contact rather than positive-gap separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonstrict nonoverlap requires weak separation on some axis, making interiors disjoint while allowing the boxes to touch.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(o_{ik}\in\mathbb R\) and \(s_{ik}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(B_i)\cap\operatorname{int}(B_j)=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak endpoint separation is the conventional packing nonoverlap predicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Weak separation on at least one axis correctly characterizes interior-disjoint positive-size boxes while allowing contact. An authoritative source is still required because the label nonstrict nonoverlap is convention-dependent.

children.title: Boundary-Touching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric contact cases separating strict from nonstrict interpretations.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Touching Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of touching permitted by weak axis separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let closed axis-aligned boxes \(B_i\) and \(B_j\) have disjoint interiors. They touch at their boundaries exactly when \(B_i\cap B_j\ne\varnothing\). Equivalently, for every axis their closed projections intersect, and on at least one axis an endpoint equality holds: \[o_{ik}+s_{ik}=o_{jk}\quad\text{or}\quad o_{jk}+s_{jk}=o_{ik}.\] The number of axes with nondegenerate projection overlap determines whether contact is through a face, a lower-dimensional edge, or a corner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary touching occurs when box interiors are disjoint but their closed projections meet, with endpoint equality on at least one axis.
assumptions_latex: \(B_i,B_j\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are closed axis-aligned boxes of positive extent.
\(\operatorname{int}(B_i)\cap\operatorname{int}(B_j)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Boundary contact is equivalent to \(B_i\cap B_j\ne\varnothing\), characterized by intersecting projections and at least one endpoint equality.

notation.meaning: origin and extent of box i on axis k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: boundary contact of Cartesian products is determined coordinatewise

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise characterization of boundary contact is plausible for positive-size axis-aligned boxes, but no source supports the face/edge/corner classification or its dimension-dependent terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Axis-Projection Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise nonoverlap reasoning through one-dimensional coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For axis-aligned boxes \(B_i=\prod_{k=1}^{d}I_{ik}\) and \(B_j=\prod_{k=1}^{d}I_{jk}\), their interiors overlap exactly when the interiors of \(I_{ik}\) and \(I_{jk}\) overlap for every axis \(k\). Therefore nonoverlap is equivalent to the existence of an axis with disjoint interval interiors: \[\operatorname{int}(B_i)\cap\operatorname{int}(B_j)=\varnothing\iff\bigvee_{k=1}^{d}\operatorname{int}(I_{ik})\cap\operatorname{int}(I_{jk})=\varnothing.\] Any established separating axis consequently certifies pairwise box nonoverlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boxes overlap only if their projections overlap on every axis; one separating axis therefore certifies nonoverlap.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
Each \(I_{ik}\subseteq\mathbb R\) is a nondegenerate closed interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairwise box nonoverlap is equivalent to interval separation on at least one coordinate axis.

notation.meaning: projection interval of box i on axis k
Cartesian product of the projection intervals of box i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interiors of finite Cartesian products intersect exactly when all coordinate interiors intersect

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cartesian-product projection equivalence is mathematically standard and fits a principle container, but the record lacks the required authoritative constraint-programming citation for its use as axis-projection reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Shape Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: GEOST-style finite representation of a shape by shifted component boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix dimension \(d\). A shape identifier \(q\) is represented by a finite nonempty set \(K_q\) of component boxes. Each component \(r\in K_q\) has a relative offset \(a_{qr}\in\mathbb Z^d\) and positive size \(s_{qr}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^d\). At object origin \(x\in\mathbb Z^d\), the occupied region of shape \(q\) is \[S_q(x)=\bigcup_{r\in K_q}\prod_{k=1}^{d}[x_k+a_{qrk},\,x_k+a_{qrk}+s_{qrk}).\] Thus one shape may encode a nonrectangular orthogonal region as a finite union of shifted boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shape is encoded as a finite union of positive-size component boxes positioned by offsets relative to an object origin.

\(K_q\) is finite and nonempty.
\(a_{qr}\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(s_{qr}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Object Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Shape–Object Channeling
