children.title: Component Selection Configuration
children.top_down_role: Product configurations centered on selecting required, optional, or alternative components.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,A)\) is a finite rooted component tree with root \(r\).
For each nonleaf \(v\), the selected-child bounds satisfy \(0\le \ell_v\le u_v\le |C(v)|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed binary constraints define hierarchy-respecting component selections with bounded child multiplicities.

notation.meaning: one when component v is selected
lower and upper selected-child bounds at v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical rooted product-structure selection template; CP locator is general
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted product hierarchy with parent activation and conditional child-cardinality bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Associate \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\) with each \(v\in V\). A component selection configuration is specified by
\[
z_r=1,
\]
\[
z_c\le z_v\quad(v\in V,c\in C(v)),
\]
and
\[
\ell_v z_v\le\sum_{c\in C(v)}z_c\le u_v z_v
\quad(v\in V\text{ nonleaf}).
\]
Thus every selected child has a selected parent, an unselected parent has no selected children, and each selected nonleaf has between \(\ell_v\) and \(u_v\) selected immediate components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select components in a rooted product tree so every selected child has a selected parent and each active parent obeys its child-count bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Selection Configuration

children.title: Type Assignment Configuration
children.top_down_role: Configurations assigning component instances to admissible types, classes, or variants.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite component set and \(T_v\) is the finite allowed-type set for component \(v\).
The component-selection indicators satisfy \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equations give every selected component exactly one allowed type and every unselected component no type.

notation.meaning: one when component v is selected
one when component v receives type t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical conditional one-of type assignment; generalized-assignment locator is provisional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional one-of assignment of allowed types to selected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Introduce \(y_{vt}\in\{0,1\}\) for \(v\in V\) and \(t\in T_v\). Type assignment is channeled to component selection by
\[
\sum_{t\in T_v}y_{vt}=z_v\quad(v\in V).
\]
Equivalently, a selected component has exactly one type from its allowed domain, while an unselected component has none. If an implementation uses a type variable \(\tau_v\in T_v\cup\{\bot\}\), the same channel is
\[
z_v=0\iff\tau_v=\bot,
\qquad
z_v=1\iff\tau_v\in T_v.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign exactly one allowed type to each selected component and a distinguished absent value, or no active type indicator, to each unselected component.
knowledge_statements.title: Type Assignment Configuration

children.title: Cardinality Configuration
children.top_down_role: Configurations controlling component multiplicities, quotas, and occurrence ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite component set with selection indicators \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\).
\(\mathcal G\subseteq2^V\) is a finite family of component groups.
Each \(G\in\mathcal G\) has integer bounds \(0\le\ell_G\le u_G\le|G|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selection obeys the cardinality configuration exactly when every group count lies within its prescribed interval.

notation.meaning: one when component v is selected
lower and upper selection bounds for group G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-cardinality constraint over Boolean selection variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-and-upper cardinality restrictions on arbitrary finite component groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(G\in\mathcal G\), define the selected-component count
\[
n_G=\sum_{v\in G}z_v.
\]
The cardinality configuration predicate is
\[
\ell_G\le n_G\le u_G\quad(G\in\mathcal G).
\]
The special cases \(\ell_G=u_G=1\), \((\ell_G,u_G)=(0,1)\), and \(\ell_G=1,u_G=|G|\) respectively express exactly-one, at-most-one, and at-least-one selection. Groups may overlap; every displayed bound must then hold simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each designated component group, require the number of selected members to lie between specified integer lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Configuration

children.title: Cross-Level Configuration Channeling
children.top_down_role: Links among component presence, assigned type, and permitted multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Level Configuration Channeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-count channeling between branch nodes and selected terminal components in their rooted subtrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(v\in V\), impose
\[
q_v=\sum_{\ell\in L(v)}z_\ell
\]
and
\[
z_v=1\iff q_v\ge1.
\]
Because \(0\le q_v\le|L(v)|\), an equivalent linear channel is
\[
z_v\le q_v\le |L(v)|z_v.
\]
For every nonleaf \(v\), the counts can be propagated recursively by
\[
q_v=\sum_{c\in C(v)}q_c.
\]
These constraints synchronize terminal selections, aggregate counts, and activation indicators across hierarchy levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activate a hierarchy node exactly when at least one terminal component in its subtree is selected, and propagate selected-terminal counts upward through the product tree.
assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,A)\) is a finite rooted tree, and \(C(v)\) is the set of children of \(v\).
\(L(v)\) is the set of terminal vertices in the subtree rooted at \(v\), including \(v\) itself when \(v\) is terminal.
\(z_v\in\{0,1\}\) indicates activation and \(q_v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) counts selected terminals in \(L(v)\).
Every active branch is required to contain an active terminal component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The channel makes activation equivalent to a positive selected-terminal count at every hierarchy level.

notation.meaning: terminal vertices in the subtree rooted at v
number of selected terminal vertices in the subtree rooted at v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Boolean-count channel across a configuration hierarchy; exact locator is general

children.title: Compatibility Configuration
children.top_down_role: Configurations governed by permitted component, option, or type combinations.

assumptions_latex: \(I,J\) are finite source and support component sets.
\(C(i)\subseteq J\) is the set of components compatible with \(i\in I\).
Selection indicators satisfy \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected source component has at least one selected component from its compatibility set.

notation.meaning: one when component v is selected
components compatible with source component i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical implication-to-supported-choice compatibility constraint; CP locator is general
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed compatibility requiring selected support for each selected source component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The compatibility configuration predicate is
\[
z_i\le\sum_{j\in C(i)}z_j\quad(i\in I).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
z_i=1\Longrightarrow\bigvee_{j\in C(i)}(z_j=1).
\]
If compatibility means that every selected pair across two component classes must be allowed, let \(R\subseteq I\times J\) be the allowed-pair relation. Then the pairwise form is
\[
z_i+z_j\le1\quad((i,j)\in(I\times J)\setminus R).
\]
The supported-choice and allowed-pair forms encode respectively existential and universal interpretations of compatibility and must not be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Require each selected source component to have selected compatible support, or forbid every selected cross-class pair absent from the allowed compatibility relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility Configuration

children.title: Exclusion Configuration
children.top_down_role: Configurations governed by forbidden combinations, mutual exclusions, or incompatibility groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Exclusion Configuration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise and higher-order exclusion predicates for selected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Pairwise exclusion is imposed by
\[
z_i+z_j\le1\quad(\{i,j\}\in E).
\]
For each higher-order forbidden set \(H\in\mathcal H\), exclusion of the complete combination is imposed by
\[
\sum_{v\in H}z_v\le |H|-1.
\]
This constraint forbids simultaneous selection of all members of \(H\) but permits every proper subset. If at most one member of \(H\) may instead be selected, the correct stronger constraint is
\[
\sum_{v\in H}z_v\le1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forbid conflicting component pairs, forbid complete higher-order combinations, or impose the stronger at-most-one rule when required.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite component set with indicators \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\).
\(E\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in V,i\ne j\}\) is a pairwise conflict set.
\(\mathcal H\subseteq\{H\subseteq V:|H|\ge3\}\) is a family of higher-order jointly forbidden component sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities prevent every declared pairwise or higher-order forbidden combination.

notation.meaning: one when component v is selected
family of higher-order jointly forbidden sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conflict and forbidden-set inequalities over Boolean choices

children.title: Compatibility–Exclusion Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of positive compatibility requirements and negative exclusion restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility–Exclusion Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective compatibility after pairwise exclusions remove nominal supporting choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose compatibility requires
\[
z_i\le\sum_{j\in C(i)}z_j
\]
and exclusion requires
\[
z_i+z_j\le1\quad(j\in X(i)).
\]
Under these exclusion constraints, the compatibility inequality is equivalent to
\[
z_i\le\sum_{j\in C(i)\setminus X(i)}z_j.
\]
Thus the conjunction of the original compatibility inequality and the exclusions is equivalent to the conjunction of the reduced compatibility inequality and the same exclusions. Consequently, if \(C(i)\subseteq X(i)\), propagation forces \(z_i=0\); if another constraint forces \(z_i=1\), the configuration is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: While retaining the exclusion constraints, remove excluded choices from each compatibility set; a selected component then requires at least one selected compatible, nonexcluded support.
assumptions_latex: \(I,J\) are finite component sets and \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\).
\(C(i)\subseteq J\) contains the nominal supports compatible with \(i\in I\).
\(X(i)\subseteq J\) contains supports excluded whenever \(i\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the exclusion constraints, compatibility for \(i\) is equivalent to requiring selected support in \(C(i)\setminus X(i)\).

notation.meaning: nominal compatible supports for source i
supports excluded when source i is selected

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct logical reduction of compatibility support under retained pairwise exclusions; locator is general

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite set of selectable components and \(R\) is a finite set of resources.
Each component \(i\in I\) has consumption \(a_{ri}\ge 0\) for every \(r\in R\).
The feasible configuration set \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I}\) encodes all structural, compatibility, and exclusion constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A resource-balanced configuration is any minimizer of \(\Delta\) over the displayed feasible system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax balancing of finite resource use within a feasible product configuration.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive scales \(s_r>0\), a resource-balanced configuration is a pair \((x,\Delta)\) satisfying \(x\in F\), \(\Delta\ge 0\), and
\[
-\Delta s_r\le \sum_{i\in I}a_{ri}x_i-b_r\le \Delta s_r\qquad(r\in R),
\]
with \(\Delta\) minimal. Thus component choices remain feasible while the largest normalized deviation of aggregate resource use from its target is minimized. If only upper capacities are prescribed, one may set \(b_r\) to the desired load and retain the upper-deviation inequalities appropriate to the application.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible component selection is resource-balanced when it minimizes the largest normalized deviation of aggregate resource consumption from prescribed target levels.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Balanced Configuration

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax definition is mathematically coherent and the content kind fits, but the cited resource-allocation section does not specifically support this product-configuration balancing template or its target-deviation formulation.

children.title: Open Product Configuration
children.top_down_role: Configuration settings where component sets, option catalogs, or structural choices remain extensible.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set of currently known component variables with finite domains.
\(C\) is a constraint set over \(V\), and \(E\) is a specified class of admissible future extensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The configuration is open precisely when every committed assignment has at least one admissible consistent completion after extension.

notation.meaning: an admissible extension introducing variables and constraints
solution set of a constraint system

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extension-based definition of openness for constraint configurations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension-based openness for partial finite-domain product configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An open product configuration is a partial assignment \(p\) on variables \(U\subseteq V\) such that
\[
\forall e=(W,C_e)\in E\;\exists q\in\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup C_e):\quad q|_U=p,
\]
whenever \(C\cup C_e\) belongs to the declared admissible extension class. The quantifier over \(E\) is part of the template: it may restrict future modules, interfaces, or parameter domains. Openness therefore means that present commitments are preserved and remain extendable under every extension covered by the specification; it does not assert compatibility with arbitrary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open configuration preserves current commitments while guaranteeing a valid completion for every future extension admitted by its declared extension class.
knowledge_statements.title: Open Product Configuration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, but universal extendability over every admissible future extension is a strong, specification-dependent meaning of open configuration and has no cited source.

children.title: Reconfigurable Product Templates
children.top_down_role: Product models supporting controlled changes to an existing valid configuration.

assumptions_latex: \(T=\{0,\ldots,m\}\) is a finite sequence of configuration stages.
Each stage \(t\in T\) has a feasible set \(F_t\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I_t}\).
For consecutive stages, \(c_t(x^{t-1},x^t)\ge 0\) is a specified reconfiguration cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reconfigurable product template is the feasible multistage system together with its transition relation and transition-cost model.

notation.meaning: allowed transition relation from stage t-1 to t

review_flags: reconfiguration semantics require domain-specific source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-stage template with feasible configurations and explicitly constrained changes.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Multiple plant, product and period models p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A reconfigurable product template consists of stage-feasible sets \(F_t\), transition relations \(K_t\subseteq F_{t-1}\times F_t\), and transition costs \(c_t\). Its admissible evolutions are
\[
\mathcal R=\{(x^0,\ldots,x^m):x^t\in F_t\ (t\in T),\ (x^{t-1},x^t)\in K_t\ (t=1,\ldots,m)\}.
\]
For an admissible evolution, \(C_{\mathrm{chg}}=\sum_{t=1}^{m}c_t(x^{t-1},x^t)\). Persistence, replacement, and bounded-change requirements must be represented explicitly in the relations \(K_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reconfigurable template specifies feasible configurations at each stage, allowed transitions between stages, and the total cost of changing the product.
knowledge_statements.title: Reconfigurable Product Templates

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Multiple plant, product and period models p. 45

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-stage representation is coherent and definition is an appropriate kind, but the cited multiperiod-modeling section does not establish the claimed product-template and transition semantics.

children.title: Configuration Evolution Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Persistence, change-cost, and validity boundaries across successive product configurations.

assumptions_latex: \(V_t\), \(D_t\), and \(C_t\) describe the variables, domains, and constraints at version \(t\).
Each update is applied atomically and returns either acceptance or rejection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is correct when accepted updates produce exactly the declared successor model and rejected updates leave the previous model unchanged.

notation.meaning: configuration model state at version t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: transactional update contract for evolving constraint models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transactional interface contract for finite-domain configuration-model evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A configuration evolution interface is correct if every update \(u_t\) has a declared transformation \(U_{u_t}\) and satisfies
\[
\operatorname{accept}(M_t,u_t)\Longrightarrow M_{t+1}=U_{u_t}(M_t),
\qquad
\operatorname{reject}(M_t,u_t)\Longrightarrow M_{t+1}=M_t.
\]
For an accepted update, all added, removed, or modified variables, domains, and constraints must occur exactly as specified by \(U_{u_t}\), and the interface must expose whether a retained assignment \(p\) remains extendable, namely whether \(\{q\in\operatorname{Sol}(M_{t+1}):q|_{\operatorname{dom}(p)}=p\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A configuration-evolution interface applies declared model updates atomically and reports whether retained decisions still extend to a solution of the updated model.
knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Evolution Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed transactional correctness contract. The extendability query also requires an explicit condition that every variable in the retained assignment remains present in the successor model. The condition kind is plausible for an interface-correctness leaf but needs domain-specific support.

children.title: Constraint-Specific Solver Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces needed to execute, explain, decompose, and relax global propagators without duplicating general solver-search architecture.

children.title: Matching State Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Incremental state retained for matching-based global propagators across domain changes.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(X\cup V,E)\) is the current bipartite value graph, with \((i,v)\in E\) exactly when \(v\in D_i\).
\(M\subseteq E\) is a matching valid before a finite set of domain-edge deletions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained state is valid exactly when the returned \(M'\) is a maximum matching of the updated value graph.
review_flags: incremental maintenance details extend beyond the cited matching section
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental maximum-matching state for bipartite value graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete invalid edges from \(G\) and from \(M\). For each newly exposed vertex \(i\in X\), search the alternating graph of the updated graph \(G'\) for an \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\). If one is found, replace \(M\) by \(M\triangle P\); otherwise retain the current matching and report that no augmentation from \(i\) exists. Continue until every exposed vertex has been processed. Return the resulting matching \(M'\), together with the alternating-search labels needed by the propagator. The state invariant is that \(M'\) is a maximum matching of \(G'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After domain-edge deletion, remove invalid matched edges and repair the matching through augmenting paths until a maximum matching of the updated value graph is restored.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching State Maintenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The citation supports bipartite matching generally, not this incremental state-maintenance algorithm. Processing each initially exposed vertex only once does not explicitly guarantee repeated augmenting-path searches until no augmenting path remains, so the asserted maximum-matching invariant is insufficiently justified.

children.title: Flow State Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Incremental residual, capacity, and feasibility state retained by flow-based propagators.

assumptions_latex: \(N=(V,A,\ell,u,b)\) is a finite capacitated network with node balances \(b\).
A feasible flow \(f\) is stored before capacities, bounds, or balances receive a finite update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maintenance succeeds exactly when it returns a flow satisfying every updated bound and node-balance equation; otherwise it returns an infeasibility cut certificate.

notation.meaning: excess at vertex v after an update

review_flags: incremental repair procedure requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental feasibility repair for a capacitated network flow.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First clamp each changed arc flow to its updated interval \([\ell_a,u_a]\), producing node excesses and deficits. Construct the residual network \(N_f\), including forward residual capacity \(u_a-f_a\) and backward residual capacity \(f_a-\ell_a\). Repeatedly send residual flow from vertices with \(e(v)>0\) to vertices with \(e(v)<0\) until all imbalances vanish. Return the repaired \(f\). If no residual path can discharge a positive excess, return the residual reachable set \(S\); the corresponding saturated cut certifies that the updated balance requirements cannot be met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a network update, clamp invalid arc flows and route resulting imbalances through residual paths, returning either a repaired feasible flow or an infeasibility cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow State Maintenance

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited max-flow material does not specifically support the proposed repair procedure for arbitrary changes to lower bounds, upper bounds, and node balances. The excess convention and the balance terms required for the claimed cut certificate are not defined sufficiently to validate the conclusion.

children.title: Residual-Network State Sharing
children.top_down_role: Reusable residual structures and invalidation boundaries connecting matching-based and flow-based maintenance.

assumptions_latex: Two propagator views encode the same capacitated network and stored feasible flow \(f\).
All state changes are serialized as atomic capacity or flow updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shared residual state is sound when every client observes residual capacities derived from the same current flow and current bounds.

notation.meaning: residual capacity of a forward arc
residual capacity of the corresponding backward arc

review_flags: state-sharing invariant is only indirectly supported by the cited flow material
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency invariant for propagators sharing one residual-network representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every original arc \(a\), the shared residual state must satisfy
\[
r_f(a)=u_a-f_a\ge 0,
\qquad
r_f(\bar a)=f_a-\ell_a\ge 0.
\]
An atomic update of \(f_a\), \(\ell_a\), or \(u_a\) must update both residual capacities before any client performs reachability, augmentation, or cut analysis. A client may cache search labels but must invalidate every label whose correctness depends on a changed residual arc. Consequently, all clients reason about one residual graph \(G_f\), and a residual path or cut computed after synchronization is valid for the common network state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagators may share a residual network only when every arc update is atomic and all clients see residual capacities derived from the same flow and bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Network State Sharing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-capacity equations are standard, but the cited network-flow section does not support the concurrency, atomic-update, cache-invalidation, or multi-client state-sharing contract asserted here.

children.title: Tuple-Residue State
children.top_down_role: Remembered tuple supports used to accelerate repeated extensional-constraint checks.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite table of allowed tuples over variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\).
Each variable has a current finite domain \(D_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residue map is valid when every stored tuple is either a current support for its indexed literal or is explicitly marked stale.

notation.meaning: residue stored for literal Xi equals a

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional residue invariant for extensional-constraint propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cached tuple supports for an allowed-table constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the currently valid tuples by
\[
T_D=\{\tau\in T:\tau_j\in D_j\text{ for every }j\},
\qquad
S_{i,a}=\{\tau\in T_D:\tau_i=a\}.
\]
A tuple-residue state is a partial map \(\rho\) assigning to each literal \((X_i=a)\) either a tuple \(\rho(i,a)\in S_{i,a}\) or a stale marker. A stored tuple is only a witness cache: after any domain deletion it must be revalidated. If it is stale, the propagator searches for another member of \(S_{i,a}\); failure establishes that \(a\) has no table support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tuple residue caches one supporting allowed tuple per variable-value literal, with stale residues revalidated or replaced after domain changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Tuple-Residue State

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cached-support definition is coherent and fits the state leaf, but no source is supplied for the residue convention, stale-marker semantics, or propagation consequence.

children.title: Bitset State
children.top_down_role: Packed tuple-compatibility state used for word-level filtering and support queries.

assumptions_latex: \(T=\{\tau^1,\ldots,\tau^m\}\) is a fixed indexed allowed-tuple table.
The machine word size is \(w\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bitset state is correct when set bits correspond exactly to tuples compatible with every current domain.

notation.meaning: static support bitset for literal Xi equals a
number of machine words storing a table bitset

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard indexed-bitset representation of extensional supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-word representation of currently valid table tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every literal \((X_i=a)\), define a static bitset by
\[
B_{i,a}[k]=1\iff \tau^k_i=a.
\]
The current-live bitset is
\[
L=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}\left(\bigvee_{a\in D_i}B_{i,a}\right).
\]
Thus \(L[k]=1\) exactly when tuple \(\tau^k\) is compatible with all current domains. Each bitset occupies \(q=\lceil m/w\rceil\) words. Domain deletion is reflected by recomputing or incrementally intersecting the affected masks, and literal \((X_i=a)\) has support exactly when \(L\wedge B_{i,a}\ne 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static bitsets index tuples supporting each literal, while a live bitset marks exactly the allowed tuples compatible with all current domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Bitset State

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bitset identities are mathematically consistent and representation is the correct content kind, but no inspectable source supports this extensional-constraint representation or its maintenance claims.

children.title: Residue–Bitset Integration
children.top_down_role: Hybrid state organizations combining remembered supports with packed compatibility indexes.

assumptions_latex: A correct live-tuple bitset \(L\) and support bitsets \(B_{i,a}\) are maintained.
Each residue \(\rho(i,a)\) is either a tuple index or a stale marker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integrated update removes exactly those literals whose support intersection with the live bitset is empty.

notation.meaning: support bitset for literal Xi equals a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrated support checking for an allowed-table propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After each domain change, update \(L\). For every affected literal \((X_i=a)\), first test whether the cached index \(k=\rho(i,a)\) satisfies \(L[k]=B_{i,a}[k]=1\). If so, retain the residue. Otherwise compute
\[
W=L\wedge B_{i,a}.
\]
If \(W=0\), delete \(a\) from \(D_i\). If \(W\ne 0\), choose any set bit \(k\) of \(W\), set \(\rho(i,a)=k\), and retain \(a\). Repeat until no deletion changes \(L\); output the resulting domains, live bitset, and residues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate each cached support against the live bitset; on failure, find a new set bit or delete the unsupported value, repeating to a fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Residue–Bitset Integration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is plausible and its content kind fits, but no source supports the combined residue-bitset procedure, fixpoint requirement, or exact-support conclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)\) is a finite automaton, with possibly partial transition relation \(\delta\).

Variables \(X_1,
\ldots,X_n\) have finite domains contained in \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state is correct when forward and backward sets equal the states reachable through domain-compatible prefixes and suffixes, respectively.

notation.meaning: states reachable after positions 1 through i
states from which an accepting suffix after position i exists

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: layered automaton reachability used by regular-language propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered forward-backward state for a finite-automaton constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The automaton reachability state is defined by \(R_0=\{q_0\}\), \(S_n=F\), and
\[
R_i=\{q'\in Q:\exists q\in R_{i-1},\exists a\in D_i,
(q,a,q')\in\delta\},
\]
\[
S_{i-1}=\{q\in Q:\exists a\in D_i,\exists q'\in S_i,
(q,a,q')\in\delta\}.
\]
A value \(a\in D_i\) is supported exactly when there exist \(q\in R_{i-1}\) and \(q'\in S_i\) with \((q,a,q')\in\delta\). Incremental maintenance recomputes every layer whose predecessor, successor, or contributing domain changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward state sets record domain-compatible automaton reachability; a value survives exactly when it labels a transition joining compatible prefix and suffix states.
knowledge_statements.title: Automaton Reachability State

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-backward reachability equations are coherent for a finite transition relation and representation fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for the exact support characterization or incremental-maintenance claim.

assumptions_latex: Activities form a finite set \(J\), with start variables \(s_j\), positive durations \(p_j\), and nonnegative demands \(r_j\).
A renewable resource has capacity \(C\), and each \(s_j\) has current bounds \([\underline s_j,\overline s_j]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource-profile state is valid when its stored compulsory load equals the displayed sum at every relevant time point.

notation.meaning: compulsory execution interval of activity j
compulsory resource load at time t

review_flags: scheduling-profile specialization is only indirectly supported by the resource-allocation locator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compulsory-part profile for one discrete renewable resource.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each activity \(j\), define its compulsory interval by
\[
K_j=[\overline s_j,\underline s_j+p_j)
\]
when \(\overline s_j<\underline s_j+p_j\), and let \(K_j=\varnothing\) otherwise. The compulsory resource profile is
\[
P(t)=\sum_{j\in J:\,t\in K_j}r_j.
\]
It is stored as breakpoints with constant load between consecutive breakpoints. Any bound change that modifies \(K_j\) removes the old contribution and adds the new one. If \(P(t)>C\) for some \(t\), the current domains are infeasible; otherwise the profile is a lower bound on unavoidable resource use.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource-profile state stores the aggregate demand of all compulsory activity parts, updating breakpoints as start bounds change and detecting capacity overloads.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Profile State

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compulsory-part profile is mathematically coherent and representation fits the state container, but the generic resource-allocation citation does not support the scheduling-specific interval, overload, breakpoint, or incremental-update claims.

children.title: Hall-Set Explanations
children.top_down_role: Propagation reasons organized around Hall sets, value scarcity, and cardinality bottlenecks.

knowledge_statements.title: Hall-Set Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explanation certificate for Hall-set propagation of an all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables \(x_i\), \(i\in I\), have finite domains \(D_i\), and impose \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_i:i\in I)\). A Hall-set explanation consists of \(S\subseteq I\) and \(H=\bigcup_{i\in S}D_i\) satisfying \(|H|=|S|\). Every satisfying assignment must assign the variables indexed by \(S\) bijectively to \(H\); consequently, for each \(j\in I\setminus S\), every value \(a\in D_j\cap H\) is unsupported and may be removed. The premises \(D_i\subseteq H\) for all \(i\in S\), together with all-different, therefore certify each conclusion \(x_j\ne a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight Hall set consumes all its neighboring values, certifying removal of those values from every variable outside the set.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and every \(D_i\) are finite.
\(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_i:i\in I)\) is enforced.
\(S\subseteq I\) satisfies \(|\bigcup_{i\in S}D_i|=|S|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\notin D_j\) is valid for every \(j\in I\setminus S\) and \(a\in D_j\cap H\).

notation.meaning: Union of the domains indexed by S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hall-set certificate is mathematically plausible and the certificate kind fits, but no source supports the explanation interface. The conclusion should ultimately be stated as the valid inference x_j≠a rather than a∉D_j, which otherwise conflates the pre-propagation and updated domains.

children.title: Matching-Certificate Explanations
children.top_down_role: Reasons derived from matching structure, alternating reachability, or matching failure.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Certificate Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching-based certificate for inconsistency or value removal in all-different propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the bipartite value graph \(G=(I\cup V,E)\), where \((i,a)\in E\) exactly when \(a\in D_i\). Inconsistency is certified by a set \(S\subseteq I\) with \(|N_G(S)|<|S|\). To certify removal of \(a\in D_i\), force \((i,a)\), delete \(i\) and \(a\), and let \(G_{i,a}\) be the residual graph. A set \(S\subseteq I\setminus\{i\}\) satisfying \(|N_{G_{i,a}}(S)|<|S|\) proves that no matching covering all variables can contain \((i,a)\), hence \(x_i\ne a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deficient neighborhood in the value graph certifies failure; after forcing an edge, such a deficiency certifies that the corresponding value is unsupported.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains are finite.
Feasibility of the all-different constraint is represented by a matching covering all variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|N_{G_{i,a}}(S)|<|S|\) implies that \(x_i=a\) has no support.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-matching deficiency is a sound finite-domain certificate and the content kind fits, but the matching-based explanation and forced-edge construction have no cited source.

children.title: Hall–Matching Certificate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections and translation boundaries between Hall-based reasons and matching-derived certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Hall–Matching Certificate Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bipartite correspondence underlying all-different failure certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(I\cup V,E)\), the following are equivalent: there is no matching covering \(I\); there exists \(S\subseteq I\) with \(|N_G(S)|<|S|\); and the standard unit-capacity matching network has an \(s\)-\(t\) cut of capacity less than \(|I|\). Thus a Hall-deficient set, a maximum matching of cardinality below \(|I|\), and a subcritical minimum cut are mutually convertible infeasibility certificates for the associated all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hall deficiency, failure of a variable-covering matching, and a matching-network cut below the required cardinality are equivalent certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(I\cup V,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph.
The matching network assigns unit capacities to source-variable, variable-value, and value-sink arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(G)<|I|\iff \exists S\subseteq I:\ |N_G(S)|<|S|\iff \lambda_{s,t}<|I|\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cut capacity in the matching network.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Cut Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cut explanations for propagation in capacitated-flow representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have arc capacities \(u_a\ge0\), source \(s\), sink \(t\), and required flow value \(F\). For any cut \(S\subset V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), the inequality \(F\le\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\) is necessary. Hence bounds implying \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a<F\) form a verifiable conflict explanation. More generally, if assuming a candidate literal tightens capacities so that a cut has capacity below \(F\), the same cut and the capacity-bound literals certify deletion of that literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut whose available capacity is below the required flow explains infeasibility or removal of any assumption that creates the shortfall.
assumptions_latex: The represented constraint requires an \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value at least \(F\).
All relevant arc capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a<F\) certifies that the required flow is infeasible.

notation.meaning: Current upper capacity of arc a.

children.title: Automaton Explanations
children.top_down_role: Reasons based on state reachability, transition support, and accepted-path loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Automaton Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability-cut explanations for regular constraints represented by layered automata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent an automaton constraint on \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) by its layered graph, whose arcs from layer \(k-1\) to \(k\) are labeled by values in \(D_k\). A value \(a\in D_k\) is supported exactly when an initial-to-accepting path uses an arc at layer \(k\) labeled \(a\). If every such path contains an arc disabled by a current domain exclusion, the disabled arcs form a path cut. The corresponding exclusions certify \(x_k\ne a\); a cut meeting every initial-to-accepting path certifies failure of the entire constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disabled transitions that cut every relevant accepting path certify either an unsupported value or total automaton-constraint failure.
assumptions_latex: The automaton and sequence length are finite.
Layered arcs are enabled exactly by current variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absence of an enabled accepting path through label \(a\) at layer \(k\) certifies \(x_k\ne a\).

notation.meaning: Current domain at sequence position k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The layered-path support characterization and cut explanation are plausible and certificate is the correct kind, but no source supports the explanation construction or its precise domain-literal interpretation.

children.title: Table Explanations
children.top_down_role: Reasons based on surviving tuples, support loss, and tuple incompatibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Table Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional no-support explanations for table constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq A_1\times\cdots\times A_n\) be the allowed tuples and let \(D_i\subseteq A_i\) be current domains. For \(a\in D_k\), define \(T_{k,a}=\{t\in T:t_k=a\}\). A table explanation for deleting \(a\) selects, for every \(t\in T_{k,a}\), an index \(i(t)\) such that \(t_{i(t)}\notin D_{i(t)}\). The conjunction of these witnessed domain exclusions intersects every potential supporting tuple, so no tuple consistent with all current domains assigns \(a\) to \(x_k\), certifying \(x_k\ne a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One excluded component from every allowed tuple containing a candidate value forms a checkable no-support explanation for deleting that value.
assumptions_latex: The allowed-tuple set \(T\) is finite.
Current domains satisfy \(D_i\subseteq A_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall t\in T_{k,a}\ \exists i:\ t_i\notin D_i\) implies that \(a\) is unsupported for \(x_k\).

notation.meaning: Allowed tuples assigning a to position k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tuple-hitting no-support certificate is precise and appropriate for the leaf, but it lacks a source for table-constraint explanations.

children.title: Representation-Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions affecting whether explanations transfer effectively between automaton and table representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on transferring explanations between automaton and explicit-table representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Explanation validity transfers between an automaton and a table only when both encode the same relation under the same current domains: any certificate must still imply absence of a supporting tuple or accepting path. Certificate size need not transfer polynomially. A layered deterministic automaton may represent exponentially many accepted tuples with polynomially many states and arcs, so expanding an automaton cut into tuple-by-tuple exclusions can be exponential. Conversely, compiling an arbitrary table into a deterministic automaton can require a number of prefix states proportional to the number of distinct tuple prefixes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent representations preserve explanation validity, but conversion can expand a compact path cut or tuple witness exponentially.
assumptions_latex: The automaton and table encode the same finite-arity relation.
Explanation size is measured by listed transitions, tuples, or domain literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semantic equivalence does not imply polynomial-size transfer of explanation certificates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic-validity distinction is plausible, but the claimed exponential certificate-conversion boundary requires a cited construction or lower-bound family. Failure_boundary is the correct content kind.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Overload Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-energy certificate for infeasibility of a cumulative resource constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider nonpreemptive activities with start times \(s_i\), durations \(p_i>0\), demands \(r_i\ge0\), and renewable capacity \(C\). For an interval \([a,b)\), let \(e_i(a,b)\) be a valid lower bound on the processing energy of activity \(i\) that must occur inside that interval under current start-time bounds. If \(\sum_i r_i e_i(a,b)>C(b-a)\), no schedule satisfying those bounds can respect capacity. The interval, the contributing activities, and the bounds establishing each \(e_i(a,b)\) constitute a directly checkable overload explanation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory activity energy exceeding an interval's capacity certifies infeasibility, with the responsible bounds serving as the explanation literals.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive with fixed positive durations.
At every time, total active demand may not exceed \(C\).
Each \(e_i(a,b)\) is a sound lower bound on processing inside \([a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i r_i e_i(a,b)>C(b-a)\) certifies infeasibility under the cited bounds.

notation.meaning: Mandatory processing of activity i within the interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The overload inequality is sound if e_i(a,b) denotes mandatory processing time, with r_i e_i(a,b) its resource energy. A scheduling source is required for the exact bound and explanation-literal interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Decompositions of Global Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended linear formulation and its continuous relaxation for a finite-domain global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) be a global constraint, and let \(X_R\) be the set of its one-hot encodings. A linear decomposition is a mixed-integer system \(Ay+Bz\le b\) whose feasible points, with all prescribed integrality restrictions imposed, satisfy \(\operatorname{proj}_y\{(y,z):Ay+Bz\le b,\ (y,z)\text{ integral as prescribed}\}=X_R\). Dropping all prescribed integrality restrictions gives the projected continuous relaxation \(P=\operatorname{proj}_y\{(y,z):Ay+Bz\le b\}\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\subseteq P\), and the decomposition is ideal exactly when \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear decomposition projects its prescribed integral feasible points to the encoded global relation. Dropping all integrality restrictions gives an outer relaxation of the relation's convex hull, and the decomposition is ideal when the two sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: Every domain \(D_i\) is finite.
The one-hot encoding and all prescribed integral variables are fixed.
The mixed-integer formulation projects exactly to \(X_R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\subseteq P\), with equality exactly when the decomposition is ideal.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected continuous flow relaxation of a global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_R\) be the assignment encodings satisfying a global constraint. Suppose a directed network uses flow variables \(f\), assignment variables \(y\), balance equations \(Af=b\), integral bounds \(0\le f\le u\), and linking equations \(L_f f+L_y y=d\), and suppose its prescribed integral feasible points project exactly to \(X_R\). The network-flow relaxation is \(P=\operatorname{proj}_y\{(f,y):Af=b,\ 0\le f\le u,\ L_f f+L_y y=d\}\), obtained by omitting the prescribed integrality restrictions. Then \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\subseteq P\). If the full linked constraint matrix, including the linking rows and bound representation, is totally unimodular and all right-hand sides are integral, the extended polyhedron is integral; together with exact encoding, this implies \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\). Total unimodularity of the node-arc incidence matrix alone does not establish this conclusion when the linking rows destroy total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-flow relaxation projects the continuous full linked flow formulation onto assignment variables. It contains the convex hull of feasible assignments and is ideal under exact encoding when the complete linked formulation, not merely its incidence submatrix, has the required integrality property.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed integral network formulation projects exactly to \(X_R\).
Capacities, balances, and other right-hand sides are integral when total unimodularity is invoked.
All linking constraints are included when assessing total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\subseteq P\), and \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\) under exact encoding and integrality of the full extended polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Diagram Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-flow relaxation induced by a layered decision diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(N,A)\) be a layered acyclic decision diagram whose root-to-terminal paths encode a superset \(R_B\) of the feasible assignments \(R\). Assign nonnegative arc flows \(f_a\), impose one unit of root-to-terminal flow and conservation at internal nodes, and link \(y_{i,v}=\sum_{a\in A_i(v)}f_a\), where \(A_i(v)\) contains layer-\(i\) arcs labeled \(v\). The projected path-flow polytope contains \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\). It equals \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\) when the diagram represents exactly \(R\); merging states or adding arcs generally yields a weaker outer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit flow through a layered decision diagram gives an assignment relaxation, exact for an exact diagram and weaker after state merging or arc addition.
assumptions_latex: The decision diagram is finite, layered, and acyclic.
Every feasible assignment has a root-to-terminal path in the diagram.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(X_R)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_y(P_B)\), with equality when the diagram represents exactly \(R\).

notation.meaning: Layer-i arcs labeled by value v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-flow formulation, outer-relaxation inclusion, and exact-diagram equality are mathematically plausible, and representation is the correct kind. No source supports the decision-diagram formulation or state-merging claim.

children.title: Resource Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations based on aggregate capacity, load, or resource-profile information.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-only relaxation for cumulative scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For activities with start variables \(s_i\), durations \(p_i>0\), demands \(r_i\ge0\), and resource capacity \(C\), introduce occupancy variables \(z_{it}\in[0,1]\) indicating whether activity \(i\) executes at time \(t\). A resource relaxation retains \(\sum_i r_i z_{it}\le C\) for every time period and suitable equations such as \(\sum_t z_{it}=p_i\), while dropping some sequencing, contiguity, or integrality requirements connecting \(z_{it}\) to \(s_i\). Every feasible nonpreemptive schedule maps into this polyhedron, so violation of any retained capacity or aggregate-resource inequality is a valid infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing contiguity or integrality while retaining timewise capacity produces an outer approximation of feasible resource schedules.
assumptions_latex: Time is discretized into a finite horizon.
Durations and demands are nonnegative, with \(p_i>0\).
The retained linking equations are valid for every feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The occupancy vector of every feasible schedule satisfies \(\sum_i r_i z_{it}\le C\) and \(\sum_t z_{it}=p_i\).

notation.meaning: Relaxed occupancy of activity i at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The occupancy formulation gives a plausible outer relaxation under the stated discrete-time assumptions, and representation fits the leaf. A source and a more specific declaration of which linking, contiguity, and integrality conditions are retained are needed before the precise relaxation can be relied upon.

children.title: Energy Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations based on workload energy within scheduling intervals or resource windows.

assumptions_latex: Each activity \(i\in I\) has release time \(r_i\), deadline \(d_i\), processing time \(p_i\ge 0\), and constant demand \(q_i\ge 0\).
A renewable resource has constant capacity \(C\), and activities are nonpreemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in I}q_i e_i(a,b)\le C(b-a)\) for every \(a<b\).

notation.meaning: Minimum processing time of activity i forced into interval [a,b].

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard energetic necessary condition for a cumulative scheduling constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpreemptive cumulative-resource energetic relaxation over arbitrary time intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), define the compulsory energy contribution of activity \(i\) by \[e_i(a,b)=\max\!\left\{0,\ p_i-\max(0,a-r_i)-\max(0,d_i-b)\right\}.\] Any feasible schedule must satisfy the energy relaxation \[\sum_{i\in I}q_i e_i(a,b)\le C(b-a).\] Violation for any interval certifies infeasibility, while satisfaction of all such inequalities is only a relaxation and need not produce a feasible nonpreemptive schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every interval, the resource energy unavoidably consumed by activities cannot exceed capacity times interval length.
knowledge_statements.title: Energy Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The energetic necessary condition is mathematically plausible and fits the Energy Relaxations leaf, but no inspectable source is cited for the compulsory-energy formula or its scheduling hypotheses.

children.title: Resource–Energy Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Comparative strength and applicability boundaries for capacity-based and energy-based relaxations.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a base resource relaxation of a global constraint.
\(E\) is obtained from \(R\) by adding valid interval-energy inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_E\subseteq F_R\), with strict inclusion whenever some point in \(F_R\) violates an added energy inequality.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the resource relaxation.
Feasible set after energy inequalities are imposed.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adding valid energy inequalities can only strengthen a relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion comparison between resource-only and resource-plus-energy relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_R\) be the feasible set admitted by a resource relaxation \(R\), and let \(\mathcal E\) be a family of valid energy inequalities. Define \[F_E=F_R\cap\bigcap_{e\in\mathcal E}\{x:e(x)\le 0\}.\] Then \(F_E\subseteq F_R\), so optimization over \(F_E\) gives a bound at least as strong as optimization over \(F_R\) in the same objective direction. The regime is strictly stronger exactly when there exists \(x\in F_R\) and \(e\in\mathcal E\) with \(e(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding valid energy inequalities to a resource relaxation yields a contained feasible region, and is strictly stronger when it cuts off a resource-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource–Energy Strength Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion property is correct and the content kind fits the strength-regime leaf, but the record has no citation supporting the resource-versus-energy terminology or optimization-bound interpretation.

assumptions_latex: Finite-domain literals encode current variable-domain restrictions.
A global propagator can return a conflicting or pruning explanation as a clause over those literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every learned clause is entailed by the global constraint and the encoding, and unit propagation applies its asserted consequence.

notation.meaning: Current conjunction of asserted domain literals.
Explanation literals sufficient for a consequence or conflict.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explanation-producing propagation for one finite-domain global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global propagator explains every pruning or conflict by an entailed clause, which the SAT engine learns and propagates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches the lazy-clause-generation interface and distinguishes propagation from conflict explanations, but its entailment and learning contract requires an authoritative LCG source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: Each finite-domain value test has a Boolean literal \(b_{i,v}\) representing \(x_i=v\).
The selected clauses and pseudo-Boolean constraints encode both variable domains and the global relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is projection-equivalent when \(x\in G\iff\exists b\,\Phi_G(x,b)\).

notation.meaning: Boolean equality indicator for value v of variable i.
SAT or pseudo-Boolean encoding of the global constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-equivalent Boolean and pseudo-Boolean encoding; propagation strength is separate.

source_refs.locator: 4.4 Parsimonious MIP Representation of Disjunctive Sets p. 59

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\), impose \[\sum_{v\in D_i}b_{i,v}=1,\qquad b_{i,v}\in\{0,1\},\] and link \(x_i\) by \(x_i=\sum_{v\in D_i}v b_{i,v}\). A CP-SAT global encoding is a formula \(\Phi_G(b,z)\), possibly using auxiliary Boolean or integer variables \(z\), such that \[x\in G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists(b,z)\;\Phi_G(b,z).\] This projection equivalence preserves feasible assignments; it does not by itself imply that unit propagation matches domain consistency of a dedicated global propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CP-SAT encoding is exact when its satisfying Boolean and auxiliary assignments project precisely to tuples satisfying the global constraint.

assumptions_latex: The global relation is a finite union \(G=\bigcup_{k=1}^K P_k\) of bounded polyhedra.
Valid finite constants are available for an indicator or big-M formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed-integer formulation projects exactly to \(G\) when its selector and linking constraints are valid in both directions.

notation.meaning: Polyhedral alternatives whose union is the global relation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact disjunctive MIP interface for a union of bounded polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k=\{x:A_kx\le b_k\}\) and introduce \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\). The interface \[\sum_{k=1}^K y_k=1,\qquad A_kx\le b_k+M_k(1-y_k)\quad(k=1,\ldots,K)\] is an exact CP–MIP representation of \(G\) when every \(M_k\) is finite and valid for all admissible \(x\), and the displayed inequalities enforce membership in \(P_k\) whenever \(y_k=1\). Consequently, projection onto \(x\) equals \(G\). Relaxing \(y_k\) to \([0,1]\) may be weaker than the convex hull of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary selectors expose a global disjunction to MIP; valid linking constants make the integer formulation exact, though its continuous relaxation may be weak.

assumptions_latex: Variables are partitioned into a master vector \(y\) and CP subproblem vector \(x\).
For fixed \(y\), the CP oracle either returns a feasible \(x\) or a valid cut excluding the current master assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite termination follows when the master domain is finite and every infeasible iteration excludes its current assignment.

notation.meaning: Variables handled by the CP subproblem.
CP constraints parameterized by the master assignment.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a master model over \(y\) with no CP-derived cuts. Repeatedly obtain a master assignment \(\bar y\) and solve the CP subproblem \[\text{find }x\text{ such that }G(x;\bar y).\] If feasible, return \((x,\bar y)\). If infeasible, derive a master-valid cut \(c_{\bar y}(y)\le 0\) that is satisfied by every \(y\) admitting some \(x\) with \(G(x;y)\), but violated by \(\bar y\); add it and continue. If the master becomes infeasible, report infeasibility. With finite master domain and exclusion of each rejected assignment, the procedure terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master proposes assignments; a CP subproblem accepts them or returns valid cuts, terminating finitely when rejected finite-domain assignments are excluded.

children.title: Constraint Selection Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Constraint-specific boundaries governing representation choice, propagation strength, resource reasoning, explanations, and template suitability.
