assumptions_latex: An extensional table lists every allowed tuple explicitly.
The constraint is \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(D_i=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The allowed table contains }n!\text{ tuples and therefore requires }\Omega(n\,n!)\text{ stored value occurrences.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: allowed tuples of AllDifferent are exactly permutations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit allowed-tuple representation of an all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D_i=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a tuple satisfies \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) exactly when it is a permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Hence an allowed-tuple table has \(n!\) rows. Because each row stores \(n\) values, its explicit size is \(n\cdot n!\) value occurrences, excluding indexing overhead. Thus a polynomial-size intensional global constraint can require factorial space under complete extensional enumeration; the failure boundary is reached even though every individual domain has only \(n\) values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit allowed table for n-variable all-different contains every permutation, requiring n! rows and factorial storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Table-Size Explosion

children.title: Automaton State Explosion
children.top_down_role: State-space growth caused by language structure, state products, or expanded sequence context.

assumptions_latex: The alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\).
\(L_n\) contains exactly the words whose \(n\)-th symbol from the right is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every deterministic finite automaton recognizing \(L_n\) has at least \(2^n\) states.

notation.meaning: Language testing the n-th symbol from the right.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Myhill-Nerode distinguishability yields the exponential lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal deterministic automata for a suffix-position language family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), define \[L_n=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*:|w|\ge n\text{ and the }n\text{-th symbol of }w\text{ from the right is }1\}.\] Any deterministic finite automaton recognizing \(L_n\) must distinguish all \(2^n\) binary suffixes of length \(n\), and therefore has at least \(2^n\) states. Consequently, a regular global constraint may have a concise parameterized language description while its deterministic automaton interface requires exponential state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Testing a symbol at a fixed distance from the word end requires a deterministic automaton to remember exponentially many binary suffixes.
knowledge_statements.title: Automaton State Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The suffix-position language is clearly defined and the exponential deterministic-state lower bound fits the failure-boundary leaf, but no formal-automata source with a theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: MDD State Explosion
children.top_down_role: Node-width or layer growth caused by weak merging, variable ordering, or domain structure.

assumptions_latex: Variables are ordered \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\) and are binary.
The relation requires the binary numbers encoded by \(x\) and \(y\) to be equal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every exact ordered MDD has width at least }2^m\text{ after layer }m.\)

notation.meaning: Number of bits in each encoded number.
Equality relation on two binary numbers.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinct x-prefixes induce distinct residual functions on y
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact ordered MDD under a block variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_m\) be the binary relation \[\sum_{i=1}^m2^{m-i}x_i=\sum_{i=1}^m2^{m-i}y_i\] under ordering \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\). After the first \(m\) decisions, each of the \(2^m\) assignments to \(x\) requires a different residual condition on \(y\), namely equality to its encoded value. Thus no two such prefixes can share an exact MDD node, so layer \(m\) has width at least \(2^m\). Variable ordering can therefore turn a compact relation into an exponentially wide exact MDD.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With all x bits before all y bits, an equality relation needs a distinct MDD state for every x value, giving exponential width.
knowledge_statements.title: MDD State Explosion

children.title: Automaton–MDD Scaling Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation-dependent size, sharing, and propagation boundaries between automata and MDDs.

assumptions_latex: A sequence relation has both an exact deterministic automaton \(A\) and an exact ordered MDD \(M\) for a fixed horizon.
Propagation scans each representation once using adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The propagation costs are compared through }T(|Q_A|+|E_A|)\text{ and }|V_M|+|E_M|\text{, and neither representation uniformly dominates.}\)

notation.meaning: State and transition sets of the deterministic automaton.
Node and arc sets of the layered MDD.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graph-scan propagation is linear in the represented graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size comparison for exact finite-horizon sequence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a horizon \(T\), unrolling an automaton \(A\) yields at most \((T+1)|Q_A|\) layered state copies and at most \(T|E_A|\) transition copies. An exact MDD \(M\) instead stores \(|V_M|\) layered nodes and \(|E_M|\) arcs, potentially merging horizon-specific equivalent prefixes that an unrolled automaton keeps distinct. A reachability-based propagation pass costs \(O(T(|Q_A|+|E_A|))\) on the unrolled automaton and \(O(|V_M|+|E_M|)\) on the MDD. Either quantity can be smaller; exponential lower bounds can occur for either representation under an unfavorable language or ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automaton and MDD propagation scale with their graph sizes; horizon-specific merging may favor an MDD, while compact transition structure may favor an automaton.
knowledge_statements.title: Automaton–MDD Scaling Tradeoffs

assumptions_latex: A graph-based propagator explicitly materializes one vertex per variable and value and one edge for each admissible variable-value pair.
Each of \(n\) variables has the same domain of size \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The explicit incidence graph has }n+d\text{ vertices and }nd\text{ edges, requiring }\Theta(n+d+nd)\text{ storage.}\)

notation.meaning: Number of values in the common domain.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct counting in a complete bipartite incidence graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit bipartite variable-value graph for dense domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\) represent variables and let \(V\) contain the \(d\) domain values. If every variable admits every value, then the incidence graph is complete bipartite: \[E=U\times V,\qquad |U\cup V|=n+d,\qquad |E|=nd.\] Any explicit adjacency-list representation therefore uses \(\Theta(n+d+nd)\) space, and a full edge scan costs \(\Theta(nd)\) time. This overhead can dominate a compact intensional constraint whose input consists only of the \(n\) identical domain bounds and a constraint identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense variable-value graph contains nd edges, so explicitly materializing it can dominate the compact global-constraint input.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Representation Overhead

assumptions_latex: Every pairwise conjunction \(x_i\land x_j\) is materialized by a distinct auxiliary variable \(y_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The extension introduces }\binom{n}{2}\text{ variables and }3\binom{n}{2}\text{ linear linking inequalities.}\)

notation.meaning: Auxiliary variable representing a pairwise conjunction.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct counting of pairwise auxiliaries and exact binary-product inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic overmodeling caused by materializing all binary pairwise conjunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(1\le i<j\le n\), introduce \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) and encode \(y_{ij}=x_i\land x_j\) by \[y_{ij}\le x_i,\qquad y_{ij}\le x_j,\qquad y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1.\] This construction adds exactly \(\binom{n}{2}\) auxiliary variables and \(3\binom{n}{2}\) linking inequalities before any constraint using the conjunctions is imposed. Thus a model with \(O(n)\) original variables acquires \(\Theta(n^2)\) representation size. When most pairwise conjunctions are not required by propagation or the objective, this is an auxiliary-variable overmodeling boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Materializing every pairwise conjunction of n binary variables creates quadratically many auxiliaries and linking inequalities, even when most are unused.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Overmodeling
Weak Primitive Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes propagation loss from independently filtering a logically equivalent primitive decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak primitive decomposition occurs when there are \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(a\in D_i\) such that, for every primitive \(C_j\) whose scope contains \(x_i\), there is an assignment \(y^j\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) with \(y^j_i=a\) that satisfies \(C_j\), but no assignment \(y\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) with \(y_i=a\) satisfies every primitive: \[\forall j\ (x_i\in\operatorname{scope}(C_j)\Rightarrow \exists y^j:\ y^j_i=a\land y^j\models C_j),\qquad \nexists y:\ y_i=a\land\bigwedge_{j=1}^m y\models C_j.\] Independent generalized-arc-consistency filtering therefore retains \(a\) in every primitive containing \(x_i\), whereas generalized arc consistency on the conjunction deletes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primitive decomposition is propagation-weaker when each component separately supports a value but no complete assignment satisfying all components supports it.
assumptions_latex: Variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite current domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
Primitive constraints \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) have scopes drawn from these variables, and their conjunction represents the global constraint.
Each primitive is filtered independently to generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The independently filtered decomposition is strictly weaker on the stated domain state.

notation.meaning: complete assignment witnessing support in primitive j

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Complete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional complexity boundary for complete domain filtering of succinctly represented global constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a global-constraint family whose designated-value support problem is NP-complete, a generalized-arc-consistency filter must determine for each \(i\) and \(a\in D_i\) whether \[\exists t\in R\cap(D_1\times\cdots\times D_n):\ t_i=a.\] If such complete filtering ran in time polynomial in the instance encoding length \(N\), a designated support query could be answered by running the filter and testing whether \(a\) remains. Therefore, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time generalized-arc-consistency filtering algorithm exists for that family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When designated-value support is NP-complete, complete generalized-arc-consistency filtering cannot run in polynomial time unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: Instances of a fixed global-constraint family have succinct encodings of length \(N\).
Deciding whether a designated value \(a\in D_i\) has a support is NP-complete for that family.
Filtering must establish generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the family has no polynomial-time complete generalized-arc-consistency filter.

notation.meaning: relation represented by the global-constraint instance
polynomial-time and nondeterministic polynomial-time complexity classes

knowledge_statements.title: Nonincremental Recomputation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-level cost boundary for propagators that discard reusable state after each domain event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a branch contains \(q\) successive domain transitions and the nonincremental propagator performs a full recomputation after every transition. If each recomputation costs at least \(T(N)\) on instances of encoding size \(N\), then the total propagation work is at least \[\sum_{k=1}^{q}T(N)=qT(N)=\Omega(qT(N)).\] This bound applies even when each transition deletes only one value and an incremental implementation could update less information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recomputing from scratch after each of q domain changes incurs at least q times the full-recomputation cost.
assumptions_latex: A search branch produces \(q\) successive domain transitions.
The instance encoding size remains \(N\) throughout the branch.
After each transition, a nonincremental propagator performs a full computation costing at least \(T(N)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The branch incurs \(\Omega(qT(N))\) propagation work.

notation.meaning: lower bound on one full recomputation at size N

assumptions_latex: Two sound propagators \(P\) and \(Q\) operate on redundant views of the same domain state.
Their closure operators coincide on every reachable state: \(P(D)=Q(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scheduling both propagators adds no pruning but pays both execution and synchronization costs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where redundant views duplicate propagation without strengthening the common fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P(D)=Q(D)\) for every reachable \(D\), then applying both yields \[Q(P(D))=P(D)=Q(D).\] Thus the second propagator performs no additional deletion. A propagation round costs at least \(c_P(D)+c_Q(P(D))\), plus any channel-maintenance cost, while either propagator alone reaches the same state. Redundant-view contention occurs when this duplicated work and event traffic exceed any benefit from different implementations or wake-up schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent propagators on redundant views can reach the same fixpoint while duplicating execution, events, and synchronization.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-View Contention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Given that P and Q are closure operators and coincide on all reachable states, the no-additional-pruning conclusion is mathematically consistent. No inspectable source supports the redundant-view cost and contention characterization.

assumptions_latex: Nonpreemptive tasks use one unit-capacity renewable resource over the integer horizon \([0,5)\).
Three tasks have processing time \(2\) and start domains \(S_i=\{0,1,2,3\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compulsory-part filtering is silent although the instance is infeasible.

notation.meaning: earliest completion time of task i
latest start time of task i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete cumulative-scheduling failure of compulsory-part timetable reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every task, \(\operatorname{ect}_i=2\) and \(\operatorname{lst}_i=3\), so its compulsory part \(K_i=[\operatorname{lst}_i,\operatorname{ect}_i)\) is empty. A compulsory-part timetable therefore has load zero everywhere and derives no contradiction. Nevertheless, the tasks require total processing energy \(3\cdot2=6\), whereas the unit-capacity horizon supplies only \(5\). Consequently no feasible nonoverlapping schedule exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three length-two tasks cannot fit in five slots, yet all compulsory parts are empty and timetable propagation detects nothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Compulsory-Part Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally correct: all compulsory parts are empty while six units of processing cannot fit in a unit-capacity horizon of length five. A scheduling source with a specific locator is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Activity Dilution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by reasoning separately about optional activities and an aggregate presence requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the cardinality constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^{4}z_i\ge3\), each individual value \(z_i=0\) has a cardinality support obtained by setting the other three presence variables to \(1\), and each value \(z_i=1\) also has a support. Thus cardinality propagation alone need not fix any task present. An optional timetable that includes only tasks with presence fixed to \(1\) then sees no compulsory load. Nevertheless, any feasible presence assignment must select at least three tasks, requiring processing energy at least \(3\cdot2=6\), while the unit-capacity horizon supplies only \(5\). The conjunction is therefore infeasible although the two weak propagators can each remain silent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four optional length-two tasks with at least three required are jointly infeasible in five slots, although neither the cardinality constraint nor a timetable using only fixed-present tasks need detect this alone.
assumptions_latex: Four optional nonpreemptive tasks have duration \(2\), unit demand, and start domains \(S_i=\{0,1,2,3\}\) on a unit-capacity horizon \([0,5)\).
Binary presence variables satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^{4}z_i\ge3\).
The optional timetable counts only activities whose presence variable is fixed to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate cardinality and optional-timetable propagation can reach a nonfailing state although their conjunction is infeasible.

notation.meaning: binary presence indicator of task i

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Resource Reasoning Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of propagating a multi-resource scheduling model independently by resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independent resource-wise generalized-arc-consistency propagation is incomplete on a domain state when every current value has a support for every resource separately, \[\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\ \forall i\ \forall a\in D_i\ \exists s\in F_k:\ s_i=a,\] but the joint feasible set is empty, \[\bigcap_{k=1}^{r}F_k=\varnothing.\] Each resource propagator then retains every current value, while no common start vector satisfies all resources. Detecting the contradiction requires reasoning across resource-specific alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent resource propagators can retain every value because it has support on each resource separately even though no start vector satisfies all resources together.
assumptions_latex: The common start vector lies in \(D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\).
For each resource \(k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), the set \(F_k\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) contains the start vectors feasible for that resource.
Each resource constraint is propagated independently to generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resource-wise generalized arc consistency can reach a nonfailing fixpoint while the joint multi-resource model is infeasible.

notation.meaning: current domain of start variable i
start vectors feasible for resource k

children.title: Setup Fragmentation
children.top_down_role: Reasoning loss caused by sequence-dependent setup intervals, transition diversity, or setup placement.

assumptions_latex: Three nonpreemptive tasks of duration \(1\) must execute on one unit-capacity resource within \([0,5)\).
Every transition between distinct consecutive tasks requires a nonpreemptive setup of duration \(2\) on that resource.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A setup-oblivious energy test accepts the instance, but every complete sequence is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss from ignoring setup time in aggregate scheduling reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Processing alone consumes \(3\) units, so the setup-oblivious condition \(3\le5\) holds. Every permutation of the three tasks, however, contains two transitions. Since each transition consumes \(2\) resource-time units, every complete sequence has length at least \[3+2+2=7>5.\] Thus setup fragmentation makes the instance infeasible even though processing-energy and compulsory-part reasoning that omits setups can report no overload.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processing fits the horizon, but the setups forced between tasks make every complete sequence too long.
knowledge_statements.title: Setup Fragmentation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical counterexample is correct under the stated setup convention and fits the Setup Fragmentation leaf. No inspectable scheduling source is cited.

children.title: Calendar Fragmentation
children.top_down_role: Reasoning loss caused by discontinuous availability, shutdown periods, or variable capacity calendars.

assumptions_latex: A nonpreemptive task has duration \(3\) and requires one unit of a unit-capacity resource.
The resource is available only on \([0,2)\cup[3,5)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregate available capacity is sufficient, but the task has no feasible placement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of aggregate-capacity reasoning under a fragmented availability calendar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The total available resource-time is \(|A|=4\), which exceeds the task energy \(p=3\). Nevertheless, nonpreemptive execution requires some start \(s\) satisfying \([s,s+3)\subseteq A\). Each connected component of \(A=[0,2)\cup[3,5)\) has length \(2\), so no such \(s\) exists. An aggregate energy test that replaces the calendar by its total availability therefore accepts an infeasible instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four available time units are insufficient for one nonpreemptive length-three task when availability is split into two length-two windows.
knowledge_statements.title: Calendar Fragmentation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calendar-fragmentation counterexample is mathematically correct and matches the leaf: total capacity is four, but neither availability component can contain a nonpreemptive length-three task. No source is supplied.

children.title: Combined Fragmentation Effects
children.top_down_role: Scheduling regimes where setup structure and calendar discontinuities jointly weaken propagation.

assumptions_latex: Two nonpreemptive unit-duration tasks and their intervening unit-duration setup require the same unit-capacity resource.
The resource is available only on \([0,2)\cup[3,5)\), and the setup must be contiguous with its adjacent tasks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Setup and calendar constraints are individually plausible but jointly infeasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined fragmentation under a setup-contiguity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ignoring the calendar, the task-setup-task block has length \(|B|=1+1+1=3\le5\). Ignoring the setup, the two unit tasks can be placed in the available windows. Joint feasibility, however, requires a contiguous interval \(B\subseteq A=[0,2)\cup[3,5)\) of length \(3\). Since every connected component of \(A\) has length \(2\), no such block exists. Separate setup and calendar checks can therefore miss the combined contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tasks fit the calendar without setup, and the setup fits the horizon without closures, but their required contiguous block cannot fit.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined Fragmentation Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct if the task-setup-task sequence must form one contiguous block, but that modeling convention is material and requires an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Coarse Global Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-strength loss caused by explaining a global deduction with unnecessary antecedents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The coarse explanation produces \(C_A=\bigvee_{a\in A}\neg a\vee\ell\), while the smaller valid reason produces \(C_M=\bigvee_{a\in M}\neg a\vee\ell\). If \(M\subsetneq A\), then \(C_M\models C_A\), while the converse need not hold. Thus the coarse explanation yields a logically weaker learned clause and may propagate later or contribute less effectively to conflict analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding unnecessary antecedents to a valid explanation produces a weaker learned clause that may propagate less effectively.
assumptions_latex: A deduction literal \(\ell\) is implied by a set \(A\) of currently true antecedent literals.
A proper subset \(M\subsetneq A\) is also a valid reason, so \(M\models\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clause learned from \(A\) is logically weaker than the clause learned from \(M\).

notation.meaning: clauses generated from the two reasons

assumptions_latex: A propagator may return any valid reason \(A\) satisfying \(A\models\ell\) for the same deduction \(\ell\).
Conflict processing cost is at least linear in the number of literals in the returned reason.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbounded reason size or variation destroys any uniform small-reason cost guarantee.

notation.meaning: antecedent set returned as a reason
number of literals in a reason

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backend boundary created by explanations whose size or identity lacks a stable bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of equivalent deduction states, let the propagator return valid reasons \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) with \(A_t\models\ell\). Reasons are large when \(\sup_t|A_t|\) grows with the entire constraint scope, forcing \(\Omega(|A_t|)\) processing per explanation. They are unstable when equivalent states can produce many distinct incomparable sets, so neither \(A_s\subseteq A_t\) nor \(A_t\subseteq A_s\) generally holds. Then clause size, reuse, and conflict-analysis behavior lack a state-independent small bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reasons that grow with the whole scope or vary among incomparable antecedent sets impose unpredictable clause-processing and reuse costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Large or Unstable Reasons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear cost consequence for large reasons follows from the stated assumption, but the proposed notion of unstable reasons and its claimed effects on reuse and conflict analysis are source-dependent and lack a precise stability metric.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\) is a finite-domain search space.
\(G\) and a decomposition \(D=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Sol}(G)=\operatorname{Sol}(D)\).
The explanation backend accepts only reasons from a language \(\mathcal L_D\) generated by literals exposed by the components \(C_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) has a backend decomposition mismatch at domain state \(Q\) when the global propagator produces a sound pruning \(\ell\in P_G(Q)\) but no backend-admissible reason can justify it: \[\nexists E\subseteq\mathcal L_D:\quad Q\models E,\qquad D\land E\models\ell.\] Equivalently, semantic preservation of complete solutions does not preserve explanation-supported propagation. The mismatch boundary is crossed whenever \(P_G(Q)\not\subseteq P_D^{\mathcal L_D}(Q)\), where \(P_D^{\mathcal L_D}\) denotes deductions having reasons expressible and checkable by the backend.

notation.meaning: Solutions satisfying a constraint or constraint family.
Deductions produced at domain state Q.
Backend-supported explanation language for the decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain decomposition with an explanation language restricted to component-level literals.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a global constraint and \(D\) a solution-equivalent decomposition. Relative to an explanation backend whose admissible reasons form \(\mathcal L_D\), backend compatibility requires every pruning made by \(G\) to possess a sound reason expressible through the decomposition. A backend decomposition mismatch occurs at a domain state \(Q\) if \(G\) derives some literal \(\ell\), yet no reason over \(\mathcal L_D\) both holds at \(Q\) and entails \(\ell\) with \(D\). Thus solution equivalence alone is insufficient for explanation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution-equivalent decomposition is mismatched when the global propagator makes a sound deduction that the backend cannot justify using component-level reasons.
knowledge_statements.title: Backend Decomposition Mismatch

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and restricted-reason formulation fit the node, but the cited MINLP decomposition chapter does not support claims about global-constraint propagators, explanation languages, or backend-checkable reasons. A constraint-programming or lazy-clause-generation source is required.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq X\) is the feasible set of a global constraint over a finite-domain space \(X\).
\(R\supseteq S\) is a relaxation used for bounding, while \(P_S\) and \(P_R\) are sound domain-pruning operators.
Domain states are ordered by componentwise inclusion, with smaller states representing stronger pruning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A relaxation-propagation mismatch occurs at a domain state \(Q\) when relaxation feasibility or optimization yields no corresponding propagation strength, namely \[P_S(Q)\subsetneq P_R(Q),\] where each operator returns the surviving domain state. More generally, two candidate relaxations \(R_1,R_2\) are mismatched with propagation when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) but there exists \(Q\) such that \(P_{R_1}(Q)\not\subseteq P_{R_2}(Q)\). Hence relaxation dominance does not, without a compatible inference procedure and representation, imply propagation dominance.

notation.meaning: Exact feasible set and its relaxation.
Surviving domain state after propagation based on a set or relaxation.
Current Cartesian product of variable domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares relaxation strength with domain-pruning strength under a fixed representation.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Continuous Relaxation and Lagrangian Relaxation p. 24
5.4 Duality results and convex relaxation p. 60
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the exact feasible set and \(R\supseteq S\) a relaxation. Although a tighter relaxation can improve bounds, propagation also depends on the inference algorithm and exposed variables. A relaxation-propagation mismatch is present when the relaxation ordering fails to induce the expected ordering of surviving domain states. In particular, failure occurs if exact propagation gives \(P_S(Q)\subsetneq P_R(Q)\), or if \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) while \(P_{R_1}(Q)\not\subseteq P_{R_2}(Q)\) for some state \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation is propagation-mismatched when its apparent set or bound strength does not translate into correspondingly stronger domain pruning.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Propagation Mismatch

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Continuous Relaxation and Lagrangian Relaxation p. 24
5.4 Duality results and convex relaxation p. 60
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited relaxation sources address optimization relaxations, not the asserted ordering of finite-domain propagation operators. Moreover, strict separation between exact and relaxed propagation is ordinarily expected, whereas failure of propagation monotonicity under tighter relaxations is a different phenomenon. A specialized source is needed to determine the intended boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq X\) is the intended relation on the modeled variables.
Each candidate template \(G\) has a solution relation \(S_G\), propagation operator \(P_G\), and nonnegative implementation cost \(c_G\).
Candidate templates are compared on a specified family \(\mathcal Q\) of reachable domain states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The choice of \(G\) is misaligned if either \(S_G\ne R\), or there exists a semantically exact template \(H\) such that \[S_H=R,\qquad P_H(Q)\subseteq P_G(Q)\ \text{for every }Q\in\mathcal Q,\qquad c_H\le c_G,\] with at least one strict inequality. Here smaller propagated states mean stronger pruning. The first case is semantic misalignment; the second is operational domination. The boundary therefore depends on the intended relation, reachable states, and declared cost criterion rather than on the template name alone.

notation.meaning: Intended relation and relation represented by template G.
Surviving state after propagating template G at Q.
Declared implementation cost of template G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and operational boundary for selecting among alternative global-constraint templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an intended relation \(R\), a selected global constraint \(G\) must first satisfy \(S_G=R\). Among semantically exact candidates, selection is misaligned when another template \(H\) is no more costly and leaves no larger propagated domain at every reachable state, with strict improvement somewhere. Formally, misalignment holds if \(S_G\ne R\), or if such an \(H\) dominates \(G\) on the declared state family \(\mathcal Q\) and cost measure \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global constraint is misaligned when it models the wrong relation or is dominated in pruning and implementation cost by an exact alternative.
knowledge_statements.title: Misaligned Global-Constraint Choice

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but defining template misalignment through joint propagation-and-cost Pareto domination is a substantive, context-dependent criterion with no cited support. A source must establish the relevant selection criterion and cost model.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\) are primary variables and \(y\in Y\) are auxiliary view variables intended to satisfy \(y=\phi(x)\).
\(C_x\) and \(C_y\) are constraints expressed in the two views.
A channel is a constraint family \(K\subseteq X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The views are correctly channeled when \[K=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y=\phi(x)\}.\] A missing channeling view occurs when the posted model \(M=C_x\land C_y\land K'\) uses \(K'\ne K\). If \(K'\supsetneq K\), then some feasible pair has inconsistent views; if \(K'\subsetneq K\), then some consistent pair is incorrectly excluded. Even when complete solutions are repaired elsewhere, propagation communication is missing whenever a deduction in one view has no sound image in the other under \(K'\).

notation.meaning: Primary variables and auxiliary view variables.
Intended view map from primary to auxiliary values.
Exact channel relation between the views.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact functional channeling between primary variables and auxiliary global-constraint views.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an auxiliary view \(y\) is intended to represent \(\phi(x)\). Exact channeling posts the graph relation \(K=\{(x,y):y=\phi(x)\}\). A channeling view is missing or incomplete when the posted relation \(K'\) differs from \(K\): a strict superset admits inconsistent pairs, while a strict subset removes consistent pairs. At the propagation level, a missing channel also occurs when a sound deduction expressed in one view cannot be transferred into its sound counterpart in the other view.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A channeling view is missing when auxiliary variables are not constrained to represent exactly their intended functions of the primary variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Channeling Views

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Exact graph channeling is mathematically clear, but the record treats every relation unequal to the exact channel—including an overly restrictive channel—as a missing view. It also invokes transfer of deductions without defining the correspondence between literals. Specialized channeling evidence is needed to fix the intended boundary.

children.title: Overconstrained Templates
children.top_down_role: Templates whose combined restrictions exclude intended solutions or encode unintended commitments.

assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq X\) is the intended feasible relation.
\(T\subseteq X\) is the relation imposed by the instantiated template.
All side constraints relevant to the intended template semantics are included in \(R\) and \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The template is overconstrained exactly when \[T\subsetneq R.\] Equivalently, it is sound with respect to the intended relation, since every accepted assignment is intended, but it is incomplete because there exists a witness \(x^
atural\in R\setminus T\). Such a witness certifies that the template forbids at least one intended assignment. If \(T\not\subseteq R\) also holds, the error is not purely overconstraint; it additionally contains an underconstrained component.

notation.meaning: Relation imposed by the instantiated template.
An intended assignment rejected by the template.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic boundary for templates that reject intended feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the intended feasible relation and \(T\) the relation enforced by a template. The template is overconstrained precisely when \(T\subsetneq R\). Thus every assignment admitted by the template is intended, but at least one intended assignment is rejected. Any \(x^\natural\in R\setminus T\) is a finite, directly checkable witness of overconstraint. When \(T\) also contains assignments outside \(R\), the mismatch has both overconstrained and underconstrained components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A template is overconstrained when its feasible assignments form a strict subset of the intended relation; a rejected intended assignment is a witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Overconstrained Templates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-theoretic characterization and failure-boundary kind are precise, but the cited hard-versus-soft-constraints section does not directly support overconstrained global-constraint templates or the stated witness characterization.

children.title: Underconstrained Templates
children.top_down_role: Templates lacking restrictions needed to exclude invalid, incomplete, or semantically unintended solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Underconstrained Templates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic boundary for templates that admit unintended assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the intended feasible relation and \(T\) the relation enforced by a template. The template is underconstrained precisely when \(R\subsetneq T\). Hence every intended assignment is admitted, but at least one unintended assignment is also admitted. Any \(x^\flat\in T\setminus R\) is a finite, directly checkable witness of underconstraint. When the template also rejects assignments in \(R\), the mismatch has both underconstrained and overconstrained components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A template is underconstrained when it strictly contains the intended relation; an admitted unintended assignment is a witness.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq X\) is the intended feasible relation.
\(T\subseteq X\) is the relation imposed by the instantiated template.
All side constraints relevant to the intended template semantics are included in \(R\) and \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The template is underconstrained exactly when \[R\subsetneq T.\] Equivalently, it is complete with respect to the intended relation because it admits every intended assignment, but it is unsound because there exists a witness \[x^\flat\in T\setminus R.\] If the template also rejects an intended assignment, then the error additionally has an overconstrained component.

notation.meaning: Relation imposed by the instantiated template.
An unintended assignment admitted by the template.

children.title: Constraint-Balance Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between excessive restriction, adequate modeling coverage, and insufficient restriction.

assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq X\) is the intended feasible relation.
\(T\subseteq X\) is the relation imposed by the selected template and its channeling constraints.
Template correctness is judged by equality of complete assignments in the common ambient space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact constraint balance holds if and only if \[T=R.\] The constraint-balance failure boundary is therefore \(T\triangle R\ne\varnothing\), where \[T\triangle R=(T\setminus R)\cup(R\setminus T).\] Points in \(T\setminus R\) witness underconstraint, and points in \(R\setminus T\) witness overconstraint. If both sets are nonempty, neither relation contains the other and the template has a two-sided semantic mismatch. Propagation strength may still differ when \(T=R\); that operational issue lies outside this semantic boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic equality boundary separating exact, overconstrained, underconstrained, and two-sided templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) denote the intended relation and \(T\) the relation imposed by a complete template instantiation. The template is semantically balanced exactly when \(T=R\). Failure begins when their symmetric difference is nonempty. An assignment in \(T\setminus R\) witnesses underconstraint, while one in \(R\setminus T\) witnesses overconstraint. Nonempty differences in both directions constitute a two-sided mismatch. This boundary concerns complete-solution semantics and does not assert equality of propagation algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint balance holds exactly when template and intended relations coincide; either side of their symmetric difference supplies a failure witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Balance Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric-difference boundary is internally correct and clearly excludes propagation equivalence, but the hard-versus-soft-constraints citation does not directly support this taxonomy of global-template balance failures.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the assignment space and \(v:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is the intended violation cost.
The intended optimization problem minimizes \(f(x)+v(x)\), with \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
A hard encoding admits only \(H\subseteq X\); a soft encoding retains assignments having finite violation cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
A soft requirement is incorrectly hardened when there exists \(x
otin H\) with \(v(x)<+\infty\); the hard model deletes an assignment that the intended model merely penalizes. A hard requirement is incorrectly softened when there exists \(x
otin H\) assigned finite penalty by the soft model; then sufficiently favorable \(f(x)\) may make an intendedly forbidden assignment optimal. Exact alignment is obtained by representing hard violation with \(v(x)=+\infty\) and soft violation with its intended finite penalty.

notation.meaning: Assignments admitted by the hard requirement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value formulation distinguishing forbidden assignments from finitely penalized violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a requirement by a violation cost \(v:X\to[0,+\infty]\). A hard requirement assigns \(v(x)=+\infty\) to every forbidden assignment, whereas a soft requirement assigns a finite cost to each permitted violation. A soft-hard boundary mismatch occurs when a finitely penalized assignment is deleted by a hard template, or when an intendedly forbidden assignment receives finite cost in a soft template. In the latter case, the base objective can outweigh the penalty and select an assignment that should be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mismatch occurs when a finite-cost violation is forbidden outright, or when a truly forbidden assignment receives only a finite penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Soft–Hard Boundary Mismatch
